(P3a Heading) {The Dispelling of Objections Regarding Non-existence}.

Homage to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti! In this work composed for the delight of the learned by Śaṅkara—the jewel of wisdom remaining on the serpent’s body whose heart blossomed at the sight of the lotus-feet of the lordly sacrificer Rāmasvāmī—having established that the term "Nārāyaṇa" is proven by the multitude of all Purāṇas and Śāstras, [the author] sets aside those who hold [other] interpretations...

I, Śeṣaśāstrin, the son of the learned Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa, [compose] this *Śrī-tattvamālā-maha*, which consists of the sacrificial lore flowing from the lotus-mouths of the preceptors headed by Rāmasvāmin and Makhiṃdra; which is like the celestial river being tasted by the mountain Śeṣādri, whose head bows at the feet of the gods; and which, like a lion with its claws, performs the act of prostration (*ṇatva*) before the one named Śrī Nārāyaṇa—[who, like a lion, acts] upon the heap of dūrvā grass [of ignorance] and the breaking of the elephant’s frontal globes [of doubt], and who moves within the enclosure of the [Vedic] syllables. *Śrī-tattvamālā-maha* By Śeṣaśāstrin, son of the scholar Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa.
This is composed for the purification of my own words and for the delight of the learned.

Having bowed to the glorious moon-crested Lord, the life-giver of the Daughter of the Mountain, the ocean of compassion, and to the Goddess of Speech who bestows the playful eloquence upon those who prostrate;
and having cleansed my own intellect— which warbles with the impurity of praise— by means of this *Tattvamālā*, [I shall compose it].
Instantly producing the cleansing of the affliction of the loss of the *ṇatva* [substitution] by means of the waters of this commentary;

Having bowed to the one who has bestowed auspiciousness upon me, I compose this primary commentary titled *Vidhūnanā*, which is adorned with the word "Nārāyaṇa" and shines with the essence of reality. May the virtuous, casting aside envy, examine this work of mine with favor;
for if a fault is to be sought, it is easy to find everywhere even in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works.
If that bold assertion were to be censured by the great ones in the principal treatises such as the *Bhāṣya*,
then this work of mine too should rightly be treated with compassion, as merely the talk of a child.

Indeed, here, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to undertake, [the author] composes [this verse]: "He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine so for the Guru—for such a great soul, these truths that have been told become manifest... Through a multitude of scriptural passages such as "A person who has a teacher knows," it is established that devotion to the Guru is the consecrated foundation for the entire succession of welfare and the supreme human goal.

Because it establishes that the work under discussion—which bears the responsibility of sustaining the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, which is the primary cause of the highest good (niḥśreyasa)—bestows the knowledge of the essential nature of Supreme Śiva, [it is praised] by such scriptural passages as: "The gods generated divine speech;

animals of all forms speak it; yielding for us low-toned refreshment and vigor, may that cow Speech come to us well-praised," and so forth, wherein the word *ūrj*—derived from the verbal root *ūrj* meaning "strength" and "vital breath"—is employed.

By means of the majesty of the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevī*), he demonstrates her status as the knower of the cause for attaining all human goals and as the bestower of the power of the sun; thus, for the sake of maintaining the tradition of the learned, he composes at the beginning of his work a benediction consisting of salutations to his Guru and the Goddess of Speech, and declares his intended undertaking: "Having bowed to the lotus-feet of my Guru and also to the Goddess of Speech, for the pleasure of Sadāśiva, I compose this garland of devotion adorned with the word 'Nārāyaṇa'. The phrase "adorned with the word 'Nārāyaṇa'" refers to Nārāyaṇa...

Because the word *ṇa* illuminates the splendor consisting of the attainment of the supreme union with Paramaśiva, it possesses a state of being an ornament (*bhūṣaṇabhāva*). By means of that [ornament], the "garland of principles" (*tatvamālikā*) shines and blazes. Regarding this, the term "principles" (*tattva*) refers to the number thirty-six—the principles well-known in the Śaiva Āgamas beginning with Śakti and ending with Pradhāna; thus, by the word *tattva*, the number thirty-six is expressed. It does not refer to the Sāṃkhya enumeration accepted by astronomers, as seen in verses from the *Sūryasiddhānta* and other texts such as: "The principles, horses, oceans, and the moon... and so forth.

The number twenty-five is stated as being based on the *tattvas* (principles). This is because, since this present work is devoted to the majesty of Paramaśiva, the enumeration taught in the Śaiva Āgamas is what is most relevant here. Thus, the syntactical connection is as follows: "I compose this garland of thirty-six verses, which constitutes the present work, for the pleasure of Sadāśiva. In this context, there exists a relationship between the object of adornment—well-known in the world and obtainable through the metaphorical expression of the word *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament)—and the standard of comparison consisting of ornaments such as a priceless red garland (*anargharaktamālā*), which serves to sustain that relationship.

By stating that the *Tattvamālā*, the work under discussion, is illuminated by being adorned with the word "Nārāyaṇa," there is established a specific distinction consisting of its own beauty being sustained by the object in the form of the venerable word "Nārāyaṇa. This constitutes the figure of speech *Vyatireka* (Distinction), which is intermingled with *Rūpaka* (Metaphor). For it is said: "When the coloring of the subject [the upameya] toward the likeness of the object [the upamāna] occurs due to a difference between them, that is *Rūpaka*; however, when there is a distinction between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, it is *Vyatireka*."

Furthermore, because this treatise possesses the characteristic [of establishing] the attainment of a most exalted yoga pertaining to the term *Nārāyaṇa*—which refers to Paramaśiva—by means of effecting the substitution of the letter *ṇa*, it serves as an ornament to the word *Nārāyaṇa* precisely by manifesting such splendor; it does not do so merely by producing some other kind of beauty. This point is established by the fact that the splendor consisting in the attainment of a most exalted yoga pertaining to Paramaśiva, which belongs to the word *Nārāyaṇa*, is proven through the statements of the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, and others to be in accord with the consensus of the venerable Vyāsacaraṇa and others. Such is the truth.

This is suggested by the statement that the present work, titled *Lākṣya*, shines with the ornamentation of the word "Nārāyaṇa. Here, a contradiction appears regarding the fact that the *Tattvamālā*—which is an ornament for the feet of Govinda, the referent of the word "Nārāyaṇa" from head to foot—is intended for the pleasure of Sadāśiva. That contradiction is rendered apparent by taking the word "Nārāyaṇa" to mean the term "Nārāyaṇa" itself; thus, there is also a combination of the figure of speech known as *Virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction), since its definition states: "When a contradiction is apparent [rather than real], it is called *Virodhābhāsa*. This subject matter of the work is further specified in five [verses].

He demonstrates this through verses: "I do not exert myself in elucidating the supreme nature of Śiva, for that has been established without obstruction by learned men such as Dīkṣita Haradatta and others, whose fame extends to the very ends of the earth. Rather, when the mantra 'tama āsīt' (there was darkness) determined—by the illustrious Dīkṣitas, by Nāpāyaṇa, and even by those who composed the Purāṇas through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—that the purport of all creation-texts lies in Śiva accompanied by Ambā (*Sāmbaśiva*), some fools prattle that this was stated by the eminent Dīkṣitas merely because it does not contradict [their own views]."

"That is false" thus it flashes forth. Now, regarding the views of Śivāditya, the author of the *Dīpikā*, and others—if [the name] "Nārāyaṇa" is etymological (*yaugika*) even when preceded by "Cūḍa," yet the impossibility of the suffix *ṇatva* persists, we shall speak according to our understanding. "The Dīkṣita" means the venerable Appayadīkṣita. Regarding "vāṅmukha," Amara states that "vāṅmukha" means an introduction (*upanyāsa*). In the phrase "entire creation" (*samastasṛṣṭi*), the mention of "creation" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for maintenance and dissolution as well. "Etymological" (*yaugika*) refers to what is to be established within the respective contexts of the Purāṇic statements.

The sense is this: if someone should think that the conventional usage of the term *nārāyaṇa* found in the Purāṇas could possibly apply to Śiva—since such texts, being intent on praising their own deities, lack the power to establish the primary meaning of a word, much like a lexicon (kośa)—[the author replies: O Glorious One! That which is the cause of the supreme human goals, characterized by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), and the agency in the creation and so forth of the universe—all that resides in You alone, O Lord of the Mountain, as established by the garland of Śruti scriptures. Therefore, Your pair of feet alone is our supreme refuge. This is the meaning: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow; having known Him thus... [and so on].

"He goes to death; there is no other path for the journey," and so forth—by such scriptural passages, it is understood that liberation, which constitutes the supreme human goal, is obtained through the knowledge of Brahman alone, and not by any other means. Furthermore, regarding that Brahman, its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) has been stated in scriptures such as, "From which indeed these beings are born," namely, its being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe. And that characteristic is expressed thus: "When there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed; that is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent [quality] of Savitṛ, and from Him the ancient creation issued forth."

By means of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* mantra, the eminent Dīkṣitas have established in works such as the *Śivādityadīpikā*, the *Śivatattvaviveka*, and the *Śivakarṇāmṛta* that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of all passages concerning creation and so forth refers exclusively to Paramaśiva, and not to any other; this is understood. Here too, we shall briefly describe the manner of that establishment. In the mantra "When darkness was," the first half states: "Darkness alone existed here at first, impelled by that [which is beyond], it moves toward differentiation."

"Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning; there was neither day nor night. He moved about in this blinding darkness. 'Neither non-existence nor existence existed then; there was only the Unmanifest, enveloped by darkness, in the beginning'—thus, as established by the Maitrāyaṇī and other Śrutis, there was a time consisting of mere darkness, devoid of the distinction between day and night. Since the abiding of Paramaśiva is ordained therein, the terms such as 'Pitāmaha', 'Brahmā', and 'Parameṣṭhin', which designate the presiding deity of that temporal darkness, are determined to refer to Paramaśiva himself. [The creation... was thus described.

The purport [of the Gāyatrī] is established as being the Supreme Śiva. By the second half [of the verse], through the words "that syllable" (*tadakṣaram*) and others, it is shown that by means of this [Gāyatrī], that syllable is attained. Thus, the verses concerning creation and so forth found in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*—beginning with "That syllable which is to be attained"—demonstrate, by means of the phrase "that which is more excellent than the excellent" (*tatsaviturvareṇyam*), the characteristic of being the inner controller of all (*sarvāntaryāmitva*), namely the state of being the impeller of all intellects and the creatorship of the entire universe, in the Supreme Śiva who is denoted by the word "Cave" (*garta*). Furthermore, by the words "and from Him issued forth the ancient wisdom" (*prajñā ca tasmāt prasṛtā purāṇī*), [it is shown that He is the source of] "He thought: 'May I become many, may I procreate'"; "He desired. (Note: The provided text contains fragments of Vedic citations and philosophical commentary. The translation reflects the technical terminology of Advaita Vedānta and Śaiva Siddhānta exegesis.)

The purport of the passages concerning creation and so forth—such as those found in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* beginning with "May I be many, may I procreate," which establish the creative resolve (*prajñā*) consisting of the intention to become manifold—and of other such texts, is demonstrated to reside in Paramaśiva. Thus, it is quite clear that the mantra used for the ritual bathing is that which establishes the purport of all the passages regarding creation and so forth in Paramaśiva. Now, as for the doubt raised by the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra of the final section of the sixth book, "In the injunction regarding the animal, there is no restriction because there is no specific [indication]," concerning the word "animal" (*paśu*) occurring in the injunctive sentence "One should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma":

Since there is no evidence for such a restriction, the word "goat" (*chāga*) occurring in the subordinate mantra—"the omentum and fat of the goat"—cannot logically restrict the word "animal" (*paśu*) found in the principal injunctive sentence. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that either a goat or any other animal whatsoever may be sacrificed. However, by the sūtra establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of that section—*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt* ("It is the goat, because of the wording of the mantra")—it is established that through the power of the word "goat" in the mantra "the omentum and fat of the goat," the general term "animal," which denotes animals in general, is restricted to the specific type of animal that is the goat.

It is logical that [the word *paśu*] culminates in the specific [animal, the goat]; otherwise, in the alternative view where the ritual application pertains to animals other than goats, there would be an absolute lack of syntactic connection (*atyantānanvaya*) for the word *chāga* occurring in the mantra, resulting in the fallacy of a dilemma corrupted by the eight defects of having no other recourse (*nāgatikagatikāṣṭadoṣa*). Even though it culminates in the specific form of the goat, the word *paśu* found in the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) maintains its syntactic connection with the subordinate element (*aṅgabhūti*). In that case as well, since the generic property of being an animal (*paśutva*) does not depart [from the goat], therefore—according to the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinyāya*)—even the word *paśu* found in the primary injunctive sentence maintains its connection with the word *chāga* found in the subordinate mantra.

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, in accordance with the requirements of the context, [the term] refers specifically to a particular animal in the form of a goat. Now, if it is asked, "What is this 'Kāṃsabhojin-nyāya' (the maxim of the eater of bronze)?"—listen: "When there is no contradiction, a quality belonging to a superior [category] may apply to a common [category], just as the eating from bronze applies even to what is not primary. This is stated in the penultimate section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the second quarter (*pāda*) of the twelfth chapter, based on the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) regarding the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī-yāga*) within the *Āśrayaṇeṣṭi*, as well as the *Svarasāman* and the single-pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*) and curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) offerings, according to the seventh chapter, third quarter.

By establishing through the *raṇa* [reasoning] that this is a modification of the *vaiśvadevika* *dyāvāpṛthivya*, the rule that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) must consist of flowers is obtained by extension (*atideśa*). Regarding other sacrifices such as the *aindrāgna* and so forth, where the grass may be either flowering or non-flowering, since the *aindrāgna* and others are primary and more numerous, the primary [rule] applies because of the priority of the original injunction, as in common worldly practice: "In a conflict of contradictory properties, that which belongs to the majority shall prevail. This is established by the two [sūtras] located in the second quarter of the twelfth chapter.

The properties of the *aindrāgna* and other offerings arise through both the principle of the primary (*mukhya*) and the principle of favor (*anugraha*). Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that any *barhis*—whether flowering or non-flowering—is to be taken without restriction, there is no contradiction for the *aindrāgna* and others who are satisfied with obtaining the mere *barhis* common to both flowering and non-flowering varieties; even though the *dyāvāpṛthivīya* offering possesses a greater degree of primacy and accepts the restrictive rule of using only flowering *barhis*, this does not conflict with the others. This is like the case of a disciple who observes the rule of eating from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), while his teacher, being free from such a rule, does not.

And just as when there is the occasion for eating from a single vessel, the teacher’s eating from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) is not prohibited in accordance with the rule for disciples, so too it is established as the final position (*siddhānta*) that here, in the *prasūnābhi* sacrifice, the rule alone must be accepted. However, the body of the section [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*] beginning with "The *svarasāman*s and the *ekakapāla* and *āmikṣā*, because of the observation of indicative marks" is as follows: in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, it is stated, "There are seventeen *svarasāman*s," and thus three *svarasāman*s named after the *viṣuvat* day are placed before and after the *divākīrtya* day.

Specific days have been prescribed; likewise, in other contexts such as the *aṣṭarātra* and others, the *svarasāman* days are prescribed, namely "two sets of six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*) and two *svarasāmans*. Similarly, in the *vaiśvadeva* section of the *cāturmāsya*, the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā* and the *dyāvāpṛthivya ekakapāla* cake are prescribed. In another place, in the position of the *anūbandhyā*, the *maitrāvaruṇī āmikṣā* is prescribed, and in the *avabhṛtha* and other rites, the *vāruṇa ekakapāla* cakes are prescribed. [The terms] *svarasāman*, *ekakapāla*, and *āmikṣā* [refer to] the *svara*-named *sāman*, the single-pot cake, and the curd-mixture, respectively.

Since [the term *svarasāman*] functions as an injunction regarding specific qualities and thus lacks the status of a name (*nāmadheya*), it does not extend its application (*anatideśaka*). Consequently, the previous position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was reached that the *svarasāman* chants occurring in the eight-night sacrifice (*aṣṭarātra*) and so forth, the *anubandhyā* animal sacrifice, the *maitrāvaruṇī-āmikṣā*, and the *vāruṇa-ekakapāla* cake in the *avabhṛtha* rite, are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *nāgā-vā madhanika-svarasāman* and the *vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā-ekakapāla*. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Even though there is no extension of application by way of a name when it is merely a name, [the modification is established] by the quality of being a *svarasāman* and the *ekakapāla* [cake], supported by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) mentioned in the Bhāṣya.

Because an injunction regarding the nature of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) can be extended [to other sacrifices] by means of the general characteristic (*liṅga*), the *Bhāṣya* states that those [other sacrifices] are indeed modifications (*vikāra*) of that [model sacrifice], and thus such characteristics (*liṅga*) have been stated. Regarding the *Svarasāman* days: after stating that in the *Aṣṭarātra* and other [sacrifices] there are two sets of six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*) with the *Praṣṭhya* chants and two *Svarasāman* days, it is heard [in the scripture]: "In that regard, on the third day, which is the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) day, one shifts the position of the twenty-four-fold (*caturviṃśa*) [stoma] so as not to interrupt the sequence of the three subsequent stomas."

The meaning of this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is that there is a sequence of seventeen [stomas]. It refers to the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* sacrifice, which possesses the *pṛṣṭhya-stotras* characterized by the stomas of *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, *ekaviṃśa*, *triṇava*, and *trayastrimśa*. In that context, the third day, known as the *saptadaśa*, must be performed immediately after the *trayastrimśa* [day]. This being so, the *pañcadaśa* exceeds the *trivṛt* by six; the *ekaviṃśa* exceeds the *pañcadaśa* by six; and [the *triṇava*] exceeds the *ekaviṃśa*...

Three [days] plus six; with respect to the triṇava, the thirty-three [stoma] is six more. Thus, all five days become characterized by the *ṣaḍuttara* stoma and are rendered unseparated (*avyavahita*). Likewise, because the third [day], which is the *saptadaśa*, occurs immediately after the *trayastrimśa*, and because it possesses the *saptadaśa* stoma by its very nature (*svarasāmana*), the sequential and uninterrupted succession of the three *saptadaśa* stomas is established. And this is the nature of the two *svarasāmans*, the Gāyatrī and the Mahānāmnī.

The observation of the three seventeen-fold stomas being arranged in sequence is a *liṅga* (indicative mark) for the fact that the Svarasāmans have the Mādhuchandasa as their model, because it is only when the seventeen-fold stoma is obtained through the modification of the Mādhuchandasa-Svarasāman that this [sequence] is possible, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, in the sentence—"Having prescribed the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth in the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, 'That which he offers entirely is one reproach; that which, once offered, turns back is the second; therefore, one should sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with clarified butter alone'"—which is intent upon enjoining clarified butter (*ājya*), [the mention of the Āgrayaṇa serves as a further indicative mark].

The restatement of the *vaiśvadevika* and *ekapāla* rites as being performed with all oblations (*sarvahoma*) and without the ritual circumambulation (*paryāvṛtti*) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that all *ekapāla* offerings are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *vaiśvadevika-ekapāla*. "Paricakṣā" means censure. The statement, "In the *maitrāvaruṇa-amikṣā*, they do not proceed with the whey (*vājina*)," which prohibits the addition of whey to the *vaiśvadevika-amikṣā*, is an indicative mark that all *amikṣā* offerings are modifications of the *vaiśvadevika-amikṣā*. Alternatively, according to the principle "the primary [is followed] because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice," the actual performance is as follows; it is heard in the *adhvarakalpā*: [Text fragment omitted for brevity] ...therefore, the whey is not used in the *maitrāvaruṇa-amikṣā*. Thus, the whey is excluded from the *vaiśvadevika-amikṣā* and its modifications. Furthermore, the rule regarding the *ekapāla* cakes is stated: "One should offer the *ekapāla* cakes with all oblations and without the ritual circumambulation. This indicates that these are modifications of the *vaiśvadevika-ekapāla*. Moreover, the prohibition of whey in the *maitrāvaruṇa-amikṣā*—stated as "they do not proceed with the whey"—indicates that all *amikṣā* offerings are modifications of the *vaiśvadevika-amikṣā*. "One performing malevolent magic (*abhicaraṇ*) should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, and he should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with clarified butter. However, some roll about here [in confusion], thinking that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* could occur solely on the basis of the principle of *yoga* (etymological connection).

For them, whose intellect is devoid of an investigation into the status of being a "single word" (*samānapada*), how can there be the cause for the substitution of *ṇ*? The underlying intention here is as follows: by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that by which something is stepped upon (*padyate*) or understood (*bodhyate*) is a *pada*," the term refers merely to a signifier; or else, it refers to the technical definition (*paribhāṣika*) "a *pada* is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*"). Nor can it be the second [definition].

In the case of the word *nārāyaṇa*, since the word *ayana* functions as the final member (*uttarapada*), the prohibition [of the rule regarding the status of being the beginning of a word] applies by the Vārttika stating that there is a prohibition against applying rules concerning the beginning of a word when a suffix follows. Consequently, because the status of being a word (*padatva*) is absent—due to the impossibility of being a *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix) by relying on the internal case-suffix—and because it is easily established that the letter *n* does not reside in a word distinct from the word containing the cause [for the application of the rule], one might object: "Even so, by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ*..."

Since the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.3] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), and because the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) has been excluded from non-technical names (*asaṃjñāśabda*) such as *rāmanāma* and others, how can the substitution of *ṇ* be established in the derivative (*yaugika*) word *nārāyaṇa*? Nor should it be argued that the rule "from a preceding member" (*pūrvapadāt*, Pāṇini 8.4.3) is intended solely to prescribe the substitution of *ṇ* in technical names like *sūtrasādi*, and not to exclude the substitution of *ṇ* in non-technical names. For even in those cases, by the Vārttika—"When the latter member is a pada, there is a prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics in rules concerning what does not begin with a pada"—there is an absence of the status of being a finished word (*subanta*). Consequently, the *n* residing in the latter member lacks the status of being situated in a pada distinct from the cause [of the rule], and thus the substitution of *ṇ* cannot occur.

Since the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is already established by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi*, and since it must be stated that [the rule] serves as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*)—specifically regarding the word *vyaktāt*—the author says: "Some say that this rule, *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ*, blocks even the *ṇatva* that would otherwise have been obtained, for the purpose of restriction here. However, Śaṅkara strikes them with the realization that there is indeed no possibility [of *ṇatva*] in words such as *druṇasa*; what can I do? This is the intention: because the *n* in words like *druṇasa* is at the beginning of a word (*padādi*), the prescription of *ṇatva* applies to the beginning of a word; and according to the Vārttika, "And when it is the latter member of a compound, provided it is not a prescription for the beginning of a word," [the rule does not apply].

Since it must necessarily be stated that the rule *pūrvapadāt* [Pāṇini 8.4.3] regarding the application [of the suffix *ṭa*] there serves as an injunction (*vidhi*), the injunction would apply only when preceded by the utterance of the word "beginning of a word" (*padādi*) in the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca*.

Thus, one relies on the injunction for the beginning of a word in rules such as *padādyoḥ*; and consequently, because the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) lacks the status of being an injunction for the beginning of a word, the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca* applies to technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *druṇasa*.

Since the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is already established by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* alone, the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām am-nagarayoḥ* serves merely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* would not be established in the word *nārāyaṇa*. To this, [the author] says: "The statement of Kātyāyana, 'in the prescription of what is not at the beginning of a word,' would apply only if it were situated in the context of the mention of that specific word. Who could possibly remove the weakness of that doubt and its refutation found within that portion of the Bhāṣya? This is the intended meaning regarding the form of Mahilārtha.

There is no evidence for the intention that [the rule] is preceded by the utterance of words such as *pada*, and there is unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, this contradicts the context of the Bhāṣya on the Vārttika: "And when it is a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), it is not a prescription regarding what does not begin with a word (*apadādividhi*). For in that [Bhāṣya], having raised the objection—"If it is stated 'when it is not a prescription regarding what begins with a word,' then the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'subsequent word' (*uttarapada*) cannot be established; what would be the fault in that? The rule 'karṇo varṇalalāṭayoḥ' would not be established"—it is replied: "The governing heading of 'subsequent word' will apply by virtue of the specific statement."

The doubt regarding that [objection] in the Bhāṣya is as follows: if it is said, "if [the rule] is stated as 'in the case of an operation concerning what begins with a word' (yady apadādividhau)," then the Vārttika "yadi uttarapadatve ca" must be commenced; this is the meaning. This is because a part can serve as an indicator for the whole, otherwise the meaning of the sentence would be untenable. For this very reason, in the *Laghuvivaraṇa*, it is stated regarding the Bhāṣya's phrase "if it is stated as 'in the case of an operation concerning what begins with a word'" that by this, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the prohibition is expressed as an exception (*apavāda*). It should be understood that [the question] "what then [is the purpose] of the prohibition? is intended [only] if the rule were preceded solely by the utterance of the term "beginning of a word" (*padādi*).

If it were intended as a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), then in the case of *śvetakarṇam agradātrā*—derived from *śvetakarṇa-* according to the rule *avarṇāllakṣaṇād ity atra*—the rule *uttarapadatve ca* would not apply because the accentuation rule is a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*) due to the governing context *ity atra uttarapadādi*. Consequently, by relying on the internal case-ending (*antarvatīṃ vibhaktim*), [the desired result follows].

In examples such as *karṇaḥ*, since the accentuation consisting of the acute on the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) would be established without hindrance for the word *karṇa* following words denoting color (*varṇa*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), both the doubt raised in the Bhāṣya and its subsequent refutation would be untenable by virtue of the force of that [Bhāṣya] statement.

If, however, by the term "rule concerning the beginning of a word" (*padādividhi*) what is intended is actually a rule concerning the beginning of a *pada*, then—since the letter *ka* alone constitutes the beginning of a *pada* while the letter *a* does not—the present rule for vowels would indeed be a "non-rule concerning the beginning of a *pada*" (*apadādividhi*). Consequently, both the doubt regarding the application of the Vārttika and its resolution become logically consistent.

Nor should it be argued that because "a consonant is treated as non-existent in the application of vowel rules" (*svaravidhau vyañjanam avidyamānavat*), the letter *a* must be considered the very beginning of the word due to the presence of the letter *ka*; for even though the [consonant] is present in the application of vowel rules, it is not non-existent with respect to the designation of "beginning of a word" (*padāditva*) contained in the Vārttika phrase "and when it is the latter member of a compound, provided it is not the application of a rule regarding the beginning of a word. Precisely for this reason, Kaiyaṭa raised the objection: "This is a vowel-rule and it is a rule regarding the beginning of a word," and then resolved it by stating: "The letter *ka* is the beginning of the latter member of the compound, but the letter *a* is not; in the application of vowel rules, even a consonant is treated as existent, but there is no designation of it as being the 'beginning'. This has been explained in detail.

In the *Laghuvivaraṇa*, it is stated that when [the word] *grandha* (or *grantha*) stands as the beginning of a subsequent member (*uttarapadāditva*), there is an exception to the prohibition regarding that rule. However, in this case, the cognition that it is the beginning of a subsequent member occurs precisely at the time of the rule for accent (*svaravidhi*), and not prior to that; such is the intended meaning. Therefore, because the intention to express the state of being preceded by the utterance of the word "beginning of a word" (*padādi*) would contradict the *Bhāṣya*, the rule for *ṇatva* in technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *druṇasa* does not apply under the *Vārttika* "and when it is the end of a subsequent member" (*uttarapadatve ca*). Consequently, since the status of being a word (*padatva*) is not lost by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) of the subsequent member, [the rule applies] even in cases where the cause [of the change] resides in something other than the word.

Since the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* in *pada-vartin* is not established by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) is intended as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) in that context. Thus, one might argue: "If [the word] *nārāyaṇa* is analyzed as *nārasyāyanam*, then even if it refers to Śiva, the substitution of *ṇ* would not be established. To this we reply: No; for, in accordance with the Bhāṣya which will be cited later—namely, the statement "one employs a grammatical rule according to its technical definition" (*yathā-lakṣaṇaṃ prayuṅkte*)—the substitution of *ṇ* is accepted in cases such as *nārasyāyanaṃ nārāyaṇam*.

Because of this [absence of the *ṇatva*], if the uncontrived usage "Nārāyaṇa" is observed precisely due to the absence of the quality of being a *guṇa*, then—following that precedent—one should assume that the word "Nārāyaṇa," when used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*) with respect to Śiva or any other object possessing a specific *ṇatva*, is characterized by a different meaning from that [quality-based] one. For this very reason, in the sixth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, after establishing even the four-faced Brahmā’s state of reclining upon the waters through a lengthy textual exposition, [the author] applies it to him by way of etymology (*yogena*).

The application of the specific term "Nārāyaṇa" has been demonstrated. For his text (grantha) states thus: "When that single ocean existed and all things mobile and immobile had perished, there then arose Brahmā—the thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and beyond the senses. Then the one called Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa slept upon the waters. And here he recites this verse concerning the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is the very nature of Brahmā, the omnipresent source of the universe: 'The waters are called *nārāḥ*...'"

"Water indeed is the *nara* (the offspring), and that [Viṣṇu] has it as his *ayana* (abode); because of that, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, in certain specific *kalpas*, even though Viṣṇu alone performs the office of Brahmā, he is called "Brahmā. In the immediately following text: "Then, having perceived within that water the earth situated inside, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), desiring to lift her up by means of inference, assumed for a long time the form of a boar with flaming tusks—an invisible form even to others through the mind, consisting of speech, designated as Brahman—for the sake of lifting the earth."

"Having entered the netherworld for that purpose, the Supporter of the Earth, who sustains himself by his own power, lifted her up with his tusk"—by such statements, it is declared that he assumed the form of a boar for the sake of lifting the earth.

However, one must say that the assumption of the boar-form for the purpose of lifting the earth belongs to Viṣṇu alone, as this is established by many Purāṇas and worldly tradition. [This is stated] after describing his abandonment of the boar-form immediately following the lifting of the earth; thereafter, it says: "Then Brahmā indeed created from his mind his mental sons: Sanaka, Sanandana..."

And likewise, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) [created] Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra from the very beginning. These five sages were yogis who had attained supreme detachment; with their minds fixed on the Lord, they set no thought upon creation. While they remained thus indifferent, that Prajāpati, the creator of the world, was suddenly deluded by the illusion (māyā) of the Great Illusionist (Māyin). Having described how he fell into this delusion after having performed the creation of the world up to the Kumāra-creation, [the text continues: "He awakened his son, the master of the world... and so forth.

The great sage Nārāyaṇa, the great yogi known as Yogicittānurañjana, demonstrated the cessation of that [son's] delusion through the instruction of his father, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa; and subsequently, the manifestation of the lotus from Nārāyaṇa’s navel was described. Following the question, "How was that Blessed One born—Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, the Lord born from the lotus? You ought to tell us this," it was further established that he too, having established himself in yoga, created the manifold universe.

Nor should it be suspected that the description of the four-faced Brahmā assuming the form of a boar is inconsistent, because we see the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa—who was previously Prajāpati—engaged in creation once again, and because there is the mention of the name "Nārāyaṇa" applied to Viriñca himself. For the Śruti states: "In the beginning, this world was indeed water; in it, Prajāpati, having become wind, moved about. He saw this earth; becoming a boar, he took her up," and so forth, showing that even Viriñca assumes the form of a boar.

Because of the presentation of the grasping and receiving of form; even so, since it begins with "Then [there was] Brahman," refers in the middle to "Brahman indeed created," and concludes with "the Lord named Nārāyaṇa, the Prajāpati as before," it is understood that the passage beginning with "then in the single ocean" and so forth refers exclusively to the four-faced one (Caturmukha). Nevertheless, because the four-faced one is designated as the son of Viṣṇu by the statement "He awakened him, his son," he is an incarnation of the manifestation (vyūha) of Viṣṇu.

It is understood that here it is the four-faced one (Brahmā) alone who is being propounded. Nor should it be said that there is a lack of evidence for Viṣṇu’s possession of manifestations (*vyūha*) and incarnations (*avatāra*); for [it is stated]: "Brahmā, Dakṣa and others, time, and likewise all living beings—these are the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Hari, the causes of the creation of the world. Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and others, time, and likewise all living beings—these belong to Viṣṇu, who is the instrumental cause of the maintenance [of the world]."

"Vibhūtis [are]: Rudra, Kāla, Antaka, and all living beings; these are the fourfold vibhūtis for the sake of dissolution, O Janārdana"—since such statements from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* are themselves the authority, one might ask: "In this context, since the etymology of the name Nārāyaṇa is introduced with the words 'the god whose nature is Brahman' (*brahmasvarūpiṇaṃ devam*), referring to Nārāyaṇa who possesses a manifestation (*vyūha*) consisting of Brahman, how can this refer to the Four-faced One (Brahmā)? To this it is replied: because previously, in the passage "Brahmā is indeed named Nārāyaṇa," the word Nārāyaṇa was applied to the Four-faced One himself.

In response to the inquiry, "How does he possess the name Nārāyaṇa on account of his application [to that goal]?", the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name Nārāyaṇa—which was introduced [in the text]—properly culminates in the very nature of Brahman as the qualifier. This is because of the maxim that when something is predicated of a qualified entity, if there is a sublation [of the whole], it leaves aside the qualificand and transfers to the qualifier; this is seen in examples such as "the heavenly-dweller perishes. Furthermore, in the present case, the absence of any such expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) serves as the proof. Therefore, in the present context, Nārāyaṇa...

This etymological derivation [of the name Brahmā] applies to the four-faced one who constitutes the manifestation (*vyūha*) of Viṣṇu. However, in reality, regarding the statement that Brahmā—whose nature is established in the textual passage of the sixth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* beginning with "Then, when that ocean was a single expanse and all moving and non-moving beings had perished, Brahmā came into being"—is an incarnation (*avatāra*) from the manifestation (*vyūha*) of Viṣṇu, there is nothing [to contradict this].

Furthermore, we do not see any valid means of knowledge [for such a claim]. The statement that he awakened his son is justified even by the mere fact of his being born from the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu; on the contrary, it is the four-faced Brahmā himself—who is included within the three Guṇamūrtis that constitute the līlā-avatāras of Paramaśiva—who, at the end of the Kalpa, took the form of Viṣṇu, lay upon the couch of Śeṣa, and after lifting the earth in the form of a boar, abandoned that Viṣṇu-form and again performed the creation of the world through his own self. This is according to the Sūtasaṃhitā, which shares a common context with the Kūrmapurāṇa regarding the greatness of Śiva.

This is understood from a detailed examination of that [text]. Indeed, the textual composition therein begins with such questions as, "O Brahman, how is the number of time units designated by those who know time? and so forth, and subsequently establishes in the eighth chapter that Śiva is not limited by time, whereas others—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest—are so limited.

Having established that [the Lord] is delimited by time, [it is said]: "Śiva alone, for the sake of accomplishing creation, maintenance, and dissolution, manifests through the conceptual constructs known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. O best of scholars, when enveloped by the quality of *rajas*, Brahmā presides over that quality and becomes the creator of the entire world. O wise ones, when enveloped by the quality of *tamas*, Viṣṇu presides over the quality of *sattva* and becomes the Lord, the protector of the entire world. Likewise, O Brahmins, Rudra is enveloped by the quality of *sattva* [and presides over] the quality of *tamas*."

Having presided over [the world] through his non-existence as its sustainer, he—speaking the truth—through Nandin and others, established that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who possess the colors yellow, blue, and white respectively, are veiled by the qualities of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva* according to the suitability of their respective specific colors; and that, according to the suitability of their respective specific tasks in the form of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, *rajas* presides over the qualities of *sattva* and *tamas*. Thus it is said: "O you of excellent vows, infinite forms of Brahmā arise from the differentiation of the qualities; likewise for Viṣṇu and likewise for Īśa, due to the differentiation of the qualities."

Having described how even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra each possess intermediate forms characterized by the predominance of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas respectively, [the text states]: "Who else is the Lord to be worshipped and the liberator for those submerged in saṃsāra, other than Mahādeva himself? This is the eternal Vedic revelation. By this verse, which expresses the Vedic teaching that "when men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, without knowing Śiva, there will be an end to suffering," it is established that Paramaśiva alone is the bestower of liberation.

Having established this point, it is subsequently explained in the ninth chapter that Brahmā, assuming the form of Viṣṇu and taking on the form of a boar, lifted up the earth; then, abandoning that Vaiṣṇava form and assuming the form of a man-lion (mehara), he created the gods and others who had been destroyed in the previous creation by the grace of Mahādeva—thus answering the question posed at the beginning of the chapter by the residents of Naimiṣa: "O Blessed One, how was the earth raised from the waters by Viṣṇu?"

If it is argued that—upon examining such passages as "Then, when the world of stationary and moving beings had perished in the single ocean, Viṣṇu himself appeared in that great ocean"—it is understood that Viṣṇu alone is the subject taught there, and not Viṣṇu as an emanation (guṇamūrti) of Viriñca (Brahmā)—we say no; for in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, which belongs to the same context, the opening refers to Viriñca: "The Lord, Prajāpati, knowing the earth to be submerged in water within the single-oceaned universe, desired to lift it up by means of inference. Thus, [the subject] is indeed Viriñca.

By the employment of the word *prajāpati* in its conventional sense, this is supported by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a vast expanse; therein Prajāpati, having become wind, moved about. He beheld this earth; becoming a boar, he took her up. Having cast off his boar-form, Hari himself became Brahmā. O Brahmins of excellent vows, that earth stood upon the water like a ship. Upon it, by the very grace of Mahādeva, the Lord Brahmā [established] all the immortals who had been destroyed in the previous creation, just as before.

The twice-born [Brahmā] set his mind upon creation, thinking, "I am Prajāpati. Upon a careful consideration of the conclusion of the ninth chapter of the Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa in the Sūtasamhitā, it is established that this ninth chapter indeed teaches that Prajāpati himself is the subject here.

This is because the use of the word "Viṣṇu" in the question and answer can be explained as referring to the Vaiṣṇava [aspect] presided over by Viriñca (Brahmā). By this, [the objection regarding] the Matsya [incarnation] from the Viṣṇupurāṇa—"Just as in former Kalpas he assumed other bodies such as the Fish and the Tortoise, so too he took on the form of a Boar"—is also addressed.

Even by the power of the analogy of the emergence [of the world] from the tortoise (*kūrma*) and others, the suspicion that [the text] independently establishes Viṣṇu is refuted; for even that [analogy] is consistent with the intention of referring to a Vaiṣṇava form presided over by Viriñca (Brahmā). And this very point has been established by Mādhavācārya in the *Tātparyadīpikā* on the *Sūtasaṃhitā*. His text runs as follows: "Viṣṇu is directly [the creator]"—for indeed, at the end of the day, Brahmā, having taken the form of Viṣṇu and lain upon the couch of Śeṣa, lifted up the earth in the form of a boar (*varāha*), and then again created the three worlds by his own self. Therefore, he will say later: "that which is to be emitted..."

It should not be argued that because Brahmā himself became Hari by assuming the form of a boar (*vārāha*), there is no emergence of a *vetāla* (a ghost or demonic spirit) in this rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*). This is because the application of the term "Nārāyaṇa" to Viriñca (Brahmā) and the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name Nārāyaṇa are both consistent only with the intention of referring to the Vaiṣṇava form presided over by Viriñca; thus, the claim that the passage refers to Viriñca is refuted. For after describing how the four-faced one (Brahmā), having lifted up the earth and abandoned his Vaiṣṇava boar-form, performed the creation of the world up until the Kārttikeya-creation (*kaumārasarga*), and then spoke of his manifestation from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa, [the text] describes the subsequent creation again...

When the four-faced one had come forth, he too, having concentrated his yoga, created the manifold world; for since the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa was previously the Prajāpati, and because the application of the word "Nārāyaṇa" to the four-faced one himself is directly established, it follows that—given the absence of any contradiction in applying the term "Nārāyaṇa" to Viriñca—the requirement for an explanation of its etymological basis (pravṛttinimitta) is satisfied by the fact that even the ancient etymological derivation of the name "Nārāyaṇa" must appropriately refer to Viriñca as its presiding deity.

However, the term *nārāyaṇa* used there does not have as its primary referent the Vaiṣṇava being who is to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*), because its well-known usage does not require an explanation of its etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*). Therefore, the etymological derivation of the name *Nārāyaṇa* found in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* refers exclusively to Viriñca (Brahmā). As Āśvalāyana states: "From that staff was born the four-faced Śivātmā, Brahmā, the creator of all worlds and lord of the progenitors. And he, the Prajāpati who is Śivātmā, having long resided upon the waters by his own will, assumed the name Nārāyaṇa in the form of Śakti."

In the *Dharmaśāstra*, the etymological derivation of the name Nārāyaṇa from Viriñca is to be seen. Furthermore, by Śaṅkarānanda Yati, on the occasion of commenting on the auspicious verse in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*—specifically "Nārāyaṇa is beyond the manifest"—and in his commentary on the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*—"Puruṣa is indeed Nārāyaṇa"—he demonstrated that even the term "Nārāyaṇa" applies to the undifferentiated Brahman. He explains: "Nārāyaṇa is the one whose path (*ayana*) is the *nārāḥ*, that is, the individual souls (*jīva*) who are reflections; he is Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, [the term applies] to Śiva as well.

Or, in another instance where the derivative word *nārāyaṇa*—characterized by the nasalization (*ṇatva*)—is employed, one must assume that the status of being a *bhūmādi* (belonging to the class beginning with *bhuvaḥ*) applies only to that form of *nārāyaṇa* which is qualified by a different meaning. This principle does not apply solely to the word *nārāyaṇa*; rather, it should be applied in the same way to any other word containing the element *-āyana* that is capable of such nasalization. For this very reason, in the *Praśnopaniṣad* and other texts, expressions such as "the flowing rivers have the ocean as their *āyana*" (*samudrāyaṇāḥ*) and "the sixteen digits have the Person as their *āyana*" (*puruṣāyaṇāḥ*) are used. In those cases, the nasalization must be justified precisely according to the method we have described, and not otherwise.

Nor can this be resolved by appealing to Vedic archaic usage (*chāndasatva*), for that would apply equally here; moreover, according to the reasoning stated previously, the word *Nārāyaṇa* occurring in the *Subālopaniṣad* and other texts must necessarily refer to Śiva. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the specific mention of the particle *ca* with particular meanings in the list of *gaṇa*-rules is not defective, because one might resort to splitting the rule *tindogotrāt* (Pāṇini 8.1.27) into *tindo gotrāt* and *kutsanābhīkṣṇayoḥ*, thereby establishing that the particle *tiṅ* following words such as *gotra* functions as a cause for the suppression of accent (*nighāta*).

Furthermore, by relying on the fact that the portion [of the rule] beginning with *kutsanābhīkṣṇayoḥ* is a *paribhāṣā*, and by carrying forward (*anuvṛtti*) the term *gotrādīni* from that context, it should be understood that wherever *gotra*-type suffixes are heard, they must always pertain specifically to the domains of contempt (*kutsanā*) and repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*). Consequently, even in the rule *cānaci divagotrātaddhitāmreḍiteṣvagateḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.57), which prescribes the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent for a word ending in contempt when followed by *van*-type suffixes and so forth, as well as for a word preceded by *agati*, those [suffixes] must likewise pertain to the domains of contempt and repetition.

The inclusion of the term *nāmnaḥ* alone is established; however, it is explained by all grammarians that if [the rule] were formulated as a single yoga (*ekayogakṣema*), it would not be established. Consequently, the recitation of [the word] *gotra* and so forth results in [the rule] being restricted solely to the specific meanings of "contempt" (*kutsana*) and "repetition" (*abhīkṣṇya*). For this very reason, the *Kāśikā* states: "And this [refers to] the mention of contempt and repetition."

It has been stated that this should be understood as a qualification of the *pāṭha* (the list). Furthermore, what is excluded from the *pāṭha*? It is said that the *saṃjñā* (technical names) are formed from those items already recited; for, by the *vārttika* on the sūtra "sarvādīni sarvanāmāni" (Pāṇini 1.1.27), it is stated that only those items beginning with *sarva* that are distinct from technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) are included in the list of pronouns (*sarvanāman*). And since that [statement] concludes that only those items beginning with *sarva* which are qualified by specific meanings are included in the list of pronouns, for this very reason Kaiyaṭa says there: "In the example *yathā dindro gotrādīn*, the phrase 'in the sense of contempt and repetition' (*kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ*) is a qualification of the inclusion [of the word] in the list of the *gotra*-class."

The very list of roots distinguished by specific grammatical markers (*viśeṣaviśiṣṭagaṇapāṭha*) has been cited as the illustrative example. Furthermore, having read "bhidā vidā(dhā)raṇe" in the *Bhidādi-gaṇa*, all grammarians have accepted that the form *bhitti* occurs only in senses other than "supporting," and not the form *bhide*. Moreover, regarding the rule *antaraparigrahe* (Pāṇini 1.4.70), Kaiyaṭa’s commentary and the *Kaustubha* on the Vārttika "ārhadika-vidhi-ṇatveṣu saṅkhyānam" (which prescribes the inclusion of the forms *antardhā*, *antardhiḥ*, *antarṇayati*, *antarbhavāṇī*, etc. cite the rules *ātaścopasarge* (3.3.106), *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (3.3.92), and *upasargādasamāse’pi* (8.4.14).

Since the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *arbhaka* must necessarily be commenced by means of the sūtras beginning with *āni loṭ*, the Vārttika—"The addition of *antaḥ* to the rules for the suffix *vid*, *ṇatva*, and *iṣ*"—is sufficient to establish the *ṇatva* in forms such as *antarhaṇyate*, *antarhaṇanatvam*, and *antarayaṇam*.

This is because, once the designation *upasarga* is applied to the word *antaḥ*, the *ṇatva* is already established there by the rule *hanter atpūrvasya kṛtyacaḥ*. Therefore, the two sūtras *antaradeśe* and *ayanaṃ ca* [are unnecessary] in that regard.

Having stated that the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) need not be formulated because [the required forms] are established by the two preceding sūtras, an objection is raised: even if the words *antarhanana* and *antarayaṇa* denote "place" (*deśa*), *ṇatva* would still apply there. Anticipating this, the objection is resolved by stating that in the case of "place," there is an absence of *ṇatva* because these words belong to the *kṣubhnādi* group. Thus, it is clear from both Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa* and the *Kaustubha* that the status of being in the *kṣubhnādi* group must be attributed specifically to the words *antarhanana* and *antarayaṇa* as qualified by their particular meanings. Therefore, with the intention that the connection with the word *nārāyaṇa* is not exclusive to Viṣṇu, he says [verse 8].

In the case of Padmodbhava and others, there is a connection characterized by the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; in the case of Kūrma and others, he remembers the connection with the suffix *-tva*. That fool who prattles on clearly out of hostility—alas!—would even deny the divinity of Śaṅkara.

If it is argued that even so, such an etymological derivation of the word "Nārāyaṇa" for Śiva—similar to the one given for Viṣṇu as "the waters (nārāḥ) are called nārāḥ"—is not seen anywhere in the Purāṇas, we say no. For there are thousands of statements found in the Kūrma Purāṇa and other texts which show the etymology of the name Nārāyaṇa applied to Śiva as well: "Hara is so called because he removes (harati) worldly existence; he is called Viṣṇu because of his all-pervasiveness (vibhutva); and since the 'nāra' [waters] are declared to be his abode (ayana), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, [there are many others].
He states that there are indeed thousands upon thousands of other [etymologies] as well, such as: "That whose abode (ayana), or place of worship, is the lotus-heart belonging to men (nara)."

Even so, it may be argued that the pre-eminent among all grammarians, the crest-jewel Appayadīkṣita, in his *Śivāditadyadīpikā* on the *Janmādisūtra*, accepts a secondary figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Nārāyaṇa" to Paramaśiva—who is Śiva himself in a future state—as evidenced by the statement of Śiva to Kṛṣṇa in the *Harivaṃśa*: "O Govinda, those names which exist in the world as yours are indeed my names; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter."

Since it is established that all names here are indeed his name—supported by the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Āśvalāyana and by the lexicon (*kośa*) which states "known as Ghanasāra and Candra"—just as the name *Aṅkapura* is [derived] from the name *Candra*, so too other world-renowned names of Viṣṇu are determined to be names of Śiva; and since in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of that name is seen for Paramaśiva in the passage beginning with "not the path (*ayana*) of passion (*arasa*)" (*nāramasyāyanam*), the substitution of the nasal *ṇ* has been proven by accepting both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*). By the aforementioned method, according to the grammatical system (*vaiyākaraṇarīti*), what is the formal derivation (*prakriyā*)?

To the objection that [the word] is not heard [in this way], he says: "Appayadīkṣita and others, whose devotion is directed toward the ancients, follow the path of the former and latter [grammarians] regarding the suffix -aṇ. Having propitiated [the deity]... since his diminution here consists in the abandonment of Hara by relying on the mature power (śakti) of the word. By the mention of the word 'power' (śaktim), the capacity of the term 'word' (padasya)... "

Their intention is as follows: although it is stated in the *vārttika* "when [a suffix] occurs after the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*) that "in the case of a rule for an *an-ādi* [suffix]" (*anādividhau*), when the expectation arises as to "of what? (*kasya*), the word *pada* from the current context is obtained, whereby the phrase "in the case of a rule not concerning the beginning of a *pada*" (*apadādividhau*) is established; nor should it be argued that *pada* is not part of the original context, because of the *vārttika*: "when [a suffix] occurs after the second member of a compound."

At the conclusion of the commentary, Kaiyaṭa states that the word *uttarapada* refers to the final member of a compound, just as one says "Bhīma" for "Bhīmasena," since it is possible to denote a whole by means of a part. Therefore, the meaning is that when the designation of a *pada* is to be applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) on account of its being a *pada*, the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply.

Since the word [in the rule] is understood as having the nature of an explanation (*vyākhyāna*), it is already established that [the operation applies] in this way; nevertheless, the explicit mention of the word "pada" (*padagrahaṇa*) is made to indicate that the rule intended by the term "pada-ādi-vidhi" (a rule concerning the beginning of a *pada*) is one that is preceded by the utterance of the word "pada" or similar terms. Consequently, because the rule for *ṇatva* (nasalization) is not a *pada-ādi-vidhi*, the prohibition regarding the application of suffixal markers (*pratyayalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) does not apply, and thus the *ṇatva* of words such as *druṇasa-* is established by the rule *aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi*. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the context of the previously cited *Bhāṣya*, for even though that accentuation rule (*svaravidhi*) is preceded by the utterance of the word "uttarapada," it is in reality a *pada-ādi* [operation].

Because there is an absence of prescriptiveness—since, in reality, there is an absence of prescriptiveness regarding words and so forth—the aforementioned passage of the Bhāṣya proceeds precisely with the intention of expressing such a lack of prescriptiveness; therefore, the rule *pūrvapadāt* is intended solely for the sake of the *nayama* (the prohibition of doubling), and thus, if the word *nārāyaṇa* is taken as etymological (*yaugika*), the substitution of *ṇa* is not established.

We, however, say that in reality, by the term "prescription regarding word-initial [sounds]" (*padādividhi*), only the prescription concerning what constitutes a word-initial is intended for the sake of brevity; it is not necessary to intend the requirement of being preceded by the utterance of the word itself. This is because such an intention would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and lack supporting evidence (*mānābhāva*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "word" (*pada*) in the rule *apadādividhau* is merely for the sake of clarity. This is because the maxim "the acquisition of a foot [is better than] the acquisition of a measure, and the acquisition of a son [is better than] the acquisition of wealth" applies specifically to the context of *sūtras*. Indeed, the definition of a *sūtra* stated by the learned—namely, "those who know the *sūtras* recognize a *sūtra* as that which consists of few syllables, is free from ambiguity, is substantial, has a universal application, is devoid of redundancy, and is irreproachable"—is precisely fulfilled by a formulation composed of few syllables.

"Those wise ones who know the nature of a *vārttika* call that work a *vārttika* wherein there proceeds an investigation into what has been stated, what has not been stated, and what has been poorly stated. Since this definition of a *vārttika* provided by the author of the commentary on Sureśvara’s *Vārttika* is both too brief and incomplete, whereas upon reflection the definition of a *vārttika* as consisting of an inquiry into what has been stated, unstated, or ill-stated appears to possess an abundance of syllables that is actually conducive to its excellence; in reality, however, in the absence of the mention of the word [itself], it would be the object of negation.

If the suffix (*pratyaya*) were also considered to be "present in the intellect" (*buddhistha*) by virtue of being a constituent of the definition of a suffix, then [the rule] *nar-pratyayād-vidhau* (P. 8.4.12) would also apply; consequently, in forms such as *paramadaṇḍinā*, there would be the undesirable contingency (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *ṅamuṭ* for the vowel *ā* of the suffix *ṭā*. In the present case, since the prescription of *ṅamuṭ* would not be a "rule concerning the beginning of a suffix" (*pratyayādividhi*), and because the prohibition *uttarapadatve ca* (P. 8.4.13) does not apply, the status of *daṇḍin-* as a word (*padatva*) is not lost. Nor should it be argued that there is no harm in the contingency of *ṅamuṭ* here because of its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); for this is precluded by the present Vārttika, which consists of the phrase *apadādividhi*.

For those commentators (*vārttikakṛt*) who provide such an interpretation (*rambha*), the intention is clearly that [the rule] would be incorrect; for, since it is impossible to reject [the rule] when there is a difference in result, the inclusion of the term *pada* must have a purpose. Thus, it is simply not possible for it to indicate the intention to express the fact that [the suffixes] are preceded by the utterance of words such as *pada*. [Objection: But even so, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have explained this very *vārttika*. They did so by dividing the two rules—*svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* and *yacibham*—into three separate rules: *svādiṣu*, *asarvanāmasthāne*, *yaci*, and *bham*.

In the rule *sarvanāmasthāne*, having accepted that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of prohibition, and having carried forward [the terms] "that which begins with what [is the cause of] the prescription of an affix" and "ending in a case-ending" (*subanta*) into these rules: when *svādi* (case-endings) follow, that which begins with what [is the cause of] the prescription of an affix is termed a *pada*, as is [that which ends in a case-ending] when *svādi* follow.

Having explained the first rule—that even that which ends in a *sub* suffix is designated as a "word" (*padam*)—he then explains the second rule: when a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with *yaj* follows, that which is the basis for the derivation of the suffix is not a "word," nor is the *sub*-ending form itself a "word" when it stands before a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with *yaj*.

In the third application (*yoga*), following the two preceding applications and by resorting to the governing context of the term *śabda*, one adopts the view that the negative particle (*nañ*) in the rule *asarvanāmasthāne* functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Thus, when a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ja* follows a base other than a *sarvanāmasthāna*, that which begins from the element after which the suffix is prescribed is designated *bha*, as is [the base] itself when followed by a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ja*.

Having explained that a word ending in a *sup* suffix is also designated as *bha* when followed by the *svādi* group of suffixes—excluding those that are *sarvanāmasthāna*—one must refute the occurrence of *kutva* and other such changes (which would otherwise apply because the word is a *pada* due to the internal presence of a case-ending) in examples such as *paramavācau* and *paramavācā*, by means of the Vārttika: "And [the designation *bha* applies] when the following element is the second member of a compound."

These [objections] have been refuted by this very analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For instance, although the substitution of *ṇ* is established in forms such as *dṛṇasena* because the subsequent member lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*) when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel, it would still not be established in forms such as *dṛṇasābhyām* where the case-ending begins with a consonant. Therefore, he says: "The illustrious [author]... [the status of being a word]..."

Since the status of the following member as a *pada* remains unchanged, the substitution of *ṇ* is already established; therefore, it must be stated that the rule *pūrvapadāt* serves to provide a specific injunction in that context. Consequently, although the substitution of *ṇ* is established for the word *nārāyaṇa* when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel (such as *aja*), it is not established at all when followed by a case-ending beginning with a consonant (*hal*); hence, he says:

The illustrious Patañjali, having first criticized the statement of Kātyāyana, then recited this very same sentence—devoid of the negative particle (*nañ*)—with reference specifically to the intention of Madanāntaka (Śiva) regarding the rule for establishing the *ṇatva* substitution. This is the underlying intent: that such [objections] arise by their own force immediately after the rejection of the Vārttika.

That very *vārttika*, namely "nañ-iva-nirmukte uttarapadatve ca apadādividhau," was accepted by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*), such that the status of being a word (*padatva*)—based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) of the second member (*uttarapada*)—occurs only when there is a rule regarding the beginning of a word (*padādividhau*) and not otherwise. For those authors of the *Bhāṣya* who accept this, the substitution of *ṇ* (the *ṇatva*) is indeed intended even for derivative words (*yaugika*) such as *nārāyaṇa* and others. Otherwise, if the aforementioned *yogavibhāga* were sufficient to prevent [the application of] *kutva* in cases such as *paramavācau* and *paramavācā*, then the acceptance of such a *vārttika* in the *Bhāṣya* would be redundant.

[The effort] made [to justify the rule] would indeed be in vain. Now, it might be argued that for this reason the authors of the Bhāṣya do not accept the Vārttika; rather, the Vārttika is rejected by means of the previously mentioned *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). However, in the case of *dadhi-secau*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). This is because, since the word *seca-* lacks the status of being a *pada* (an inflected word), the prohibition "not before *si* or when it begins a *pada*" (*na si-syoḥ*) would not apply. In the rule *sāt-padādyoḥ*, if one accepts the compound *padādi-pada-ādiḥ*, then in examples such as *dadhi-secau*, [the suffix] follows immediately after the member *dadhi*.

Furthermore, because [the word *bahvacaḥ*] begins with a portion that is difficult to cross (*dut-tara-bhāga*), the prohibition in the rule *sāt-padādyoḥ* applies, and thus there is no occurrence of the substitution of *ṣ*. Having raised the objection that this solution fails because in the example *bahu-secau*, since *bahvac-* is a suffix, it lacks the status of a *pada*, and thus the prohibition does not apply—leading to the undesired occurrence of *ṣ*—the two Vārttikas, "When the second member is a *pada*" (*uttara-pada-tve*) and "And when a prescription for the beginning of a *pada* applies, if the preceding member has many vowels" (*padādi-vidhau bahv-acaḥ pūrvasya ca*), were composed precisely to resolve that issue. In both cases, even though the prescription concerns the beginning of a *pada*, one relies on the intervening case-ending (*antar-vartinī vibhaktiḥ*) by means of the principle of *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*.

The prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is established because [the word *bahusecuḥ*] is a *pada* by virtue of being the latter member of a compound. It should not be argued that the second *vārttika* is redundant, given that the first *vārttika*—which states that the designation *pada* applies by relying on an internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), and that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule applies only to operations concerning the beginning of a *pada* and not to operations concerning the end of a *pada*—is sufficient to prevent *ṣatva* and to block *kutva* in the example *bahusecuḥ*. For if the term "latter member" (*uttarapada*) were used in its purely etymological sense (*yaugika*), then even in the sentence *paramaṃ carma*, the word *carman* would be considered a "latter member," and consequently, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would apply there as well.

The elision of *n* would not occur. For this very reason, while explaining the statement by Kaiyaṭa in the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca*, which says "for [the rule applies] when there is the status of being an *uttarapada* (final member) in a compound," the authors of the *Laghuvivaraṇa* stated that the sense is that the word *uttarapada* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) with respect to the final constituent of a compound. And thus, in the case of *bahusecau*, because the word *sec* lacks the status of being the final constituent of a compound, the status of being an *uttarapada* is absent; consequently, since the first Vārttika does not apply, the prohibition of *ṣatva*—which arises from the status of being a *pada* by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*)—likewise applies to the change to *kutva*.

It is not difficult [to refute this]. Nor should it be argued that because there is no compound in *bahusecau*, the preceding element is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus since the previously produced case-ending is what is actually heard, an internal case-ending is impossible; for, by the rule *arthavat* (Pāṇini 1.2.45), the entire preceding aggregate is designated as a nominal stem, and when the previously produced case-ending is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), another case-ending is subsequently produced for the aggregate, whereby an internal case-ending becomes possible.

If it is argued that because [the desired form] is possible through the elision (*lopa*), the second *vārttika* is therefore necessary, we say no. For if this were the case, one could—by relying on the previously mentioned alternative of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule)—first prevent the occurrence of *kutva* in forms such as *paramavācau* and *paramavācaḥ*, and then, in the rule *sāt padādyoḥ*, split the rule as *sāteḥ* and subsequently formulate another rule, *bahurcapadābhyām*. In this way, since the prohibition of *ṣatva* would be established for forms like *dadhisecau* and *bahusecāv* by the principle that there is no *ṣatva* for an *s* following *bahu* or *ṛca* or *pada*, the acceptance of the *vārttika* would be redundant.

Since the suffix *kāra* would be purposeless, the authors of the Bhāṣya, by accepting that [suffix], have clarified the very intention stated previously. Thus, even for the authors of the Mahābhāṣya, the substitution of *ṇa* for the etymologically derived word *nārāyaṇa* was indeed intended; and so, at the time of accepting the Vārttika, the author of the Bhāṣya [expressed] this very intention.

The author of the *Rāḥnodakīghaṭa* says constantly: "Considering my own intention to be something that must not be revealed to foolish people who lack devotion to You, this commentator [Bhāṣyakāra], O Lord of Beings, has indeed taught the *Nañ-rahi-vārtika* through the introduction of another very brief summary (*pātanikā*). Because it is the supreme secret, [he taught] Śiva-bhakti..."

This [work], which establishes the identity of the term *Paramaśiva* with *Paranārāyaṇa*, is not to be disclosed to those devoid of devotion to Śiva nor to those whose minds lack such devotion; however, it is to be disclosed to all by those endowed with the most stainless intuition (*pratibhā*) obtained through the grace of Śiva, who can themselves infer its meaning. Having taken this as its intended subject matter, it may be elucidated by wise devotees of Śiva in another manner. [For instance,] having raised the objection that there is a flaw consisting in the failure to establish the prohibition of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in cases such as *dadhi-secau* and *bāhu-secau* because of the acceptance of the *vārtika*, one might object: "But in this way, regarding the *nakāra*s that constitute the beginning of the subsequent member [of a compound], as in *rāma-..."*

Even though the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) does not apply to words such as *nāman* when they do not function as proper names (*asaṃjñābhūta*), the substitution of *ṇ* would nonetheless be unavoidable for the *n* occurring in a subsequent member of a compound—such as in the words *śaṃkara-yāna*, *aśaṃkara*, and *vana*. This is because the rule for *ṇatva* applies to what is "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādi*) and, by the operation of the Vārttika "and when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*), the *n* in question lacks the status of residing in a word distinct from the word containing the cause [of the substitution]. To prevent this, the rule must be understood as one that applies specifically to the *n* at the beginning of a word, as indicated by the use of the term "beginning of a word" (*padādividhi*) in the formulation of the rule.

It need not be stated. Furthermore, since it is impossible for the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) to have a prescriptive (*vidhi*) purpose regarding words such as *druṇasa*, it must necessarily be taken as having a restrictive (*niyama*) purpose. Consequently, there is no possibility of the application of the substitution of *ṇ* in words such as *aśaṅkara-yāna*. Therefore, he says: "If that were the case, the substitution of *ṇ* would arise in words such as *indudhara*, *śaṅkara*, and *yānamukhya*"; as for this objection, it is caused by a forgetfulness regarding the inclusion of these words in the *kṣubhnādi* group, which was recorded by the Grammarians following the authority of the author of the *Vṛtti*.

This is the intended meaning: therein, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) has already been precluded by the sūtras beginning with *pra-nir-anta-* which will be described as having a restrictive (*niyamārtha*) purpose. However, regarding these words such as *śaṅkara* and *yāna*, the substitution of *ṇ* is precluded by the restrictive sūtras. One might argue that the preclusion of *ṇatva* is also possible by classifying them as belonging to the *kṣubhna*-group; yet, one should not say that this classification is merely a rash act because it is disapproved of by the authors of the commentaries, such as the Vṛttikāra, in the case of technical terms like *druṇasa*.

For those commentators such as the author of the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and the authors of the Vṛtti who describe the purpose of the rule *pūrvapadāt* as being for the sake of establishing [the correct form], what is actually intended by the term "rule concerning *pada*, etc. (*padādividhi*) is precisely the rule concerning *pada*, etc. This is because it must necessarily be assumed that their intention was that words such as *śaṅkara* and *yāna* belong to the *kṣubhna*-class; otherwise, the description provided by them regarding the status of rules for words like *druṇasa* would result in being groundless. Furthermore, this is supported by the fact that in the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyāmagaḥ*, the author of the Bhāṣya and others [have treated] this rule...

The nature of the *vidhi* (injunction) has been described therein. Regarding that, we shall clearly demonstrate, in the context of introducing the verse, that the textual passage from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary—which is intent on describing that [nature]—is in contradiction with the objection (*codya*) found in the eighth-century Bhāṣya.
