Furthermore, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that sūtra, even the word "api" (even/also)...

They rely on the mention of the word *samāna* [in the rule], which implies that what is always [co-occurring] with the same word as previously stated is "having the same word" (*samānapada*). For them, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva), which was not otherwise applicable, is prescribed by this rule; for it has been stated that in a compound, because of the division into prior and subsequent members, there is a state of "not having the same word. This passage has also been explained by Haradatta Miśra in the section beginning with "others, however" (*apare tu*).

[The phrase] "is the same as ours" yields the restriction that [the two] are indeed identical parts. Therefore, he says: "Because of the mention of 'samāna' (same). One should have simply said "pada" (word); since there is an absence of the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-nimittin*) regarding non-words and those situated elsewhere, the mention of "pada" is understood to be for the purpose of intending singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*). Since this is already established, the fact that the mention of "samāna" is made has this [following] purpose.

The purpose is so that it may be understood that the word is indeed the same; for those who speak thus, he says "of them" (*teṣām*) to indicate that this is understood as being for the sake of a grammatical rule (*vidhy-artha*). He establishes its status as being for the sake of a rule by saying "for in a compound" (*samāse hi*), and thus [the rule] accounts for the inclusion of words such as *śaṅkara* and *yāna* within the *kṣubhnādi* group.

This is indeed agreed upon by the author of the Bhāṣya and others; therefore, in reality, it is precisely the *padādividhi* (rule concerning what stands at the beginning of a word) that is intended by the term *padādividhi*. Now, one might object: "If this were so, then by rules such as *vanaṃ purak-* etc., the prescription of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) for words like *vana-*, *aṅga-*, *nvāhana-*, and *pāna-*, which have *latā* as their subsequent member (*uttarapada*), would be displaced. This is because in words such as *vakādi*, since the prescription of *ṇatva* would not be a *padādividhi*, the rule *uttarapadatve ca* [P. 8.4.3] would apply, and thus the *ṇatva* would already be established by the rule *aṭkupvāṅ-* [P. 8.4.2]. To this, he says: ||14||

Having bowed [to the Lord], regarding the objections concerning contradictions in the sūtras pertaining to the governing scope (*adhikāra*)—or rather, the refutations of those contradictions—within the determination of the intended meaning as we have articulated it, this is the intention of those whose minds are trained by the One who bears the crescent moon (Śiva), in the distinction between the restrictive (*niyama*) and the prescriptive (*vidhi*) intent: To begin with, the sūtra *vanaṃ puraketi* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It is established by both parties that in examples such as *sadasi patravanaṃ*, the substitution of *e* is unmanifest; however, in the case of *purakāvaṇaṃ*, since it is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*), according to your own view, the sūtra *pūrvapadādi-* would function as a prescriptive rule (*vidhyarthatva*).

By that very sūtra, this [form] is established; for, according to its restrictive (niyamārtha) purpose, it is by the sūtra *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2]. In my view, although there is the possibility of both—the application of *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ* for the sake of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*) and the application of *pūrvapadāt* for the sake of a negation (*nañ-arthatva*)—the distinction is that, because of its posteriority, it is by the sūtra *pūrvapadāt* alone. Nor is it the case that... [the previous rule applies].

It should not be asked: "Since the [term] *padatvāt* (‘because of being a word-final’) is unestablished (*asiddha*) there, the substitution of *ṇ* must be stated only by means of [the rule] *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi*; how then can it be stated thus? For this statement is made by adopting the position that "rule after rule is established" (*yoge yoge upadiṣṭaḥ siddhaḥ*), rather than the position that "section after section is established" (*prakaraṇe prakaraṇam*). It might be argued: "In this position, one must state that the inclusion of the word *api* (‘even’) in the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi ṇopadeśasya* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For instance, this sūtra is intended for the establishment of the substitution of *ṇ* in cases such as *praṇamati māṇavakaḥ*, where it is an *asamāsa* (non-compound)."

In the absence of the mention [of the word *asamāse*], since the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from the preceding member" (*pūrvapadāt*) applies only within a compound—because a "preceding member" is possible only in a compound—it would be understood that this rule operates only with respect to a compound. To indicate that the rule functions even outside that governing context, the mention of *asamāse* is made; for if the governing rule "from the preceding member" were present in the rule concerning the prefix (*upasargāt*), then the substitution of *ṇ* would already be established by that very rule, and the mention of *upasargāt* would be redundant. Therefore, it does not carry over [into the subsequent rules]. Thus, by the very explanation that it serves to provide the possibility [of the substitution] even in non-compounds, the governing rule "from the following member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*) is established.

Although one might argue that there is "non-occurrence" (nivṛtti), even so, if the inclusion [of the word *asaṃjñāyām*] were not present in the non-compound (*asamāsa*), then in a compound where it is not a name (*asaṃjñā*), such as in *pra-kṛta*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur. This is because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating "after a preceding member, when it is a name," and because this current sūtra finds its application in non-compounds like *praṇamati*.

Therefore, if the inclusion [of *asaṃjñāyām*] is indeed present, the substitution of *ṇ* is established even in a compound when it is not a name; however, when it is a name, it is already established by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi*. ||16(?)||
If every rule were established only in relation to its specific context (yoge yoge), then, with respect to the rule *pūrvapadāt*, the rule *upasargāt* would be as if non-existent (*asiddha*);

consequently, because that [former rule] could not restrict it, even if the [suffix] *ṇa* were not included when there is no compound (*asamāsa*), its inclusion would be redundant since the substitution of *ṇa* would already be established in compounds and in technical names (*saṃjñā*). Thus, it is by this principle—that "in a context, a subsequent context is as if non-existent"—and not by the principle "rule after rule," that this is made known.

If you argue: "And this is possible according to your view because the rule *pūrvapadāt* lacks the status of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*); for this very reason, Haradatta Miśra, having established all of this, stated that while this [result] follows if the rule *pūrvapadāt* is restrictive, it cannot be established if it is prescriptive (*vidhyartha*)," we reply as follows: In my view, even though the mention [of the root *stambh-*] in the absence of a compound cannot serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is nonetheless intended to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* following the reduplicated syllable in forms such as *sisikṣati* and *susūṣati*, according to the rule *stautiṇyorevaṣaṇyabhyāsāt*.

The mention of "due to repetition" (*abhyāsāt*) is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For instance, if that term were absent, then in forms such as *abhiṣiṣikṣati*, the substitution [of *ṣ* for *s*] prescribed by the rule *sthādiṣv abhyāsena cābhyāsasya* would also be prohibited by the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

However, since it is present, only that substitution which occurs due to repetition is prohibited, and thus forms such as *abhiṣiṣikṣati* are established. Furthermore, this is the purpose [of the indicator] when one grammatical operation is not considered valid (*asiddha*) with respect to another.

This is not tenable. Because the rule *sthādiṣv abhyāsena ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.64) is considered *asiddha* with respect to the restriction *stautiṇyoreva* (Pāṇini 8.3.61), it is impossible for that [former rule] to prohibit the application [of *ṣatva*] caused by a prefix (*upasarga*). Nor can it be argued that examples such as *pratiṣiṣati* and *athi ṣiṣati*, which were stated by the author of the Vṛtti, should serve as counter-examples there; for if the rule *abhyāsāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.64) were absent, it would follow that even the application [of *ṣatva*] caused by the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be prohibited in those cases. This is because the scope of the restriction (*niyama*) consists of similar classes:
it prohibits the application of *ṣatva* that would otherwise occur for a verbal root following the suffix *san* when preceded by *bhū*.
Even if one were to accept that [the prohibition] applies only to that specific case, it would still be possible to avoid the inconsistency in examples such as *pratiṣiṣati*.

Therefore, by resorting to the locative case [in the rule] as referring to the scope of the operation (*nīti-viṣaya-saptamī*), and by accepting that only the occurrence of *ṣatva* that arises when the suffix *san* is added is prohibited, one might raise the objection regarding the inconsistency in *pratiṣiṣati* and so forth; however, the removal of that [objection] by means of the word *abhyāsāt* [in the commentary] is merely a superficial clearing away (*prakṣālana*).

The rule *lanāddhiti* follows this very logic. Furthermore, the mention of "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) in the sūtra *sthādiṣu* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For that [mention] is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) to ensure that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *upasargāt* only in the case of roots beginning with *sthā*, and not elsewhere—as in forms such as *abhisusūṣati* and *abhisisīṣati*. However, if one were to argue that the application of each rule is established independently within its own context (*yoge yogasya siddhitve*), this would not be tenable; because, with respect to the sūtra *sthādiṣu*, the rule *upasargāt* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus it would be impossible for the former to be restricted by the latter. Nor can it be argued that in the two aforementioned instances, the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana-prāmāṇya*)...

It must not be said that [the rule] merely indicates that "only as much as is required is not *asiddha*," but rather that "the entire section (*prakaraṇa*) is *asiddha* within the section. For if that were the case, one could argue that with respect to the sūtra *pūrvapadāt*, the sūtra *upasargādasamāse 'pi* indicates "it is not *asiddha*" by virtue of its own capacity; consequently, the statement in the Bhāṣya and other works—that "by the capacity of the inclusion of the word *asamāse*, it is indicated that the entire section is *asiddha*"—would become inconsistent. This is the point of this indication.

Furthermore, the establishment of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in forms such as *niṣkṛtam* and *niṣpītam* would not otherwise be possible; for in those cases, the *satva* (substitution of *s*) prescribed by the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* would be considered *asiddha* (unestablished), and thus the *ṣatva* prescribed by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* would not occur. On this view, in the rule *sopadādau*, the *sakāra* (*s*) that is already under discussion is what is subsequently enjoined by later rules such as *namaspurasorgatyoḥ*. Moreover, in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*, the term *apadādau* (not at the beginning of a word) does not carry over; rather, by means of the ablative *iṇaḥ*, the nominative *saḥ* is transformed into a genitive. And thus, it is by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* alone [that the desired result is achieved].

Since it is generally accepted that the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed for what follows *iṇ*, if—out of fear of the difficulty involved in resorting to an inferential indicator (*jñāpaka*) or resorting to the genitive case as referring to the base (*prakṛti*)—one were to maintain that the word "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) is understood in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*, then the substitution of *ṣ* would be prescribed only when [the suffix] begins a word; this is the case in subsequent rules such as *namaspurasoḥ*.

In the sūtras, "sa" and "ṣa" are understood to carry over [from previous rules]. In the sūtra *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*, the status of being *svarita* (an accented vowel) is declared; and according to the rule *svaritenādhikāraḥ*, the term *adhikāra*—derived from the etymology *adhikaḥ kāraḥ* (an additional operation)—refers to that which results in the attainment of further grammatical effects. By the force of this declaration of *svarita* status, it is established that for a *visarga* following a root ending in *iṇ*, there is *ṣatva* (substitution with *ṣ*), whereas elsewhere there is *satva* (substitution with *s*). Thus, in examples such as *niṣkṛtam* and *niṣpītam*, the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed by the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* alone, and not by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*. This applies to those cases where [the condition] *tug* is present.

The *yoga* is established; however, regarding the rule *prakaraṇe prakaraṇam upasargād asamāse 'pi*, if one adopts the position that the inclusion of the word *asamāse 'pi* ("even in non-compounds") is for the sake of clarity, then in forms such as *purakāvaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* is achieved by the rule *aṭ-ku-pvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* alone. It should be understood that these two positions are clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Padamañjarī*, and other works. Therefore, in cases such as *purakāvaṇam*, the argument that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām am-nagarayoḥ* due to its higher status (*paratva*) is indeed valid. As for the rule *pra-ni-r-anaḥ...* [etc.], however...

In the case of the word *vana* following words such as *śara*, whether it denotes a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or not, this rule serves to prescribe the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) as an exception to the optional application prescribed by the subsequent sūtra, "vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ. This is common to both views. Furthermore, regarding the word *vana* following the words *pra*, *niḥ*, and *antaḥ*, even when it is a technical name—as in the example *vanaṃ purakaḥ*—the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed here because it would otherwise not have applied due to the restrictive rule established by the preceding sūtra. This point also remains undifferentiated for both views. However, in your view, when the word does not denote a technical name, since the sūtra "pūrvapadāt" functions as a prescriptive rule...

Because there is an absence of technical designation (*saṃjñā*), *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) is prescribed where it had not been previously obtained; and if [the rule] were for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthatva*), then the *ṇatva* brought about by that restriction is restored (*pratiprasūyate*). Thus, although in both these views the purpose is prescriptive (*vidhyartha*), and according to my own view its purpose is indeed prescriptive, in cases such as *pravaṇa*, since the prescription of *ṇatva* is a rule concerning what is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādividhi*), the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca* applies. Consequently, because *ṇatva* is established as not occurring in a word distinct from the word containing the cause (*nimittavat*), *ṇatva* occurs only after words such as *pra*, *niḥ*, and *antaḥ* when they are not a technical designation (*asaṃjñāyām*), but not in cases such as *rāmavanam*.

The distinction here is that it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding a specific portion [of the term]. Nor should it be argued that it is unprecedented for a single sūtra to have the sense of an original injunction (*vidhyartha*) in one part and the sense of a restrictive rule in another; for this is well known to all grammarians from the very proclamation of the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsācca*, where the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* is for the purpose of an injunction, while the mention of *samāsa* is for the purpose of a restriction, and so forth. Alternatively, in the preceding sūtra *vanaṃ puragā-*, the term *saṃjñāyām* ("in the sense of a name") does not carry over to the portion concerning the word *agre*; thus, in the case of *agrevaṇam* (which occurs when it is not a name), that sūtra applies.

For it is your view that [the rule] is for the purpose of an injunction; for this very reason, Haradatta says later, "But they say that in the case of the word *śabda* when it is not a technical term (*asaṃjñā*), it is for the purpose of an injunction. And thus, in my view, since the substitution of *ṇa* is already established there by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi*, if the substitution of *ṇa* occurs for the word *vana* when it is not a technical term, then it is restricted by the subsequent rule to occur only after the word *śabda*.

It should be understood that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, which had been set aside [by Pāṇini 8.4.34], is re-enjoined by the rule *pranirantaḥśarebhyo 'paṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19) after the words *pra*, *ni*, *antaḥ*, and *śara*. The rule *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.6) is for the sake of providing an option in cases such as *dūrvāvaṇam* and *śirīṣavaṇam*; thus, both [rules] are equal in this regard. As for the expression *aho dantāt*:

In your view, this is for the sake of the meaning of the rule (*vidhyartha*) as before in both cases; however, in my view, it is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the word *ahan* only in instances such as *pūrvāhṇe*, and not in instances such as *nirahnaḥ*. Now, one might ask: here, is there the inclusion of the word *ahan* ending in *n* in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), or is it the word *ahna* ending in *a*?

Or [it might be argued that] there is an inversion, whereby the word ending in the genitive case is taken as having the nominative case-ending. This is not the first [option]. For if the word *ahan* undergoes the change to *ṇ*, then by the restrictive rule that the change applies only when the final syllable of the compound follows a preceding member ending in a long vowel (*ā*), it would follow that the change to *ṇ* would also apply in the word *dīrghāhni*. Nor can it be said that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because in that case...

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because we see in the *Bhāṣya* that the introduction of the *Vārttika* stating "it should be stated that [the substitution occurs] after an *a*-ending [word] for an *a*-ending [word]" in order to prevent the change of *n* to *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) is rendered useless; for the prevention of *ṇatva* in that case is already established simply by relying on the fact that the word *ahnaḥ* is understood as a nominative singular form ending in *a*. This being so...

If there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) for the word *ahan-* when it ends in a vowel, then—since the rule would result in the restriction that it applies only to what follows a word ending in a vowel preceded by [another] vowel—the word *ahan-* ending in *n* would not be subject to this restriction; consequently, the fault of *ṇatva* would still apply in the case of *dīrghāhnī*. If you say "no," then for you as well, under the view that the rule *pūrvapadāt* is restrictive (*niyamārtha*), this same fault would apply equally because this present rule (*ahnaḥ*) would also be restrictive by the same logic. Therefore, both parties must resolve it in this way: [the condition is] *prātipadikāntanuṃ*... [etc.].

One should not argue that this leads to a contradiction with the *vārttika* and *bhāṣya* which state, "In the case of words beginning with *yuva*, a prohibition must be stated regarding the rule *vibhaktiṣu ca*," because those two [the *vārttika* and *bhāṣya*] function as optional injunctions (*vidhi*). For this very reason, even under the view that the rule is a restrictive one (*niyama*), in order to avoid this defect, and in both views to prevent the application of the *ṇatva* prescribed by the rule *prātipadikāntanum-vibhaktiṣu ca*, it is necessary to rely on the inclusion of *yuva* and others in the list; thus, its status as an injunction is established.

The author of the Bhāṣya says: "Alternatively, the word will be read among *vāyu*, *vāri*, and so on. His intention is that even if that fault were to occur in the alternative view (*pakṣa*), since its prevention would be established [otherwise], the labor of resorting to the word *ahan* (day) ending in the nominative case by way of transposition is in vain.

As for the rule *vāhanam āhitāt*, in your view it serves as an injunction (*vidhi*) in both alternative views; however, in my view, it is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only in cases such as *ikṣuvāhaṇam* and the like, and not in cases such as *indravāhanam*. Furthermore, the rule *pāna-deśe* serves as an injunction in both of your alternative views; however, in my view... [text continues].

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *pāna* occurs only in cases such as *kṣīrapāṇā uśīnarāḥ* ("the Uśīnara people who drink milk"), but not in cases such as *kṣīrapāno bālaḥ* ("a child who drinks milk"). For this purpose, the rule *bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.10) is intended to provide an option (*vikalpa*) in forms like *kṣīrapāṇam*. However, the distinction is as follows: according to your view, since the rule *pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) is interpreted either as an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the substitution of *ṇ* is merely optional (*vikalpate*) where it was previously unestablished. According to my view, however, although the substitution of *ṇ* is established by the previous rule *pānaṃ deśe* (Pāṇini 8.4.9), it is set aside by that very restrictive rule; thus, the present rule serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to restore it optionally. Furthermore, the rule *prātipadikānta-* (Pāṇini 8.4.11) is also for the sake of providing an option in those instances.

In your view, in forms such as *māṣavāpiṇau*, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is not obtained in the portion ending in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), whereas it is obtained in the portion that is not a case-ending (*avibhakti*), as in *māṣavāpāṇi* and *māṣavāpeṇa*, just as in *mātṛbhogīṇa*. Thus, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. In my view, however, the substitution of *ṇ* is obtained everywhere; therefore, the distinction is that this is an "option regarding what is already obtained" (*prāptavibhāṣā*). Now, one might object: if this were so, then in the case of *gargabhaginī* ("the sister of the Gargas"), the optional application of *ṇ* would have to be prevented by the present rule. To prevent this, the Vārttika states: "The mention of 'compound-final' (*samāsānta*) in the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* at the end of a nominal stem is for the purpose of prohibiting it in non-compound-final instances. This refers to the compound...

The commencement [of the rule] is seen to have the meaning that only the final element of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is to be understood; and that is logical according to your view. However, since the prohibition in that very case is effected by this sūtra itself, there would be the undesirable consequence of obligatory *ṇatva* (nasalization) by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye ’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2). Consequently, it would be necessary to assume that [the word *kṣubhna*] belongs to the *kṣubhnādi* class. Since the prevention of the application of *ṇatva* in that case is already established by that [class membership], the composition of a vārttika intended to prevent the optional application of *ṇatva* therein would be redundant. In our view, however, because *ṇatva* does not apply there by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye ’pi*, there is no need to assume its inclusion in the *kṣubhnādi* class.

The commencement of that *vārttika* is indeed absolutely necessary for the purpose of preventing the optional application (*vikalpa*) of *ṇatva* by means of the present sūtra. Nor should it be argued that the optional application of *ṇatva* there is acceptable (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the *Bhāṣya* itself has stated explicitly that in forms such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*, *ṇatva* is obligatory (as in *gargāṇāṃ bhagaḥ = gargabhagaḥ*; "she possesses this" = *gargabhagiṇī*), whereas in *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī*, *ṇatva* does not apply at all. Nor should it be argued that the prevention of *ṇatva* is achieved by accepting the inclusion [of the word] in the *kṣubhna*-group, as in the case of *gargabhago 'syā asti*.

If it is argued that even in a compound (*vigraha*), the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur because one must assume that only the word *gargabhaginī*, as qualified by a specific meaning, is read [in the *gaṇa-pāṭha*] there, we say: no. Since the introduction of that *vārttika* is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, that if the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the final of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) following a cause situated in a preceding member, then it must be the final of a compound nominal stem (*samāsa-prātipadika*) alone—it follows from that very restriction that the substitution of *ṇ* is prevented in cases such as *gargabhaginī*, according to the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*.

Since it is unnecessary to assume that the word *gargabhaginī* is included in the *kṣubhna*-class because it is intended as a *kṛt*-derivative, one should not argue that—given the possibility of the Vārttika serving a prescriptive (*vidhi*) purpose in syntactic unity with the present Sūtra—it is improper to describe it as having a restrictive (*niyama*) purpose.

For, within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the preceding member" (*pūrvapada*), the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is implied, but the base (*prātipadika*) itself is not the qualificand. Thus, by explaining the rule as "of the *n* at the end of a base that constitutes the subsequent member," the prevention of *ṇatva* in cases such as *gargabhaginī* is already established; therefore, the commencement of the Vārttika would otherwise be redundant.

For this very reason, in examples such as *māṣavāpāṇi*, since the *num* augment is part of the compound stem (*samāsaprātipadika*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is established by the rule regarding "the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikānta*) alone; thus, the inclusion of the mention of *num* indicates that the explanation [of the rule] must be understood as referring to the end of the nominal stem that constitutes the second member of the compound (*uttarapadabhūtaprātipadikānta*). This is because, according to that very explanation, in cases like *māṣavāpāṇi*, although the *num* is at the end of the compound stem, the mention of *num* is purposeful due to the absence of the end of the nominal stem *vāpa* which constitutes the second member. This is the position established in the *Vṛtti*, the *Padamañjarī*, and the *Manoramā*.

For in examples such as *prahiṇvan*, the mention of *nuṃ* is purposeful (*caritārtha*) because it serves to establish the *ṇatva* (nasalization) of the *m* following the root *hi*; thus, it has been stated that resorting to the aforementioned meaning is merely a matter of relying on the interpretation [of the rule]. Therefore, according to the maxim "when something is already established, a new formulation is for the sake of restriction" (*siddhe satyārambho niyamārthaḥ*), the present Vārttika [is intended to provide a restrictive rule regarding]... [the nasalization of the *m*].

It must be accepted that this [vārttika] is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the aforementioned restriction (*niyamārtha*). For this very reason, although the authors of the Bhāṣya—having demonstrated in other sections through subtle analysis and by means of alternative methods that the meaning stated in various vārttikas is untenable, and even while refuting other vārttikas—did not criticize this particular vārttika, despite its redundancy having been clearly established by authors such as the commentator Haradatta Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
Therefore, the fact that the present vārttika serves the purpose of the restriction we have stated is indeed the intention of both the authors of the Bhāṣya and the vārttikas.

There is no contradiction whatsoever; this is the direction [of the argument]. Both sūtras—"ekāj-uttarapade ṇaḥ" and "kumati ca"—are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the preceding optional rule (*vikalpa*) in cases such as *vṭr̥haṇau*, *kṣīravāṇī*, *kṣīrapeṇa*, *vastrayugiṇau*, *vastrayugāṇi*, and *vastrayugeṇa*. Thus, both [sūtras] serve equally to provide a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) even in compounds, by means of the sūtra "upasargādasamāse'pi. For instance, in *praṇamati* and similar forms, it serves as a mandatory rule for the compound as well. Furthermore, in *praṇāmaka* and similar forms where it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*), it serves as a mandatory rule. However, in your view, since the sūtra "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām amūrdhaprabhṛtibhyaḥ" would already be providing a mandatory rule, the *ṇatva* which was previously unobtained (*aprāpta*) is what is being enjoined there.

If, however, it were for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*), then that which was excluded by the restriction would be reintroduced (*pratiprasūyate*). In my view, because the injunction of *ṇatva* in the present context is necessarily for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*), and because the *vārttika* "when there is the status of being a subsequent member" (*uttarapadatve*) applies—since it is an injunction regarding the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*)—the *ṇatva* is enjoined there precisely where it was not otherwise obtained; this is the distinction. Regarding the term *saṃjñā*, under the view that "in each individual connection [the name] is established" (*yoge yoge siddha*), this sūtra has no scope. However, under the view that "in the context, the context is not established as valid" (*prakaraṇe prakaraṇamasiddham*), this very sūtra has scope due to its superior status (*paratva*); thus, both views are equal in this regard. [Examples: *hinumi nā*; *āni loṭ*.

The four sūtras beginning with *nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihantiyāti-vātidrātipsātivapati-vahati-śāmyaticinotidegdhiṣu* (Pāṇini 8.4.17) are also set aside by the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.4.18). This is because they serve the purpose of providing the rule for forms such as *pravavāṇi*, *praṇigadati*, and *praṇipacati*; thus, this point is equal for both views. Regarding the sūtra *aniteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19), its application for the sake of the rule in forms like *prāṇiṇīṣati* would, according to your view, also extend to forms like *prāṇanam*. In my view, however, there is a distinction: under the view that the rules are established through their connection (*yogāsiddha*), it does not apply because the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) has already established the result; whereas under the view that they are established by context (*prakaraṇāsiddha*), it does apply because it is subsequent [to the previous rule]. As for the sūtra *antaḥ*...

In rules such as *he prāṇi*, it is quite clear that [the present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning word-final [nasals]. The sūtra *ubhau sābhyāsasya* serves solely for prescriptive purposes in cases such as *prāṇīṇiṣati*. Furthermore, the sūtra *hanter atpūrvasya* is intended to ensure correctness in forms like *prahaṇyate*; however, in your view, it would apply even in cases such as *prahaṇanam*, whereas in my view, it does not apply—just as before—due to the distinction between the two positions. The sūtra *tvor va* is for the purpose of providing an option in cases such as *prahaṇvaḥ* and *prahaṇmaḥ*. [The rule applies] when there is no intervention (*antara*) by another element.

The two sūtras beginning with *ayanaṃ ca* constitute the instruction regarding internal elision (*antarhanana*). That "the region [ending] in *antara* and *ayana*" is for the purpose of prohibiting [elision] in that specific region; this is common to both views. As for the sūtra *chandasyṛdavagrahāt*, in your view it serves as an injunction (*vidhi*), whereas in my view it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—meaning that although [elision] occurs after a word ending in *ṛ* when it is the first member of a compound, it occurs only when that word is actually marked by an avagraha. Therefore, there is no contradiction with any of the sūtras starting from *ṛṣābhyām* and ending with *kṣubhnādiṣu ca*. Thus.

This is the secret. [The opponent asks: "Is not even a single sūtra rendered useless? [The author replies: Even so, in examples such as *āgnimāruta*, where the rule *devatādvandve ca* applies, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both members would not occur; for according to the application of the vārttika *uttarapadatve ca*, the portion that is the second member lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*). Having thus restated this doubt held by some, he refutes it: "But those who [hold that] there is lengthening in words such as *āgnimāruta*..."
They prattle that [the suffix] *ra* causes non-conflict; for them,
there is the acquisition of *vṛddhi* indicated by the long [vowel] in the Sūtra.
O Destroyer of Tripura, the foot of the wicked does not touch this place.

This is the intention: having raised the objection regarding [the form] *karṇo varṇalakṣaṇādityādi*, the commentators (the Bhāṣyakāras) offered a solution, stating that because of the explicit statement (*vacana*), the governing rule for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) will apply. Since this solution is equally applicable here as well, there is no problem.

Furthermore, the rule *cendravatā dvandve ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.21), which prescribes vṛddhi when the subsequent member begins with a vowel—as in *aindrāgnam* and similar forms—is already fulfilled by its specific purpose; for since the prescription of vṛddhi there is a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca* does not apply, and thus the status of the latter part as a *pada* is not lost.

And thus, it should not be said that the Sūtra has its purpose fulfilled by the Tantra, nor that there is no force in the statement. In the word *aindrāgna*, first of all, there is no difference in form whether the final member (*uttarapada*) undergoes Vṛddhi or not. A difference in form might be possible if there were a well-known Dvandva compound having a word denoting a deity with a non-*a*-final vowel as its prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the word *agni* as its subsequent member; however, such a Dvandva is not well-known. And because [the rule] *devatādvandve ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.141) mandates *ānanda* (i.e., *ān-*) for the prior member, it is unavoidable that the prior member [would have to end in *ā*].

Since it is impossible for [the word] to end in *ṛṇ*, or even if such a possibility existed, there is no established usage of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities connected with a *sūkta* or an oblation (*havir*); for it is stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that this rule for *vṛddhi* applies specifically to a *dvandva* of deities connected with a *sūkta* or an oblation. Consequently, in cases such as *āgneyabhūmi*, because of the prohibition "when *indra* follows" (*indre ca*), there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* at all. Therefore, since it is impossible for the rule prescribing *vṛddhi* to find its scope of application in the case of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) beginning with a vowel, one must state that the rule applies only to a subsequent member beginning with a consonant (*hal*), as in *āgnimāruta*.

And at that time, because the rule for *āpadādi* (words beginning with *ā*) applies when there is an *uttarapada* (subsequent member), the subsequent portion lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*) due to the operation of the *vāmatika* [principle]; thus, the force of the statement remains entirely unimpaired. However, if [the word] denotes a deity connected to a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*), and possesses a difference in form caused by *vṛddhi* when it has an *ajādi* (beginning with a vowel) as its *uttarapada*...

And how could any *dvandva* not be established in some way? Nevertheless, even though the force of the [general] rule is exhausted there, it is indicated that the Vārttika "if it is the status of being an *uttarapada*" (*uttarapadatve ca*)—which belongs under the governing heading of *uttarapada*—does not apply in cases such as *maitrāvaruṇam*, because the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "after a long vowel, in the case of Varuṇa" (*dīrghācca varuṇasya*) applies. Otherwise, that very rule would be purposeless. Thus, the Bhāṣya statement, "by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), the governing heading of *uttarapada* will take effect," should be understood as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of this kind of evidence as well. Now, even so, [in the case of] *rakṣābhyām*...

By the force of the term *samāna* (identical) in the Sūtra, the meaning is that it must be a word that is eternally identical—that is to say, incapable of being used in a mutually exclusive manner. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to a collection consisting of two words capable of being used in a mutually exclusive manner, such as in the expression *nāma nāma*. However, according to the Sūtra *pūrvapadāt*, the designation *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ* is intended as a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) for words such as *druṇasa* and others, because they consist of a collection of two words capable of being used in a mutually exclusive manner. Thus, by the Sūtra *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ...*, [the *ṇatva* is established].

He restates and refutes the doubt of certain [scholars] who argue that since the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) is not applicable by the sūtra, and because the intended meaning of "yuṣmad" (you) as defined by them—namely, being a single word distinct from the word containing the cause—is absent in the etymological (*yaugika*) word "Nārāyaṇa," the *ṇatva* cannot be established in the manner described. Some, by defining the term as a single compound word, have set out to exclude the application of the rule to words like "tvayyam" and "antakāntaka. However, setting aside their own view which is entangled in various alternatives, even they must accept what we have stated.

They descended to this state. It must be stated that "the unfitness for usage with mutual deviation" means precisely "the unfitness for usage when not co-occurring with one another," because any other kind of deviation is impossible in the present context. And that [unfitness] consists either in being distinct from a collection composed of two parts capable of being used without mutual co-occurrence, or being distinct from a collection composed of two such nominal stems (*prātipadika*), or being distinct from a collection composed of two such words (*pada*).

Nor is the first [alternative] tenable, because the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) would be impossible in cases such as *rāmeṇa*; for the stem-portion *rāma-* and the suffix-portion *-eṇa* are incapable of being used independently, since they are fit only for usage when not co-occurring with one another—as seen in examples like *rāmasya* and *kṛṣṇena*. Nor can indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) be defined as the state of being distinct from a collection consisting of two portions capable of independent usage; for "independence" means the state of not being co-occurrent with the other, and in cases such as *rāmeṇa*, the stem and the suffix are not used independently.

It might be argued that, according to the rule that "an affix should not be applied to a base that is not a base, nor should a base be employed where there is no affix," the aforementioned fault does not arise; however, this cannot be maintained, for in such cases as *rāmanāmni gandharvanagaram* ("the city of Gandharvas named Rāma"), the rule would result in the occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*).

This is because the collection of words ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is distinct from the collection consisting of the two parts—namely, *rāma* and *rāma*—which are individually eligible for separate usage. Furthermore, indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) cannot be defined as "not being part of a collection composed of two parts that are individually eligible for separate usage"; otherwise, in examples such as *rāmanāmāni*, [the definition would fail to apply to] such a collection...

It cannot be argued that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of being composed of a *dāya*-compound; for if that were the case, then in examples such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, since it is composed of a composite whole consisting of "mother-enjoyment" (*mātṛbhoga*). Nor can the second alternative hold, because it would lead to the undesired application of *ṇ* in cases such as *rāmanāmni gandharvanagare*, where there is a composite of *subanta* [words]...

There would certainly be the certainty of being distinct from a collection consisting of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that are fit for use in a construction where they do not deviate from one another; for this very reason, the third [alternative] is not tenable, because in a case such as *rāmanāmni*, the quality of being distinct from a collection consisting of two such words remains intact within the collection of inflected words (*subanta*). However, even though...

In the second alternative (*pakṣa*), [the *ṇatva*] would be established in the word "Nārāyaṇa" because it is distinct from a collection consisting of two such nominal stems (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, the third alternative is not tenable; for in cases such as "nāma nāmani," where there is a collection of inflected words (*subanta*) that is distinct from a collection consisting of two such words, the application of *ṇatva* is entirely unimpeded. Thus, the third alternative holds.

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), however, although the status of being a word (*padatva*) is possible for the initial portion by relying on the case-ending contained within it, the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule applies to the subsequent member by the Vārttika "and when there is the status of being a subsequent member" (*uttarapadasyottarapadatve ca*). Consequently, even in the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhyante*), in the case of [the name] Nārāyaṇa, which consists of two such words, [the rule does not apply].

In the word *śabda*, the substitution of *ṇ* is unimpeded; it is even more so when a *subanta* (inflected word) is being heard. Nevertheless, due to the aforementioned defect, all three positions are indeed flawed. Thus, even by those who maintain that "the word is an indivisible unit (*akhaṇḍa-pada*) on the strength of the mention of 'samāna'," and who—desiring to establish that the *nakāra* resides in an indivisible word by asserting that it lacks occurrence in a word distinct from the one possessing the cause—must necessarily admit that [the *nakāra*] lacks occurrence in a *prātipadika* distinct from the one possessing the cause, after having indicated the *prātipadika* by means of the word *pāśa*. And even so, [the flaw remains].

The meaning expressed is that [the rule applies] to the letter *na* when it possesses a suffix (*bhāvavataḥ*). And thus, one must state that the status of being Nārāyaṇa does not apply [here], because when a primary sense is possible, a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is improper; and furthermore, because in cases such as *bharāṇi*, *dharāṇi*, and *bhūdharāṇi*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, since in those instances the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself—along with its cause—is unestablished. Nor can it be argued that the nominal stem possessing the cause becomes established by taking a cause residing in another word, because it is impossible for a *na* residing in another word to function as a cause. Nor can it be argued that the cause consists in a suitability of form (*svarūpayogyatva*).

One must state that for this [rule] as well, it is "unimpaired" (*akṣata*); for if that were the case, the fault of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would arise even in examples such as *ghaṭena*. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault there because of the absence of the condition "following *ra* or *ṣa*" (*raṣābhyām paratva*); for if that were so, the fault of *ṇatva* would arise in cases such as *rāmāyām* and *etā*. Nor should it be argued that in those cases, the rule *prātipadikāntanuṃvibhaktiṣu ca* provides an optional (*vikalpena*) sublation due to its higher status; for even so, the fault of *ṇatva* would still arise for the *n* in the sentence *rāmaṃ kāmena*. Furthermore, that very thing which serves as the cause (*nimitta*) upon which the occurrence of *ṇatva* is predicated is itself the possessor of the cause (*nimittavat*).

In this context, it must be stated that the term *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is understood here due to its proximity; thus, in cases such as *bharāṇi*, the cause [for the application of the rule] resides in the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself. Consequently, the objection that the status of being a *prātipadika* is unestablished remains in force. Furthermore, even if one intends the meaning of "that which does not reside in a word distinct from the word possessing the cause" to be "that which does not reside in what is characterized by the status of being a *pada*," then, in the case of the word *nārāyaṇa*, although the status of being a *pada* is absent at that time because the word *ayata* functions as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), [the prohibition still applies].

It cannot be argued that the state of being a word (*padatva*) indeed exists [in the case of *nārāyaṇa*] and therefore the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur; for there is no evidence for such an intention [to treat it as a word], and because an "indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*) itself is difficult to define without first specifying a non-common, recurring property that serves as the delimiting factor (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka*) for that which is indicated. In reality, however, the nature of an indicator is "that which differentiates while being occasional. In the present case, since the word *ayana*—which is part of the term *nārāyaṇa*—is an "uttarapada," the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 8.4.39, *cau*] applies, and thus it never possesses the status of a word (*pada*). How, then, could the status of a word serve as its indicator?

It cannot be argued that "padavat" (like a word) does not intend to mean something similar to a word; for even though the element *ayana* within the word *nārāyaṇa* lacks the status of being a complete word (*pada*), it is similar to a word, and thus the occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would follow. This argument is invalid because there is no evidence for such an intended meaning. Furthermore, since similarity is constituted by difference, in cases such as *rāmanāma*, the rule for *ṇatva* would apply because it is a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*). Consequently, the Vārttika "not when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*) would not apply, and since the latter part [of the compound] possesses the status of a word, it would lack similarity to a word, resulting in the undesired application of *ṇatva*. Nor can it be said that [the term refers to] what is similar to a word...

It cannot be argued that "one or the other" (*anyatarat*) is intended by the term *devapada*, and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply; for in the word *nārāyaṇa*, the element *ayana* resembles a *pada*, and in names such as *rāma*, the latter part is a *pada*, so the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur. This is because if similarity were stated based on the property of being a *pada*, then even in cases like *rāmeṇa*, since the suffix *ṭā* is conditioned by its being a *pratyaya*, it would be similar to *pada*-distinct words like *ghaṭa*, and thus the substitution of *ṇ* would be unjustified. Furthermore, if similarity were stated on the basis of having the same phonetic sequence (*samānānupūrvikatva*), then in cases such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*... [the fault remains].

Because the latter portion [of the compound] "bhoginā" would incur the substitution of *ṇ* due to its having the same sequence of phonemes (*samānānupūrvikatva*) as the word "bhoginaḥ"—which occurs separately from words such as "bhinna-bhuja-ga"—if one were to state that [the rule applies] by qualifying it with both having the same meaning and the same sequence of phonemes, then the substitution of *ṇ* in the word "nārāyaṇa" would indeed be unavoidable. [Thus, the word] "nārāyaṇa" [would fall under the scope of the rule].

In the case of the word *tāyana*, if it were taken in its *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) sense, it would be meaningless; even if taken in its *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) sense, because its own meaning has been transferred to another meaning qualified by that [original] meaning, there is no similarity with the independent word *āyana* which possesses its own cause [of application] and is distinct from the word [in the compound]. Nor should it be argued that by the word "pada" (word), what is intended is "suitability for being a word," and since such suitability is common to both words and non-words, the aforementioned fault does not apply; for there is no evidence for such an intention, and furthermore, since no common delimitor of suitability (*yogyatāvacchedaka*) can be specified, suitability itself is difficult to define.

Therefore, by the word *pada*, only that which is technically defined as ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix should be understood; thus, the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *nārāyaṇa* is unimpeded. [Objection: Even so, in the rule *samānapade* ("in the same word"), by the force of the inclusion of the word *samāna* ("same"), one understands only "a non-compounded word" (*asamasta-padam*), and not "the occurrence in a word distinct from the word containing the cause.

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to assume that the infinite words such as *rāma-vana* and the word *nārāyaṇa*—when qualified by a specific meaning—belong to the *kṣubhna*-class (which prevents *ṇatva*). Consequently, just as in *rāmanāma* and similar cases, the substitution of *ṇ* would not be established even for the word *nārāyaṇa* when it is used etymologically (*yaugika*).

If this is argued, [we reply: such being the case, since the meaning obtained is "that which is a word distinct from a compound," in examples such as *rāmanāmanī*, even though the portion *rāmanāman* is a compound, the word consisting of the collection of *sub*-ending elements does not lose its status as being "distinct from a compound"; thus, the occurrence of *ṇatva* would follow. Nor can it be said that by the force of the mention of *samāna* (in Pāṇini 8.4.1), the meaning of "not a compound" is "distinct from the base (*prakṛti*) of a compound"—and thus there is no aforementioned inconsistency—because by the word "base" (*prakṛti*), it is not intended that only the base of a *sup* or *tiṅ* ending which serves as the locus for the technical designation "word" (*pada*) is meant, since that [base] is what is immediately present.

It should not be argued that in examples such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*, although the entire constituent part *mātṛbhoga* serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for the suffix *-kha*, it does not possess that status with respect to the case-ending (*sup*), and therefore the condition of being "different from that which has a compound as its base" (*samastaprakṛtikābhinnatva*) still exists; thus, the substitution of *ṇ* would not fail to occur. For what is your intention in saying this? Is it (1) being different from that *subanta* which has a compound as its base, or (2) being different from that *subanta* which ends in a case-ending having a compound as its base, or (3) being a *subanta* different from that which has a compound as its base?

Is "being in the same word" (*samānapadatva*) defined as: (1) being a *subanta* (inflected nominal) whose base (*prakṛti*) is a compound; or (2) being a *subanta* distinct from that [compound] whose base is a compound; or (3) being a *subanta* distinct from a *suptadanta* (an inflected nominal ending in a case-suffix) whose base is a compound? Not the first, because in cases such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, since the entire compound is [the base] relative to the suffix *khap*.

The second [alternative] is not tenable because [the word *gandharvanagara*] is a base form (*prakṛti*) and ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For [in a compound such as] *gandharvanagarakalpam* or *gandharvanagarajātīyam*, the occurrence of the suffix *tvā* would follow from the presence of the *n* belonging to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) ending in *-kalpa* or *-jātīya*. In that case, the word *gandharvanagara* and so forth would be the base form (*prakṛti*) only with respect to the secondary derivative suffixes such as *-kalpa*, and not the base form with respect to the case-suffix (*sup*).

The third [position] is not tenable because of the undesirable consequence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in examples such as *kāmena* in the two views regarding the meaning of the word; nor is the fourth, because of the failure to produce *ṇatva* in examples such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*; nor is the fifth, for the very same reason stated above, and because of the undesirable consequence of *ṇatva* in cases such as the conceptualization of a "city of Gandharvas" (*gandharvanagara*); furthermore, in all five of these positions, there is the failure to produce *ṇatva* for the *n* in compounds such as *priyakaraṇa*. Nor can one argue that since the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) are both attached to a single *uttarapada*, the rule does not apply to a word distinct from the original base of the compound, and thus *ṇatva* occurs here because the *uttarapada* remains intact.

It should be stated that [the objection] is easily refuted. Oh, what great delusion is yours! In that case, although the latter member of the compound *karaṇa* is distinct from its original form, there is an absence of "samānapadatva" (the state of being a single word with the same base) because the prohibition *uttarapadatve ca* prevents it from being a *pada*. Now, one might argue: "In examples such as *priyakaraṇa*, once the rule for *ṇatva* has been applied to the word *karaṇa*, the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) applies immediately thereafter; thus, at the very moment the *ṇatva* is about to take effect, the status of being an 'uttarapada' (final member of a compound) does not yet exist, and therefore the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not arise. [Response: This cannot be said. Why? Because the application of the designation *samāsa* occurs simultaneously with the application of the *ṇatva* rule. Consequently, even at the time the *ṇatva* is being introduced, the status of being an *uttarapada* is already present.
