In the view that grammatical derivation proceeds by successive analysis (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), when *priyakara* is analyzed as *priya-kara-aṇ-as*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would apply immediately after the designation of the compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*). It is precisely for this reason that, in the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3), the Vārttikakāra initiated the statement that the mention of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada-grahaṇa*) in that rule—intended to prevent the prohibition of *ṇ*-substitution established by the restriction in the same rule—is for the purpose of excluding cases where the *ṇ*-substitution applies to a word situated in the prior member of a *taddhita* derivative, such as *khārapāyaṇaḥ* and *karaṇapriyaḥ*. If the view of successive analysis (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*) is accepted, then even in examples like *karaṇapriya*, [the *ṇ*-substitution would occur].

If the word *karaṇa* were already a member of a compound (*samāsa*), the designation of "compound" would have already applied; consequently, since the status of being a "prior member" (*pūrvapadatva*) would not exist in the word *karaṇa* prior to the application of the compound designation, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would not operate, and thus that Vārttika would not serve the purpose of prohibiting [the suffix] when it occurs in a prior member. Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the view of "analytical derivation" (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*). For there is evidence in the form of the inclusion of the term "samartha" (semantically connected) in the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā*, which is formulated for the sake of producing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) from forms like *sa-utthitriḥ* and *paikṣamāṇiḥ* after the sandhi operations have taken place. To explain: *su*...

Regarding the word *utthita*: when [the suffix] *iñ* is applied after the root *iṅ* (to look), the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) will occur because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. However, since the cause for the form *ak* (the short vowel *a*) is on the verge of being destroyed, the rule *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation does not take effect if its cause is about to be destroyed) prevents the application of the long vowel rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*. Thus, once the initial *vṛddhi* has taken place, one would obtain forms such as *vṛtti*, *triḥ*, or *kṣamāṇiḥ*. To exclude these results, [the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke*] is formulated. And this [rule] is applicable only under the view of *vibhajyānvākhyāna* (analytical derivation), for otherwise, since the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would arise from the very point where the operation was already performed, both the *vṛddhi* and the long vowel would have already occurred.

Since there is no simultaneity [between the application of the rule for *vṛddhi* and the formation of the compound], the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is established without obstruction even prior to the production of the *taddhita* suffix; thus, forms such as *sa-utthitiḥ* would be free from any defect, and the requirement of the condition "having the same meaning" (*samartha-grahaṇa*) would consequently become redundant. Nor should it be argued that even under the view of "successive derivation" (*vibhajyānvākhyāna-pakṣa*), the requirement remains futile because the long vowel by position (*antaraṅga*) would apply first, after which the *vṛddhi* substitution would take effect. This is because, according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the rule that a cause for the destruction of a grammatical operation does not arise until after that operation has taken place) prevails over the *antaraṅga* rule.

Since the fact that a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) possesses the status of an exception (*bādhaka*) has been proclaimed in works such as the *Kaustubha*, the impossibility of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in forms such as *priyakaraṇa* remains unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that the word *pada* refers to a collection (*samudāya*), and thus the aforementioned impossibility does not arise; for if that were the case, *ṇatva* would undesirably apply in instances such as *rāmaṃ kāmena*, where there is a single collection distinct from its constituent base-forms. Therefore, even when one wanders everywhere, the definition of "within the same word" (*samānapada*) must be stated exactly as we have proposed, even by [the author of] the *Kāmenā*. And thus, [the forms] *śaṅkara-yāna* and so forth [are established].

Since there is no other way, one must indeed assume that words such as *arthaviśeṣaṇa* and the word *nārāyaṇa* belong to the *kṣubhnādi* group. However, even so, one might object: "In the eighth chapter, by not accepting that the rule *pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) is a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), the Vārttika—which states that the mention of 'the subsequent member' (*uttarapada*) in the context of a name (*saṃjñā*) is not for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of *ṣ*] when the preceding member ends in a *taddhita* suffix—would imply that if *pūrvapadāt* were a restrictive rule, the mention of 'the subsequent member' would have to be made in order to avoid the prohibition in cases such as *khārapāyaṇaḥ* and *karaṇapriyaḥ*. This is stated in the section on names (*saṃjñāyaṃ*)."

The *vārttika* "niyamapratiṣedha" (prohibition of the restriction) is because there is a prohibition of the restriction [itself]. For if that very sūtra were intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), then by the prohibition of *agaḥ* (non-*ga*-ending words), according to the maxim "the prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding," it would be the non-restriction itself that is prohibited. Consequently, in words such as *ṛgayanādi*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would be unavoidable by the sūtra *aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye’pi*; therefore, this present work is commenced to establish that [result], and not with the intention that the sūtra serves to accomplish something previously unestablished. Since the author of the *vārttikas* does not intend for any *vārttika* to be introduced for the sake of a new injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), [the phrase] "uttarapada... [is used].

[The author] refutes certain individuals who, suspecting that the justification for the substitution of *ṇ* being made on the basis of the *Vārttika* is actually contrary to the intention of the author of the *Vārttika*, [state as follows]. ||17||

Some [hold that] when the speech of the eighth-century Vārttika contradicts [the rule], as in the sūtra *pūrvapadāt* [Pāṇini 8.3.106], they would cite [an example]; we consider that such [an objection] is caused solely by a lack of understanding regarding the greatness of employing words that do not begin with a word [as a compound]. This is the intention: even if a certain Vārttika were commenced with the aim of being an *apūrvavidhi* (an original injunction), in cases such as *paramavāk*, the substitution of *kutva* and so forth [would still apply].

And since the *vārttika* "and when it is the latter member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*) must necessarily be commenced for the sake of rules concerning word-final elements (*padāntavidhi*), the phrase "not for rules concerning what is not the beginning of a word" (*apadādividhau*) is a pursuit of a circuitous path; for by means of extending the prohibition even to rules concerning the middle of a word (*padamadhyavidhi*), it serves to establish the *ṇatva* substitution in derivative words such as *nārāyaṇa*, etc. (the rest of the sentence is missing).

Since it must necessarily be stated that the author of the Vārttika intended the sūtra to have the sense of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) alone, rather than accepting it as having the sense of a restrictive rule (*niyama*); and because, if one were to rely on the grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*) "when the following member is a word and the operation concerns the end of a word," there would be no basis for the analysis of the compound *māṣakumbhaḥ* (a jar of beans) as *māṣāṇāṃ kumbhaḥ*, [and] its derivative *tasyāpaḥ* (the water of that).

In the case of *yaṇe māṣakumbhavāpena*, since there is an absence of being a rule conditioned by the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*), the prohibition [contained in] *uttarapadatve ca* does not apply; consequently, because the prohibition of *ṇatva* contained in *padavyavāye 'pi* would otherwise take effect, the phrase *apadādividhau* is intended to prevent the application of that prohibition of *ṇatva* in the rule *padavyavāye 'pi*.

Since following a circuitous path has been discarded, it is not possible [to justify] the establishment of the *ṇatva* (nasalization) in words such as *yaugikanārāyaṇa* based on the rule *padavyavāye 'pi*; for in the foundational treatises (*ākaragrantha*), the example "not in the case of *māṣakumbhavāpa*" is clearly intended to show that the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the sowing (*vāpa*) of a jar (*kumbha*)" (*kumbhasya vāpaḥ kumbhavāpaḥ*) and "the sowing of a jar of beans" (*māṣāṇāṃ kumbha-vāpaḥ*). This is evident from the *Padamañjarī* and other works. Furthermore, it must be stated that because the word *kumbha* cannot function as the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of sowing, it is dependent upon the word *māṣāṇām* and thus lacks syntactic independence (*asamartha*); consequently, the word *kumbha* cannot form a compound with the word *vāpa*.

Since resorting to analyses such as *kumbhasya vāpaḥ* (the sowing of a jar) for the compound *yogena* is improper, one must instead resort to the analysis *māṣāṇāṃ kumbhaḥ* (a jar of beans), and so forth. For this very reason, in the example *caturaṅgayogena*, which shares the same grammatical status (*yogakṣema*) as the present example, the *Manoramā* analyzes it as *catvāry aṅgāny asya caturaṅgam, tena yogaḥ*. Thus, because the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *padavyavāye’pi* does not apply here, and since that [analysis] is not accepted by the author of the *Ākāra* (Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita), the alternative path [proposed by others] is for the sake of that [specific point].

Because the capacity [of the rule] for following [the preceding] is exhausted; or, even if it were somehow exhausted in that manner, nevertheless, since the *vārttika* beginning with "because there is a prohibition regarding the technical term (*saṃjñā*) by way of restriction" employs the term "restriction," which implies the alternative of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), otherwise the inclusion of that term would be meaningless—since the status of being for the sake of restriction is invariable [in such cases]. Therefore, the meaning stated by us is indeed approved by the author of the *vārttika*. [Objection: Even so, in words such as *ṛgayanādi*, there is an absence of obligatory compounding (*nityasamāsa*).

Since the absence of being a single word (*padatva*) has been explicitly stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya, it is directly contrary to their intention to establish the status of "always being a single word" for the etymological (*yaugika*) term *nārāyaṇa*, which shares the same conditions as that [absence]. For the Bhāṣya on the eighth [chapter] regarding the restriction in technical names (*saṃjñā*) states: "If there were a prohibition of *ṇatva* [in the case of a name], this prohibition of the restriction would have to be understood as applying to the [word] *aga*. What is the fault in that? There would be the undesirable consequence of *ṇatva* occurring there. In that case, by the preceding rule, *ṇatva* would necessarily apply both when it is a name and when it is not a name. [Objection: It is established by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*). [Response: By splitting the rule... [and so forth]. Thus, the argument fails to account for the authorial intent.

The rule will be formulated as *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (after a prior member [ending in a vowel], when a technical name is formed). From this, it follows that after a prior member ending in *bha*, there is either a prohibition or a non-prohibition of all instances where the substitution of *ṇ* would otherwise occur. As in the case of the technical name *sarvanāman* (all-noun), what is the purpose of the prohibition? Why does the substitution of *ṇ* not occur here, just as it does in the case of the technical name *sarvanāman*? And how was it stated regarding the technical name *sarvanāman*? It was said that the absence of *ṇ* occurs due to a specific grammatical convention (*nipātana*) in the definition of *sarvanāman*. But if such a convention is established there—namely, "those beginning with *sarva* are *sarvanāman*"—then what is the convention being applied here now?

Is there an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) here? [One might ask: Is it not the case that [the rule] *arṇa-gayanādibhyaḥ* does not apply here, or rather, that the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) would not even be obtained by the preceding rule? What is the reason? It is said [in the rule] "within the same word" (*samānapade*), and this is not a single word (*samānapada*) when a compound (*samāsa*) has been formed. Only that which is always a single word is [truly] a single word; however, this is not always a single word. Should this be stated? No, for how could it be understood without being stated? By the force of the mention of "same" (*samāna*). For if it were to apply where something is both the same and not the same, the mention of "same" would be purposeless. And this has been explained by Kaiyaṭa as "same."

Furthermore, in the compound *padam eva*, when there is a requirement to distinguish between the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), there exists the state of being situated in separate words; thus, the application of the rule for *ṇatva* would not arise. Consequently, this sūtra is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). Alternatively, if it were for the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*), how then could *ṇatva* occur in the case of *khārapārāyaṇa*, given that the word *khara* [is also involved]?

Since the letter *r* resides within that [word], it does not even exist as being situated in the same word (*samānapada*) as the *n*; regarding this, they say: where there is a deviation from the condition of both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*) residing in the same word, there is an absence of *ṇatva*; however, in this case, although there is a deviation regarding the *r*, there is no deviation regarding the *n* residing in the same word.

The substitution of *ṇatva* occurs when there is a "commonality" (*samāna*) and when [the word] is "pada," because it is impossible for a cause and its effect to exist when neither is situated within a *pada*. Therefore, since commonality is already established by the force of the context through the intention to express singularity, the meaning is that the term "commonality" (*samāna-śruti*) should be understood as having the restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇa*) accepted; such is the doubt to be raised.

He refutes [the objection]: "The interpretation of the word *nārāyaṇa* in the eighth-century commentary (*Mahābhāṣya*), which you have joined with the word *tvayi*, is contradictory. The meaning is this: "This [interpretation] of the foolish-minded one is indeed rendered defective by the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of that [work], whose sound is the *jhalajhala* tinkling of the anklets upon the feet of Your Majesty—the great sage Patañjali, who is an incarnation of the King of Serpents serving as the anklets for Your lotus-feet. From the lotus-mouth of that lord of sages, there issued forth the Great Commentary (*Mahābhāṣya*) itself, which is like a flood of words; the 'bolt' (*argala*) mentioned therein refers to the introduction of that work. Thus, it is caused by a deficiency in the knowledge of its true nature. The underlying intention is as follows: the point I have stated...

Furthermore, in order to avoid contradicting the intention of the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya regarding the instruction that "in the case of a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), [the *naṭ* substitute applies] when the following member has been previously cited as an example," one must postulate a different intention for the Bhāṣya in question. For instance, although the suffix *ṇatva* in words such as *ṛgayanam* is prevented by the inclusion of *nipāta*, under the view that the rule *pūrvapadāt* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—which was intended by the Teacher who composed the sūtra *agaḥ* for modern technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*) like *ṛṅnaga* and others accepted as correct—the following would apply.

Having raised the doubt in one's mind that the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is unavoidable by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), and having set aside the aforementioned defect by relying on the fact that the [Vārttika] indicator (*jñāpaka*) relates to the general case—that there is no *ṇatva* for a *na* following a prior member ending in *ga*—one must nevertheless consider that, in reality, in forms such as *nṛbhiḥ* and *nṝbhiḥ*, since the doubling (*dvirvacana*) occurs in place of the eighth-case dual suffix, it is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, because they belong to the same word (*samānapada*), the condition of "not being the same" (*asamānatva*) does not exist; thus, the restrictive rule "from a prior member" (*pūrvapadāt*) does not apply, and the substitution of *ṇ* remains unavoidable.

Therefore, in the expression *samānapade*, "constant co-occurrence in a single word" (*nitya-samānapadyam*) must necessarily be intended. Consequently, the Sūtra becomes prescriptive in its purpose. Thus, among those words whose prior member ends in the letter *g*, in certain cases such as the words *ṛṅ* and *nagara*, because the rule for *ṇatva* is a rule governing the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), the prohibition [of *ṇatva*] by the rule *uttarapadatve ca* does not apply. Since the status of being a word (*padatva*) is based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) of the subsequent part, there is an absence of the condition of "being situated in a constant single word" (*nitya-samānapadasthatva*), which consists in the absence of occurrence in a word distinct from the word containing the cause [the *g*]. Therefore, *ṇatva* does not occur at all.

With the intention that [the rule] "it occurs" (*pravartate*) applies, he says "or rather, not here again," and so forth. Here, the word *aga* is intended as the counter-example (*vyāvartya*). The meaning is: among certain words such as *ṛṅnagara* and others, which are placed within the scope of the compound *aga*-ending words; in the case of words like *ṛgayanādi*, because the prescription of *guṇa* is a rule concerning what is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādividhi*), the prohibition "and when there is the status of being a subsequent member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*) applies. Consequently, since the condition consists in the absence of occurrence in a word distinct from the [original] word—which possesses the cause—the state of not being situated in the same word (*asamānapadasthatva*) exists, and thus the substitution of *ṇa* (*ṇatva*) would be unavoidable. To prevent that, [the word] *aga* [is used].

This derivation [of *vedya*] from *arṇa*, *gayana*, and so forth, must necessarily be resorted to as a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). Therefore, the statement that the word *gait* in the Bhāṣya passage regarding *vedya* and others is intended as a rejection [of the rule] is not correct. Furthermore, in the Vārttika *uttarapadatve ca* and its corresponding Bhāṣya, because [the application of the rule] is swallowed by the impossibility [of the condition] while [the person] is living, one might object: "It has never been observed before for you to impose a different intended meaning through a forced interpretation upon a sequence of the Bhāṣya which appears to have its literal sense. To this, we reply: No, for there are many [instances...].

Regarding the [objection] concerning *labdheḥ*: for instance, in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *halantyam*, once the *it*-designation of the letter *l* in the rule *hal* has been established, the formation of the *hal*-pratyāhāra occurs via the rule *ādirantyena saha*. Once that is established, the status of being a *hal* (consonant) for the letter *l* in the rule *laṇ* is established; and once that is established, the *it*-designation of the letter *l* in the rule *halantyam* is established by its mention in the rule *hal*. Keeping in mind what Kaiyaṭa has explained as this circularity (*anyonyāśraya*), one might raise the doubt that the *it*-designation does not even apply to the letter *l* itself. Anticipating this, [the author states] the rule *halantyam*... [and so forth].

Having formed a collective *dvandva* compound as "cal ca hal ca" (the vowels and the consonants), the final *l* is elided by the rule for the elision of the final member of a *saṃyoga*; thus, the rule "halantyam" is established. Consequently, the designation *it* must first be applied to the letter *l*, so that the *pratyāhāra* "hal" becomes possible; this is one resolution [of the objection]. Alternatively, there is another resolution: "hasya l" forms a single *tatpuruṣa* compound in the neuter gender, while the other *pratyāhāra* ("hal") is masculine. Then, by the rule "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām," a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed. Thus, by means of the word "hal" in the form of a *tatpuruṣa*, the letter *ha* [is understood] as being near [to the *l*].

Having stated the second resolution—that the *it*-designation (*itsaṃjñā*) is to be applied to the *ḷ* sound occurring in the rule *hal* (Pāṇini 1.3.3), and that the *pratyāhāra* "hal" is thus established—[the author] then states the third resolution: "Alternatively, this [mention of *ḷ*] is the inclusion of the *ḷ* sound itself as a subordinate element; in that case, since it is taught [in the alphabet], the *it*-designation will apply to it by the rule 'that which is nasalized in the instruction is called *it*'. This has been explained by Kaiyaṭa in his commentary on the rules *śaṣasar hal* and *halantyam*, where he notes that just as in the case of the mention of *tavalkāraḥ*, the substitution of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the *ḷ* sound and its status as a short vowel (*alparatva*) are effected there.

The Bhāṣya statement, "In the case of the instruction [of the vowel *ḷ*], the designation *it* will apply by the rule 'an *it* is that which has an *anunāsika* [dot above]'," is not tenable according to its literal meaning, because the circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) remains as it was. To explain: if the designation *it* applies to the *ḷ*-vowel, then the pratyāhāra *hal* exists; and if that pratyāhāra *hal* exists, then the *it*-designation applies to the *c* in *ai au c*; if that *it*-designation applies, then the pratyāhāra *aj* exists; and if that pratyāhāra *aj* exists, then by the rule "an *it* is that which has an *anunāsika* [dot above] in the instruction," the *it*-designation applies to the *ḷ*-vowel.

Thus, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, this Bhāṣya—while intending to provide the authoritative proof for the designation *it* for the sound *ḷ*—ultimately abandons the rule "In the *upadeśa*, an *anunāsika* [nasal] vowel is designated as *it*" because that proof is invalidated by the aforementioned mutual dependence. Instead, it concludes by relying on the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the form of the author of the Sūtras’ own usage, namely the expression "puṣādi" in the rule "ḷditām" (Pāṇini 3.1.55). For it was precisely in this way that Kaiyaṭa explained it. If that is so, then [the status of *ḷ* as an *it*] follows from the indicative evidence in the rule "ḷditām."

It has been explained there that the intention of the venerable Bhāṣyakāra is that since the designation "rasī" will serve its grammatical function before a vowel (*aci*), there is no mutual dependency (*itaretarāśrayatva*). However, by employing the word *bhagavat*—which denotes one who is fully endowed with the sixfold sovereignty (*aiśvaryādi-ṣāḍguṇya*)—in this statement of the Bhāṣya, it is revealed through such a usage that not even a trace of negligence is possible; rather, it is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhi*) intended for another purpose. This should be observed in many instances by those who know the true nature of the Bhāṣya.

I shall desist here for fear of prolixity; therefore, it is established that even for those who follow the *Mahābhāṣya*, it is indeed appropriate to describe [the passage] as having another meaning. In reality, however, in accordance with the previously cited *Vārttika* and the *Śikṣā-bhāṣya*, the eighth-century *Bhāṣya* must be understood as a *abhyupetyavāda* (a provisional argument). Thus, regarding the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, the *Bhāṣyakāra*—without stating the purpose of the rule itself through the preceding and following arguments such as "for what purpose is the mention of *ik*? To exclude *āt* and the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) and semivowels (*vyañjana*)"—merely says "the mention of *ik*. This is the appearance of the *Bhāṣyakāra*.

The subsequent portion of the Bhāṣya—which states that since the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [in P. 1.1.3] is already understood from the rule for *māna*, their re-mention here is redundant—is clearly an argument made on a concessive basis (*abhyupetya-vāda*). This is because, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *e oṅ* (P.

1.1.50), having raised the objection that in forms such as *khaṭvevandraḥ* and *khaṭvevādakam*, there would be the undesired application of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* due to the proximity (*āntarya*) of substituends consisting of three or four morae (*mātrā*), the author introduces the Vārttika "when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are followed by *t*" (*tapare guṇavṛddhī*) to [reconcile this with] the rules *vṛddhir ādaic* (P. 1.1.1) and *adeṅ guṇaḥ* (P. 1.1.2).

Having resolved that by the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), which states that a sound followed by *t* denotes its own duration, the designations of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* apply to vowels of three and four morae respectively—as seen in the two sūtras *aij* and *endau*—one might raise the following objection: "If a sound followed by *t* were to denote its own duration even beyond [the immediate vowel], then in the rule *ṛdorap* (3.3.57), the suffix *ap* would apply only here [to forms like *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ*], but it would not apply in cases such as *laḥ*. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "This is not so because of *takāra*..."

"What then? It is the letter *da*. This objection has been answered; for upon a careful consideration of the meaning of the section (*phakkikā*) in the Bhāṣya, it is understood that it is the letter *ta* alone that serves as the indicator of that time (the duration), and not the letter *da*. However, in the Bhāṣya concerning the svarita accent, there is a concern regarding the svarita of the affix *ti* in examples such as *kirati* and *tirati*, on the grounds that [if the rule applied], the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* would not apply.

Having resolved [the objection] by introducing the *vārttika* "pratyayagrahaṇam" and by relying on the *paribhāṣā* that when both a suffix (*pratyaya*) and a derivative (*apatya*) are mentioned, only the suffix is to be understood; and having then offered another solution by resorting to reduplication (*dvitva*), stating that the fault does not apply because it is the letter *ta* [that is doubled] and not *da*, he refutes both the *vārttika* and the *paribhāṣā*.

Having raised the objection that, after [the substitution of] *khyā*, when resorting to the vowel *da* (in *adas*), there would be a long *ī* by virtue of internal similarity (*āntarya*) due to the absence of the *tapara* designation, the solution is given that because it is being taught as a *bhāvyamāna* (an element undergoing grammatical operation), it does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*). For if this were so, then in the rule *hyadaso serdādudomaḥ*, the vowel *u*—being a *bhāvyamāna*—would likewise not include its homogeneous counterparts.

Then, one might object that in cases such as *amum*, the substitution of *u* would occur in exactly this way, but not in cases such as *amūbhyām*. To address this, as if in response to such an objection, it is established in the rule *id* (Pāṇini 7.1.11) that even an *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) is a grasper of its own class (*savarṇagrāhaka*), by means of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) consisting of the addition of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*). Having thus provided the solution, [the author] then cites *dyubhiḥ* and *aktubhiḥ*.

In the rule *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), having raised the objection that the vowel *u* would result [from the substitution of *u* for the final *v* of *div*], it was argued: "This is not the letter *t*; what then? It is the letter *d*. How then can the statement regarding its being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of what was previously mentioned be justified if *d* follows? Having raised this doubt, it was resolved by stating that in the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), the letter *d* is also indicated as being subject to the process of *cartva* (the substitution of *c*). Upon a thorough examination of the Bhāṣya, since the letter *d* is also understood to have the same duration (*tatkālatva*) as the *t*, even if one resorts to the letter *d* in the rule *ṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57), forms such as *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ* remain difficult to justify. Thus, when there is a mutual contradiction between two such Bhāṣya passages, the principle of *asañjāta-*... [is applied].

One must necessarily accept that the subsequent commentary (*uttarabhāṣya*) is a formal debate (*vāda*), either by following the preceding commentary (*pūrvabhāṣya*) which is stronger due to its contradiction [with the *tapara* rule], or by accepting the latter itself; and this is logical because the elision of the letter *d* in the *tapara-sūtra* would otherwise be purposeless. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, it would be impossible to describe the *daparatva* (the state of being followed by *d*) in the rule *diva udi* as having the aforementioned indicatory force (*jñāpakatva*). For even there, one resorts to *taparatva* itself. Nor does it follow that the accentuation of the *ti* suffix (*titsvara*) would apply there, because that [undesired] application is precluded precisely by the *pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*. Therefore, [this interpretation is supported] by the very *bhāṣya* on the *titsvara* and *svarita* rules.

It should be understood that [the status of] being an *abhyupetyavāda* (a provisional or concessive argument) applies to the *bhāṣya* on the rule in question, but not to the *bhāṣya* situated on the subsequent sūtra. Now, one might object: even so, in accordance with the *bhāṣya* on the eighth [chapter], let the very text of the *bhāṣya* and *vārttika* on the first [chapter] be assumed to be an *abhyupetyavāda*; for we see instances elsewhere where, in order to conform to the accentuation (*svara*) of a later *bhāṣya*, the status of an *abhyupetyavāda* is attributed to an earlier *bhāṣya*. For example, in the *bhāṣya* on the *yathāsaṅkhya* sūtra regarding the expression *nāḍīmuṣṭyoḥ*, although there is a rejection of the connection according to numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), [the point remains].

In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* on the rule "śca," since the absence of a correspondence between the respective numbers (*yathāsaṅkhya*) is established there, it has been stated in the *Manoramā* that the *bhāṣya* on the rule containing the *yathāsaṅkhya* principle merely establishes the possibility [of the application]. One should not argue: "In the *Kaustubha* on the *yathāsaṅkhya* rule, it was said that the *bhāṣya* on the rule concerning 'nāḍī' and 'muṣṭi' must be considered doubtful and refers to another opinion, because it contradicts the *bhāṣya* on the *yathāsaṅkhya* rule itself. This is because [the *bhāṣya*] proceeds by first presenting examples such as *nāḍindhamaḥ*, *nāḍindhayaḥ*, *muṣṭindhamaḥ*, and *muṣṭindhayaḥ*.

If it is argued that—since the Bhāṣya there, which intends to negate the application of *yathāsaṅkhya* (correspondence by order), is indicated by the subsequent Vārttika beginning with "the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are *khal*, *go*, *ratha*, etc., and *traka*, *ḍya*," and since that Bhāṣya is intent merely on removing the meaning of the Vārttika "svaragrastaṃ dhamodheṭo nāḍīmuṣṭyośca" while being devoid of insistence on the attainment of *yathāsaṅkhya* therein—it is improper to consider that Bhāṣya as an exposition of another view (*matāntara*) because it is not suitable to establish such a position; therefore, the passage in the *Manoramā* regarding that is itself unobjectionable (*ajasya*)—then [we reply]: True, there is a lack of internal consistency (*asvarasa*) in that initial Bhāṣya.

Even though it might be possible to establish that [the *bhāṣya*] has already dealt with the matter—since it is devoted solely to resolving the meaning of the *vārttika* that was swallowed up [by the *sūtra*], and because it stands within the "fist" of the *nāḍī-sūtra* which cannot be interpreted otherwise—nevertheless, in the present case, the *vārttika* "uttarapadatve ca" and its explanatory *bhāṣya*, which function with this as their primary intent (*aidaṃparyeṇa*), cannot be interpreted otherwise. These two are not yet contradicted and are impossible to interpret differently. Therefore, by means of the eighth-lesson *bhāṣya*—which possesses no such intent, can be interpreted otherwise, and is already contradicted—one must [regard the former] as a concession argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

Since reasoning itself is impossible [in this case], he says with the intention that this is merely an *abhyupetyavāda* (a concessionary argument), accepting for the sake of discussion the very passage from the commentary on the eighth [chapter] of the Sūtra: "In many places, the words of the later commentary are seen to contradict the ancient [tradition]... [He continues: "It was rightly stated by Śambhu Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita that this is a proceeding based on boldness (*prauḍhi*); therefore, what fault is mine? But even so, since the author of the Bhāṣya follows the literal sense of the statement, and since this [interpretation] is not perceived as being ungrammatical... [The ellipsis remains].

Having thus imagined the intended meaning of that [text] through such a method of interpretation, the justification of its correctness is something never before seen anywhere; therefore, he says this as a bold challenge: "O Śambhu Patañjali, speaking exactly as you have heard [the tradition], that blindness toward the state of being a fool... in many places by Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita, even this unbridled power of yoga resides in you today. The underlying intention is this: since such a method has been demonstrated by Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita himself in many places, it is not [something] unseen.

Because the form *cara* itself has been observed [in usage], for instance, in the rule *bhrasjoropadhayonyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), which prescribes the optional substitution of *ra* for the penultimate vowel of the root *bhrasj* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix—such as in *bhṛṣṭa*, *bhraṣṭa*, *bhraṣṭavān*, etc.—the Bhāṣya first states that "by prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), there is *saṃprasāraṇa*" in order to prevent the optional occurrence of *ra* in forms like *bhraṣṭa* and *bhraṣṭavān*. Immediately thereafter, it introduces the Vārttika: "It is established by the statement of *rasoḥ*," explaining that in the case of *sāckara*, either the *pha* or the *sa* becomes *ṛ*; thus, there is a conflict between *saṃprasāraṇa* and the change to *ṛ*.

Having stated this as a specific rule (*viśeṣa*), even so, because the suffix *sic* takes precedence over the *luṅ* [augment], once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, the form *īsa-* would not exist; consequently, since the substitution of *ṛ* would not apply, the form would simply be *abhārṣīt*. Therefore, one must state that here the substitution of *ṛ* occurs by means of a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). And thus, we are not released from prior conflicts in all cases; furthermore, the sūtra is split, whereas in cases such as *vāstubhraṣṭa*, because the *samprasāraṇa* is obligatory, the substitution of *ṛ* would occur first in the alternative case.

The objection raised here is merely that the body of the sūtra involves a contradiction; for in the view of the supreme opponent (*paramata-pakṣe*), in the case of the periphrastic perfect (*apilliṭ*), forms such as *babharjatuḥ* and *babharjuḥ* are established. Furthermore, due to the optional application of the rule "san-sani-antar-dhī-bhrajjat-dan-bhṛ-bhū-śri-svṛ-yū-ūrṇu-bhara-jñapi-sanām" (Pāṇini 6.4.124), one understands that forms such as *bibharkṣati* (in the desiderative), *abharkṣīt* (in the aorist with *liṅ* and *sic*), and *abhārji* (in the periphrastic aorist with *caṅ* following a causative suffix) are correct. However, in the alternative view where the substitution of *ṛ* occurs, in the periphrastic perfect one would have *babhṛjatuḥ*, and in the desiderative, *bibhṛkṣati* (since it begins with a consonant).

And because the suffix *san* is marked with the *kit* indicator, [the forms] *bhṛkṣīṣṭa* and *abhṛkṣīt* are derived; for, according to the rule "the *liṅ* and *sic* suffixes are *kit* in the *ātmanepada*," the *kit* designation applies. Consequently, since the rule *ur ūd* (Pāṇini 7.2.41)—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ir ar ārām*—takes effect when a *ṇi*-causal followed by *caṅ* is present, it is understood that these [forms] are grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*). Thus, if the authors of the Bhāṣya intended that forms such as *babhrajatuḥ* and others are incorrect, while forms such as *babharjatuḥ* and others mentioned previously are correct, then another effort must be made to establish this result.

In the view of the *Ṛbhava* school, the meaning is that [the forms] are not correct (*asādhu*), yet they do not perform [that function]. Therefore, by considering the literal statement of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, it is obtained that even for those forms intended as correct by the *Sūtrakāra*, such as *babharjatuḥ* and so forth, there is indeed only incorrectness (*asādhutvam*). Since the authority of the sages increases in descending order, this being the case, one must necessarily accept the hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisandhi*) of the *Bhāṣya*: "In order to achieve consistency with the *Sūtrakāra*, the *Sūtra* is split. Thus, according to the literal statement...

Relying on the strength of the [author's] hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisandhi*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* intended even to refute the objection regarding the occurrence of undesirable forms such as *babhrajuḥ*; thus, it has been stated in the *Manoramā*: "Whether forms such as *babhrajuḥ* possess an internal structure (*sāvayava*) or not... In this way, [the reduplication occurs] twice.

In the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "na cī" (Pāṇini 6.1.39), regarding the word *dukṣu*; and in the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "necci" (Pāṇini 7.2.8), regarding the word *dukṣu*: [one says] *cukṣāvayiṣati*. From the root *uḍ*, as in "he acts like a star," *uḍavati*, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and then the desiderative suffix (*san*), one says *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*. However, from the root *tu* as specified in the sūtra "tu-ru-śamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.3.95), when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and then the desiderative suffix (*san*), one says *tūtāvayiṣati*. From the root *śvi* with the causative suffix (*ṇau*): [one says *śeśāvayiṣati*].

Regarding the form *caṅkramyate* (from *kram*), and *śuśāvayiṣati* (from *śo*) where there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the suffix *ṇic*: since the *ṇic* is not the cause for reduplication, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) does not apply to the reduplication. Consequently, one might suspect that after the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *āv* [for *śo*], when reduplication occurs, the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79) would cause the change of the short *a* in the reduplicated syllable to *u*. Anticipating this objection, it is established by the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini 7.4.80)—which includes the letter *ja* from the *vargapratyāhāra*—that when reduplication is to be performed, the substitute *āv* for the root *śo* before the suffix *ṇic* behaves as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*). Thus, forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati* are successfully derived. For indeed, according to the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare sani*, when a suffix beginning with *pu*, *ya*, *ṇ*, or *ja* follows, and provided no other sound intervenes, [the *u* of the reduplicated syllable becomes *ū*].

If that which is a member [of a word] were to undergo the repetition of its own parts when it is a vowel, then there would be *itva* (the substitution of *i*) in cases such as *apīpavat*, *abibhavat*, *amimavat*, *adhīyavat*, *arīravat*, *alīlavat*, and *ajījavat*. In these examples, although the status of being like the *san* suffix (*sanvadbhāva*) applies by the rule "when *caṅ* follows, provided there is no elision of *a*", and although *itva* would be established here in all these examples simply by the rule "for *a* after *san*"—since the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) occurs in *ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ* after the internal operation of *vṛddhi* and *ādeśa* have been applied—nevertheless, the rule "of *oḥ puyaṇjyapare" is stated for the sake of establishing forms such as *pipaviṣate* and *yiyaviṣati*.

Only this much must necessarily be formulated in the Sūtra; for, when the optional *iṭ* augment is applied by the two rules "smi-pūṅ-rañja-svañjām sani" and "san-i-va-nta-dha-srajs-da-nbhu-śri-savṛ-yūrṇu-bhara-jñapi-sanām," the rule "a-caḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau" (P. 1.1.57) applies to the reduplication. Consequently, since the vowel 'a' is absent in the reduplicated syllable, the rule "asan-yataḥ" (P. 7.2.62) does not apply. Thus, even without the inclusion of the letter 'ja' from the *varga* (consonant class) or the *pratyāhāra*, forms such as *abibhavat* are established. Therefore, its inclusion serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned meaning.

Having thus resolved [the objection] by stating "it is indeed so," and having avoided over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *adidvat* and *akit-tat*—on the grounds that the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* applies only where the vowel *a* is heard in the subsequent portion following the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), and not elsewhere—the following are cited as the purposes of the rule (*sūtra-prayojana*):

*papatuḥ*, *tasthatuḥ*, *jaghnatuḥ*, *āṭiṭat*, *āśiśat*, and *cakratuḥ*. [These examples illustrate the necessity of the rule for the application of: (1) the elision of *ā* by *āto lopa iṭi ca*; (2) the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by *gamahanajanakhanaghasāṃ lopaḥ kṅiti*; and (3) the elision of the *ṇi*-affix by *ṇeraniṭi*.

Having stated that because of the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* regarding both the elision of the suffix *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) and the *yaṇ*-substitution by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the process of doubling (*dvirvacana*) proceeds without obstacle; he then explains that this is set aside by the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior-precedence) *vārttika* to be recited in the sixth book, which states: "Doubling [takes precedence] over *yaṇ*, *ay-ava-āy-āva*, elision (*lopa*), elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), elision of the suffix *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*), *ka*, *kit*, and *rutva*. Thus, in examples such as *dadhyatra*, the *yaṇ* substitution has its scope; in *āyakaḥ* and *lavanaṃ lāvakaḥ*, the *ay-ava-āy-āva* substitutions have their scope; in *godaḥ*, the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) has its scope; and in *śleṣmaghnaḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) has its scope, as does the suffix *kāraṇā*.

In examples such as *ityādau ṇilopaḥ* (the elision of *ṇi* in *nivṛtta*), *putratvaṃ ca* (and the state of being a son), and *etāni nava*, [these rules] are superseded by the rule for doubling (*dvitva*)—which has its own scope—as seen in *bindurityādau*. Furthermore, in cases such as *kratucikāya lulāva*, *cikayitha*, *lulavidha*, *papatuḥ*, *jaghanatuḥ*, and *āṭiṭat*, [the rules regarding] the *kikin* suffixes after the roots *gam*, *han*, and *jan* (as per *ādigamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca*) are superseded by the prohibition of the preceding operation (*pūrvaghapratiṣedha*). Having explained that in these cited examples, the doubling occurs first due to the "priority of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), making the [separate] sūtra redundant, [the author] subsequently...

Even if forms such as *padatuḥ* are established under the view of "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), in cases such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*, *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*, *tutāvayiṣati*, and *śuśāvayiṣati*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *ādeśa* would occur first because they are internal (*antaraṅga*) and thus not subject to conflict. Once these have been applied and the reduplication (*dvitva*) follows, the rule *sanyataḥ* would require that an *ik* vowel be heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). To prevent this, another rule must be stated: "The substitute for *o* and *au* occurs [before the reduplication], and for the reduplicated syllable beginning with *ca*, *ṭu*, *tu*, or a sibilant (*śar*), the substitute is *at*. First of all, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is itself inappropriate here, because the elision (*alopa*) and other operations are obligatory (*nitya*), whereas the doubling (*dvitva*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*); thus, they are not of equal strength. Furthermore, in every instance of a conflict, a subsequent rule must be formulated; therefore, in the present case, [the assumption that] it would be so [by a conflict] offers no opportunity for parsimony (*lāghava*). Moreover, even if a statement regarding a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) were to be made, it would override even obligatory and internal (*antaraṅga*) rules. Consequently, in forms such as *didivatu*, *niyuṣati*, *ninavat*, and *niyiṣati*, [the desired result would not follow].

If the letter *i* were heard [in forms such as *vāvivayiṣati*], then—because of the doubling (*dvitva*), which subverts even an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) consisting of the substitution of *ā* for the *guṇa* caused by the suffix *lyuṭ* through the words "tadavane" and "vane"—the rule would apply. In forms such as *titaviṣati*, the vowel *u* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) because there is no intervention by a *ṇi* other than the original *ṇic*. It is explained as follows: the genitive in *abhyāsasya* denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), while the genitive in *odaudādeśasya* is a genitive of general relation (*saṃbandha-sāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, both are qualifiers. The meaning is this: when there is a portion belonging to the reduplicated syllable that consists of the substitutes *o* or *au*, or a substitute [of the root] consisting of *o* or *au*, then *u* arises for that [portion]. As in *vṛkṣāvadhi*.

In forms such as *ṣaṭti*, it is an *avayava* (substitute for a part), whereas in forms such as *pasphārayiṣati*, it is an *ādeśa* (complete substitute). Therefore, what is established by its own nature is that only the temporary entry into the body of Viṣṇu is described there, and not that he possesses the status of being the cause of [Brahmā’s] having a thousand heads and so forth. Furthermore, the application of the word *Nārāyaṇa* to the four-faced one (Caturmukha) is indeed primary. Now, it must necessarily be said that the application of the word *Nārāyaṇa* to the four-faced one in the sixth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* refers to Nārāyaṇa who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of Caturmukha, according to the logic of the *Pradarśana-vidyā*; otherwise, the statement regarding his assuming the form of a boar for the purpose of lifting up the earth would be contradicted. Nor is it the case that "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" [refers to anything other than Brahman].

It should not be argued that there is no contradiction because the scripture beginning with "all was water" (*salilam āsīt*) establishes that even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) assumed the form of a boar for the purpose of lifting up the earth; for if that were the case, there would be conflict with the immediately following text which states: "Seeing Hari, whose prowess was celebrated by the earth resting upon the tip of his tusk, the Siddhas and Brahman-sages dwelling in the heavens offered praise," and "Thus was the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu praised by Sanaka and the others"—wherein the Great Boar who lifted the earth with his tusk is addressed by such terms as *Hari*, *Viṣṇu*, and so forth.

Because it would result in an inconsistency of designation and because it contradicts the well-known fact that the word "Varāha" is common to Viṣṇu, [the Lord]— the Master, the Prajāpati, having realized that the earth was submerged in the waters of the world-ocean and desiring to lift it up through inference— assumed the form of a Boar, just as he had previously assumed the forms of a Fish, a Tortoise, and others at the beginnings of previous Kalpas. He, whose nature is both stable and mobile, who is the Self of all, the Supreme Self, the Prajāpati, remained in that form consisting of divine sacrifice for the sake of the maintenance of the entire world.

Praised by the gods with gold and other offerings, he then entered the waters; for, in accordance with the *Viṣṇupurāṇa-upabrahmaṇa* which states, "The Self, the Supporter, the Supporter of the Earth," the *Śruti* passage beginning with "The waters indeed... must be declared as having Viṣṇu alone as its referent. It should not be argued that [the mantra] refers only to the four-faced Brahmā, for that would result in an inconsistency with the illustrative examples of the Fish, Tortoise, and others, since such [mantras] are universally recognized as being exclusively Vaiṣṇava, as in: "Salutations to You, the bearer of the lotus, conch, discus, and mace."

Furthermore, if [the Lord] were to accept the assumption of the form of a boar (*vārāharūpaparigraha*), it would contradict another Vedic text which states: "The earth was lifted up by Śiva-Varāha, the black one with a hundred arms. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction between these two scriptural passages on the grounds that in a particular *kalpa* even the Four-faced One (*caturmukha*) might perform the lifting of the earth; for if that were so, it would conflict with the *Varāha Purāṇa*, which says: "O Lord, in every *kalpa* you alone lift me up; O Keśava, I do not know your origin or your primal creation."

Because there would arise a contradiction with [the texts] that, in all *kalpas*, establish Viṣṇu alone as the rescuer of the earth—therefore, the word "Nārāyaṇa" occurring in the sixth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* refers only to Nārāyaṇa who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the four-faced [Brahmā], and not to the four-faced one himself.

This is the samādhi. Here, it cannot be asserted that the use of the word "Nārāyaṇa" follows the logic of the Pratardana-vidyā and refers to Nārāyaṇa as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the four-faced Brahmā; for it has been established previously that Śiva alone is the inner controller of all, and none other than he. As for Nārāyaṇa—

However, because there is no mention of [the Lord] being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the four-faced one (*caturmukha*), it has been previously established that the textual passage from the sixth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* beginning with "Then, in that single ocean" (*ekārṇave tadā tasmin...*) refers either to the four-faced one who is a manifestation of Viṣṇu’s emanations (*vyūhāvatāra*) or to an independent four-faced one presiding over a Vaiṣṇava form.

Thus, since the assumption of the Varāha form for the purpose of lifting the earth is well-known to be Vaiṣṇava, the subsequent textual sequence beginning with "Having seen [the earth] on the tip of his tusk" (*dṛṣṭvā daṃṣṭrāgre...*) serves as a corroboration (*upabrahmaṇa*) of the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* passage beginning with "He [lifted] the earth ending in the waters" (*toyāntāṃ sa mahīm...*).

There is no contradiction between the statement from another Śruti text, "You were lifted up by the Boar," and the words of the Boar himself, "In every Kalpa, you alone [are the one who lifts me]," because both proceed with the intention of employing figurative identification (abhedopacāra) between the entire manifestation and its source, or with the intention of referring to the Vaiṣṇava form presided over by Viriñca. Nor should it be argued that, even if the word Nārāyaṇa is applied to the four-faced Brahmā as an incarnation of a manifestation of Viṣṇu, this does not undermine the fact that the word Nārāyaṇa is exclusively restricted to Viṣṇu; for if that were the case, then for everything consisting of the sentient and the insentient...

In the opinion of others (*paramate*), even though the word *Nārāyaṇa* is applied here and there to the *kapra* (the primordial egg), which is considered the body of Viṣṇu, the exclusivity of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇvaikāntyam*) is not violated; thus, they hold that the word *Nārāyaṇa* denotes Viṣṇu alone and no other. However, this exclusivity of Viṣṇu as intended by the opponents cannot withstand logical reasoning. Therefore, the opponents must admit that the word *Nārāyaṇa* does not apply to anything else, whether in the form of his own *vyūha* or *avatāra*, or in the form of his own body [the cosmic egg]. Yet, that is untenable, for the word *Nārāyaṇa* is indeed applied to the four-faced Brahmā (*caturmukha*) in his capacity as a *vyūha* or *avatāra*.

Since such usage is found in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, so too in the third chapter of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, the application of the word "Nārāyaṇa" to the four-faced Brahmā is observed in the statement of Parāśara: "The Lord named Nārāyaṇa, the wise Grandfather of the worlds (Brahmā), is said to have been born, though he is eternally so, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Furthermore, the phrase "named Nārāyaṇa" does not here connect with the word "Brahmā"; rather, it means that the Lord named Nārāyaṇa, though eternal, is said to have been born as Brahmā—that is, in the form of Brahmā—by way of metaphorical designation.

This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). It must be stated that, in accordance with the preceding text, "Hari, the Lord of the Universe himself, having become Brahmā, proceeds toward the creation of this world, taking pleasure in the quality of passion (*rajas*) therein. For while it is possible for the immediately preceding word "born" (*utpanna*) alone to be the predicate, [the interpretation] of the remote word "Brahmā" [as the subject] is more appropriate.

Furthermore, since the injunction regarding the entry into the body of a Brahmin is weighty, and because there is an expectancy as to how the origination of that which is eternal occurs—given that only this much is required—it is logical to determine the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) strictly according to that expectancy. Thus, in the fourth chapter, in the words of Maitreya: "O Great Sage, please tell me how at the beginning of the Kalpa the Lord named Nārāyaṇa created all beings," the application of the word *Nārāyaṇa* to the four-faced one (Brahmā) is clearly observed. Therefore, regarding the use of the word *Nārāyaṇa*...

With the intention that there is no proof whatsoever for the claim made by the initiated (dīkṣitas)—based on the Puranic tradition—that the beauty of Gaṇeśa is indeed inconsistent with [his being] Viṣṇu, [the author states]: "In the Kūrma [Purāṇa], even though [Gaṇeśa] is the son of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), he is [described as] having a lineage from Nārāyaṇa, O Moon-crested One... [and so forth].

O lotus-eyed one, [the grammatical rule] restricts the exclusivity of this [word]; therefore, it shines upon you without dispute. As for us, however, even though the word is purely etymological (*yaugika*), there is no inconsistency in the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; since our zeal is directed precisely toward this point, we have no particular insistence on establishing a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

Consequently, when the intention is to refer to the "rule regarding the beginning of a word" (*padādividhi*) by the very term "rule regarding the beginning of a word," there is no fault whatsoever. This being the case, because it lacks the prerequisite of being preceded by the utterance of the word "beginning of a word" (*padādi*), it is not a "rule regarding the beginning of a word. Thus, by the application of the Vārttika "and when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*), the *n* becomes like its cause (*nimittavat*).

Since the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is established because it does not occur across a word-break (*padabhinnapadavṛttitvābhāvāt*), the rule "pūrvapadāt" cannot possibly serve to establish it there; therefore, it must serve solely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*). This is the "kapimuṣṭi-nyāya" (the maxim of the monkey's fist). Nevertheless, following the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," the rule "pūrvapadāt" is accepted as having a prescriptive force (*vidhyartha*) in another instance.

He says: "It is described thus. Even though this is the case, O All-pervading One, we describe it as follows: even if, according to the method of the monkey’s fist (*kapimuṣṭi*), there were a fault in the application of the rule regarding *kātyāyanīya* and so forth, that fault would not arise provided it occurs only in a context where the term *tat* is actually employed. This is the manner of description here.

In modern designative words such as *ramyabhavana* and *dhanādi*, the rule *pūrvapadāt* can indeed function as an injunction (vidhi), for in these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *bhavana*—which serves as the middle member—is not established by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*; rather, it is established by the Vārttika stating that [the rule applies] when the middle member is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

It should not be argued that the statement "the rule *pūrvapadāt* [Pāṇini 8.3.106] is for the sake of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) because the grammatical status (*padatva*) is not lost by relying on the internal case-ending as being within the scope of the prohibition of the characteristic of a suffix" is untenable; for it cannot be said that the correctness (*sādhutva*) of modern technical terms such as *ramyabhavana* is unascertained due to their non-observation in usage anywhere, either in the Veda or in common worldly speech. This is because the correctness of all correct words cannot be determined by our own observation of usage, as such usage is difficult to know for anyone who is not omniscient.

Therefore, the great sages Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali, realizing that it is impossible to teach every single word by pointing to each one individually (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), and having understood all correct and incorrect words through the vision of the seers (*ārṣeṇa darśanena*), composed the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*).

Having determined that "only those words which are explained by grammar are correct," so that everyone might easily understand this, they composed the science of grammar for the sake of favoring the world. Consequently, [the status of a word as correct] is to be understood solely through grammar alone.

And correctness (*sādhutva*) has been stated by Hari: "Correctness is non-corruption, or beginninglessness, or fitness for prosperity; or it is grammatical derivation (*vyākriyā*), or a certain universal (*jāti*) manifested here through grammar. The meaning of the verse is that correctness consists in either non-corruption, or beginninglessness, or fitness for prosperity, or a specific universal manifested by grammar which delimits the fitness for prosperity. Thus, in the present context, Pāṇini’s intention is precisely that [the rule] serves as an explanatory supplement (*vidhi*) to the rule *pūrvapadāt* (P. 8.3.106), and not as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). For if it were a restrictive rule, there would be a remainder (*śeṣa*) in the rule *agaḥ* (P. 8.3.107).

On the view that [the rule] has the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), in the case of words such as *ṛgayaṇa* which function as technical names (*saṃjñā*), there would result only an exception (*apavāda*) to the restriction (*niyama*) intended to exclude the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* would be unavoidable for both words that are technical names and those that are not, such as *ṛgayaṇa*. Nor should it be argued that one might split the rule by dividing the *yoga* after *aga*, and on the strength of this split, assume that this is an exception specifically to the substitution of *ṇ* and not to the restriction; for if that were the case, the rule *ragaṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) and the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) [would be contradicted].

It must be stated that the application of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) which has already been established is what is being prohibited; it is not the case that the rule *pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) is being applied, because that rule lacks the status of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Consequently, in forms such as *rugṇam* and *rāgeṇa*, *ṇatva* would likewise not occur. Nor should one argue that, when the word *aga* is joined [to the previous rule], the preceding sūtra (*pūrvapadāt*) is carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], and thus *ṇatva* is prohibited for a *n* following a prior member ending in *g*; this would mean there is no fault in cases like *ṛgaṇam*. For if that were so, since the prohibition of *ṇatva* would apply only to technical names (*saṃjñā*), it would be impossible to prevent *ṇatva* in non-technical words such as *ṛgayana*.

Nor should it be argued that the word *saṃjñāyām* does not carry over [from the previous rule], but rather only the phrase *pūrvapadāt* carries over, and thus the aforementioned fault does not arise; for even if, by such an extremely far-fetched assumption, the rule *pūrvapadāt* is maintained as having a restrictive (*niyamārtha*) function, [the objection remains]: if there is *ṇatva* in a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then [it must follow] from a cause situated in the preceding member.

The restriction that [the substitution] applies only to the other [word] is also unavoidable because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanā*) for the opposite restriction; nor can one accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), for if that were the case, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur in forms such as *vibhīṣaṇa*. Nor can it be argued that the word *suṣeṇa* is recited in the *śivādi* group [of names], and that the opposite restriction is impossible due to the force of that specific mention, because [in the case of] *vibhīṣaṇa*...

Since it could be argued that, just as in the case of words beginning with *ṇ*, the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *suṣeṇa* would otherwise be considered grammatically correct (*sādhutva*), and that its specific mention [in the rule] is intended to indicate that such correctness does not apply, therefore, if the rule "from a preceding word" (*pūrvapadāt*) cannot possibly serve as an injunction (*vidhi*) in any way whatsoever, then—

Having set aside the rule [of *ṇatva*] that would otherwise result from a contrary interpretation of the commentary, one must describe the purpose of the restriction as being achieved with difficulty; for when words such as *ramyabhavana* are employed as technical names (*saṃjñā*), then, because they serve as the basis for the rule regarding *ṇatva*, they remain specifically characterized by that *ṇatva* even in their status as names.

Those words are "correct" (*sādhu*), yet they are not indistinguishable from incorrect ones; rather, correctness is understood through grammar alone, because even in the case of words not currently in usage, correctness must be determined solely by means of grammar. For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kṣu-antāṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.24), regarding the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.2.84), an objection is raised based on the rule *rāyo hali* (7.2.85): "If this were so, forms such as *priyāṣṭau* and *priyāṣṭāḥ* would not occur, whereas *priyāṣṭānau* and *priyāṣṭānaḥ* would result. Anticipating this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* resolves it by stating, "Just as [the forms] are employed according to the grammatical system (*yathā-lakṣaṇa-prayukta*). By speaking thus, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has...

It has been stated that when words are employed, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) must be determined solely by grammar; for this very reason, in the *Manoramā* on the rule *rāt sasya*, having raised the objection that if the letter *t* were elided [in the reading *rat saḥ*], then forms such as *acikirat* (from the root *kīrti* with *kvip*) would also suffer the elision of the *t*, the *Bhāṣya* resolves it by stating that "it is applied according to the technical definition" (*yathālakṣaṇam aparyuktaḥ*). Furthermore, regarding the derivation of the word *kroṣṭu*, the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others, while establishing the rule as having a prescriptive force (*vidhyartha*), cite examples such as *druṇasa* and *giriṇasā*.

This same method must be adopted even in the case of words beginning with *diś*; for words such as *druṇasa* and others do not differ in their status as being unmentioned [in the rule]. Now, one might object: "Even so, we do not see any purpose for the word *aga* in your view. Nor should it be said that its purpose is merely to prevent the occurrence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in words like *ṛgayaṇa*, which are proper names (*saṃjñā*), by overriding the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* through the subsequent rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām...*. For [if that were the case], it would be necessary to state the word *aga* specifically to prevent *ṇatva* in non-proper-name forms of *ṛgayaṇa* and similar words.

If it is argued that because it is necessary to include words like *kṣubhna* in the *kṣubhnādi* group, the substitution of *ṇ* would consequently apply even to those words which are technical names (*saṃjñā*)—we say no. For in my view as well, by dividing the rule into two yogas (*aga* and so on), and by carrying over only the portion *pūrvapadāt* from the previous rule, one can explain the prohibition of *ṇ* for a word following a prior member ending in *g*. Since this interpretation serves the very purpose of preventing *ṇ* in words such as *ṛgayana*—whether they are technical names or common nouns—it is unnecessary to include words like *ṛgayana* in the *kṣubhnādi* list. Thus, the inclusion of such words in the *kṣubhnādi* group is indeed untenable.

It should not be argued that, even so, since the word *pada* in the rule for *ṇatva* actually intends to refer only to the technical term *pada* and the like, the mention of *aga* in the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) would serve a purpose by forming a single syntactical unit with that rule to exclude *ṇatva* in modern names such as *ṛgnagaram*; for if that were the case, the statement that the mention of *aga* is redundant—on the grounds that the exclusion of *ṇatva* in words like *ṛgayana* (which are intended as examples of *aga*) follows simply from the specific mention of *nṛgayanādibhyaḥ*—would be contradicted. Such [an objection]...

Since the technical designation *dhuka* is not established, and since *aga* is established [by the rule *naśca dhātu-pratyayayoḥ*], the rule is divided as "aga. Thus, the *ṇatva* (nasalization) that would otherwise apply in cases such as *ṛgnagaram* and *ṛgayanam* is entirely prevented by this term *aga*. Furthermore, just as it is generally indicated by the statement "in both ways" (*ubhayathā pakṣe*) and so forth—that there is no *visarga* at the end of a word due to its being treated as the final element of a word—so too, by the statement "from *arṇa*, *gayana*, etc.," it is generally indicated that *ṇatva* occurs after a preceding member ending in *ga* or *ra*. Therefore, in my view as well, the statement of the authoritative source (*ākara*) is indeed not contradictory; it is not merely a matter of dancing about.

In cases such as *karagranthasya*, *ṛgnagaraṃ*, and *ṛgayanam*, all instances of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) that would otherwise apply are prevented by the rule-break (*yogavibhāga*) "aga. However, this [prevention] is already established by the very mention of *arṇagayanādibhyaḥ*, which serves as a general indicator (*jñāpaka*). Therefore, the intention is not that the word "aga" is redundant; rather, since the rule *pūrvapadāt* would cause *ṇatva* to apply even to words like *ṛgayanam* when they function as proper names—just as it does in words like *druṇasa*—"aga" is intended to ensure that this [prohibition] operates as a single syntactical unit with *pūrvapadāt* specifically regarding the status of a deity.

This is the intended meaning (*āśaya*). Upon careful consideration of this intention, it is indicated that the *vārttika* "when there is the status of being a subsequent member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*) does not apply to the rule for the substitution of *ṇ*. Thus, how is the substitution of *ṇ* established in the word *nārāyaṇa*? Nor should it be argued that, due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), the very point stated by us is the actual fact; for it is possible [to explain it] within a single sentence.

If it is argued that this is not so because one must avoid the assumption of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of classifying many words as belonging to the *kṣubhna*-group, we reply: no; for this is accepted by the authors of the *Bhāṣya*, who acknowledge the *Vārttika* rule stating "when it is the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*), [the substitution occurs] even when the word begins with a consonant (*padādau*)," in order to establish the *ṇatva* substitution in the case of the word *Nārāyaṇa* when followed by case-endings beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi-vibhakti*).

It is clearly understood that the *vārttika*—"when *ṇatva* is prescribed, provided there is an *uttarapada*"—indeed applies; for, in order to avoid contradiction with that, one must necessarily maintain that the intention of the present *Ākara* (original) text is exactly as we have stated. Therefore, in reality, the rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*) is indeed [the basis].

There is no inconsistency whatsoever with the previously stated position that [the rule] is intended by the term *vidhi* (injunction). Even in the position that the injunction preceded by the utterance of words such as *pada* is intended by the term *padādividhi*, the argument that the rule *pūrvapadāt* serves an injunctive purpose regarding technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *ramya-bhavana-dhana* is indeed tenable. Nor should it be argued that, because words like *ramya-bhavana-dhana* are modern technical terms, they do not fall under the scope of the rule *pūrvapadāt* which concerns ancient technical terms; for ancient and modern technical terms are common [to both].

It is improper to assume a restriction—that the term *saṃjñā* in the sūtra "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 5.3.82), which refers to words denoting names delimited by the generality of being a name (*saṃjñātva-sāmānya*), applies only to [Vedic] technical names—because, on the contrary, in grammar, only words with modern conventional designations (*adhunika-saṅketita-śabda*) are treated as *saṃjñās*, not archaic ones. For this very reason, in the passage "be the rival wife of the southern direction" (*diśaḥ sapatnī bhava dakṣiṇasyāḥ*), the word *dakṣiṇā*, though it possesses an archaic convention regarding the directions, is accepted as not being a *saṃjñā*; thus, by the rule "pūrvaparāvaretyādi" (Pāṇini 1.1.34), it is classified as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita and others have stated that [the rule] succeeds if one accepts the designation (*saṃjñātva*) of the word *uttara* (northern) when it possesses a modern convention (*adhunikasaṅketa*), because in cases such as *uttarāḥ kuravaḥ*, there is no application of the rule due to the prohibition "not when it is a designation" (*asaṃjñāyām*). They argue that while among the directions there is an ancient convention (*cirantana-saṅketa*), among the Kurus it is modern; thus, the statement of the commentators alone is the authority here. Having considered all this, he says: "O Enemy of Smara, even though the region of Drūṇa has been uprooted, [the word] 'northern' (*uttara*)—preceded by the word 'direction' (*deśa*) and following the rule for obtaining another region—[is applied]... [The rest of the verse follows].

If [the rule] does not apply here even to an insentient thing because it obstructs the *gaṃ*, how can there be no shame for a sentient person who hates you? Indeed, even so, since the word "from the preceding member" (*pūrvapadāt*) implies the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the meaning obtained is that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *na* situated in the subsequent member when it follows a cause situated in the preceding member; thus, because the middle member lacks the status of being a "subsequent member," how can it be appropriate to say that the rule "from the preceding member" applies to words such as *ramya-bhavana-dhana*? Nor is the middle member a "subsequent member" in relation to the preceding member.

It must be said that [the term *uttarapada*] certainly exists; for it has been revealed in works such as the *Kaustubha* that the word *uttarapada* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) when applied to the final member of a compound. To this, he says: "Out of fear of obstructing your [etymological] connection, and because it is fruitless [otherwise], this sūtra indeed does not imply the *uttarapada*. Thus, having made its arrangement in the middle member, it resorts only to your connection for the sake of Umā’s form. The implication of one by either the preceding or the following member is not a matter of logic, but rather must be inferred from the power of the result; [in this case,] the preceding member..."

In the view that the rule *diti* prescribes a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), there is no need to imply a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) because such implication would serve no purpose; consequently, it is not implied. For this very reason, in the rule *anandvato dvandvaḥ*, since the subsequent member does not imply the prior member, the application of the masculine form for the word *neṣṭṛ* and others in expressions such as *hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭodgātāraḥ* is established. Furthermore, in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, since the prior member is not implied, the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the word *jaratī* is established in the three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound *citrā-jarad-guḥ*. However, where there is a specific purpose [for such implication], [the rule applies].

In this regard, the implication (*ākṣepa*) of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is established through an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) and through grammatical explanation (*vyākhyāna*). For example, in the rule *prātipadikāntanum-vibhaktiṣu ca*, the meaning is that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* at the end of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the subsequent member. If there were no implication of the "subsequent member" here, then in the case of *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī* ("the sister of the Gargas"), the optional substitution of *ṇ* would also apply [to the *n* of *bhaginī*]. Regarding this, the authors of the *Vṛtti* state that the mention of *num* in the rule is the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) for this implication. If there were no implication of the "subsequent member," then in the case of *māṣavāṇī* ("a field of beans"), the *num* [augment] would belong to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Since the optional substitution of *ṇ* would be established by the very fact of being a "desirable" (*kānta*) [suffix], the inclusion of *num* would be redundant. However, if there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of an "uttarapada" (subsequent member), then because *num*—being a part of the *aṅga*—is not a constituent of the *uttarapada*, it lacks the status of being the final element of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that constitutes the *uttarapada*; thus, the inclusion of *num* becomes as good as redundant. Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita, however, maintains that the inclusion of *num* serves its purpose in forms such as *prahiṇvan* for the sake of the substitution of *ṇ*, and therefore he asserts that the implication of the *uttarapada* here occurs precisely through the force of the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). If, however, [the rule applies] to both the preceding and subsequent members...

If the implication of one term by the other were necessarily established [by the inherent nature of the words], then the authors of the treatises would not have relied upon the authority of the *ākṣepa* (implication), *vyākhyāna* (explanation), and *jñāpana* (indication) in this context, because the implication of the preceding and following words would already be possible through their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is established that implication must be effected solely by the force of a specific purpose (*prayojana*). Consequently, in the present case, since there is no such purpose, the implication of the subsequent word is simply not possible. For this very reason, even in the case of technical terms such as *druṇasa* and so forth, the *Kāśikā* states: [and so on].

Having first described that the rule *pūrvapadāt* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—since the substitution of *ṇ* is already established by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* due to the presence of a single word (as the case-ending produced from the compound is taken along with it)—and having resolved the objection that the substitution of *ṇ* would remain unestablished even in non-technical terms such as *mātṛbhogīṇa* by assuming that the word *uttarapada* is supplied [from the previous rule], he then establishes that the rule *pūrvapadāt* actually functions as an injunctive rule (*vidhyartha*) through the passage beginning with *pare tu*. That [is the conclusion].

Keeping in mind the absence of purpose in that alternative view (*pakṣa*), the objection regarding the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) has not been even smelled. However, there is this much distinction: in the *Kāśikā* and other treatises, regarding the *vārttika* "if it is the subsequent word" (*uttarapadatve ceti*), they maintain that in reality only a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*) is excluded.
