Consequently, just as in words like *rāmanāma*, even in technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *druṇasa*, because the *n* is situated in a word distinct from the [initial] cause-conditioned word (*nimittavat-padabhinnapadasthatvāt*), the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) is not established; thus, in that regard—

It has been stated by us that the rule *pūrvapadāt* [Pāṇini 8.4.3] exists for the purpose of establishing the substitution of *ṇ*. However, even if we accept the position that the rule excludes only those operations preceded by the utterance of the word "beginning of a word" (*padādi*), then in technical names such as *druṇasa*, the substitution of *ṇ* is already established by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye ’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2], because the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies to the latter member by the Vārttika *uttarapadasyottarapadatve ca*. Consequently, since these lack the status of being "words" (*pada*) due to the absence of case-endings (*subanta*), the rule *aṭkupvāṅ* would suffice. Therefore, for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* in modern technical names such as *ramya-bhavaṇa* and *dhana-ādi*, [the rule *pūrvapadāt* is necessary].

The rule "pūrvapadāt" is stated [as a restrictive rule]; thus, since the rule "pūrvapadāt" cannot serve as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha), the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *nārāyaṇa* remains entirely unimpeded. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the substitution of *ṇ* would be unavoidable in words such as *rāma* and others—just as it is in *nārāyaṇa*—because their inclusion in the class of words beginning with *kṣubhna* (*kṣubhnādyākṛtigaṇa*) makes the avoidance of *ṇ* quite easy. This is true even according to the view of the *Kāśikā* and other authorities who maintain that the rule "pūrvapadāt" is prescriptive (*vidhi*). In their opinion, there are infinite words such as *rāmavana* and the like.

Since the status of being a *kṣubhnādi* word must necessarily be postulated, there is this distinction: in the opinion of Rāma and others, the status of being a *kṣubhnādi* is to be postulated only for words such as *rāma-vana*, where the letter *n* occurs in the non-initial portion of the subsequent member; however, in our view, the status of being a *kṣubhnādi* is to be postulated even for words such as *rāmanāman*, where the letter *n* occurs in the initial portion of the subsequent member. Furthermore, if the rule were intended as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), [the objection] that it would apply to no one...

It should be stated that there is parsimony (lāghava) in not postulating that the word *śabda* belongs to the *kṣubhnādi* group; however, according to the maxim that "an undertaking [of a rule] when [the desired result] is already established is for the purpose of restriction," it is improper to interpret it as a restrictive rule when a positive injunction is possible. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate that infinite words such as *rāma*, *nāma*, and so forth belong to the *kṣubhnādi* group—a view not accepted by the author of the *Kāśikā* and others.

It should not be said that this is improper; for on the view that the rule *pūrvapadāt* is restrictive (*niyamārtha*), it would be unavoidable to consider words such as *ananta*, *ārambhya*, *bhavaṇa*, and *dhana* to be corrupt (*apaśabda*). Therefore, by comparison with that, it is more logical to describe both sets of words as correct (*sādhutva*) according to the method I have stated. Nor should it be argued that, even under the view that these are derived (*utpatti-pakṣa*), the statement that the rule *pūrvapadāt* exists there for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *ṇa* in technical names (*saṃjñā-śabda*) like *ramya-bhavaṇa-dhana* is an untenable assertion; for if that were the case, the same would apply to technical names such as *druṇasa* and others.

If one adopts the view that words are derived (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), then the statement by the author of the *Kāśikā* and others—that the rule *tatra pūrvapadāt* is prescriptive (*vidhy-artha*)—would be inconsistent. If one attempts to justify that statement by adopting the view of derivation, it applies equally to the present case. Therefore, both under the *vārttika* "if [the compound] is the latter member" (*uttarapadatve ca*) and under the view that the rule prescribes the initial of a word (*padādi-vidhi-pakṣa*), as well as the view that the rule prescribes [the substitution] preceded by the utterance of the word "beginning of a word" (*padādi-śabdoccāraṇa-pūrvaka-vidhi-pakṣa*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *Nārāyaṇa* when applied to Paramaśiva remains entirely unimpeded, even though the word is etymological (*yaugika*). However, according to the view that the rule prescribes the initial of a word (*vastutaḥ padādi-vidhi-pakṣa*), [the form would be] *paramaścāsau carthaśca* (according to the opinion of others, *paramavā*).

Furthermore, in examples such as *paramakāpara*, the rules for changing *c* to *k* (*kutva*), changing *j* to *g* (*jatva*), and eliding *n* (*nalopa*) would apply; however, since the letter *ca* and others are in fact word-initial (*padādi*), the *vārttika* "and when there is a subsequent member" (*uttarapadatve ca*) does not apply. Consequently, because the status of being a word (*padatva*) is not lost by relying on the internal case-ending, those [rules] also must be resolved according to the method stated in the *Bhāṣya*: that they are unapplied (*aprayukta*) because they would otherwise conflict with the grammatical rules (*yathālakṣaṇam*). If, however, one were to assume that an infinite number of words possess the status of being *kṣubhnādi* simply because they exist, or if one were to assume that the specific word *nārāyaṇa*—when qualified by a particular meaning—is *kṣubhnādi*, these would be considered faults.

To avoid this fault, [it is argued that] the rule "when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*)—as stated in the Vārttika—is intended by the term *padādividhi* as a rule specifically concerning the utterance of the word at the beginning of a *pada*, following the recitation of the word *padādi*. Thus, the sūtra *pūrvapadāt* is merely restrictive (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, words such as *ramya*, *bhavaṇa*, and *dhana* are considered unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*); since the sūtra *pūrvapadāt* does not apply as a prescriptive rule (*vidhyatva*) there, the substitution of *ṇ* must be established by some other means. If this is said, then [we reply: even by another means...

He states that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is thus justified: "O Purāri, just as even a trace of the scent of the feeble refutations imagined by Your detractors does not affect You, so too, why would Your grace—which is beyond reproach—not cause today that very body called Nārāyaṇa to perform [these deeds] for You? For instance, 'Nārāyaṇa' is derived as follows: He who is approached (*īyate*) by waters (*nāra-*), or reached (*prāpyate*) as being related to them; or He who is approached (*īyate*), worshipped (*upāsyate*), or reached (*prāpyate*) by the multitude of men (*nāra-*, i.e., *narasamūhena*). This is according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), which allows for great flexibility in the application of suffixes."

By the rule that the suffix *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of an object (*karman*), and by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) stating that the prescription for compounding a word with a *kṛt*-suffix—provided the first member is a root, a verbal agent (*kāraka*), or a subordinate term (*upapada*)—occurs prior to the addition of case-endings (*sup*), the word *nāra-* is compounded with the word *ayana-* while the latter is still not a nominal stem (*asubanta*). Since the subsequent member *ayana-* is not a nominal stem, it lacks the status of a "word" (*pada*). Consequently, because the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) applies only when the *n* resides in a word distinct from the cause [of the change], the *ṇatva* of the *n* in *ayana* is established without difficulty. Thus, the occurrence of *ṇatva* in words such as *rāmanāman* and others is entirely precluded.

Their status as *kṣubhnādi* (words beginning with *kṣubhna*) should not be postulated; for even in cases such as *nārāyaṇam*, since the word *tāra* lacks the status of a *kāraka*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when a *gati* or a *kāraka* [is compounded]" does not apply. Consequently, when the word *ayana* is compounded with a *sub*-ending word, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes a *pada*, and thus the rules for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would necessarily follow in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Therefore, the status of *kṣubhnādi* cannot be postulated even for the word *nārāyaṇa* when it is qualified by a specific meaning. Furthermore, in cases such as *nārasyāyanam* (the going of Nara), where the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*) is intended, even though there is no *kāraka* status, the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) or object (*karmatva*) [is still applicable].

Or, if you intend to say that when the genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65], then because it is a *kāraka*, the substitution of *ṇa* (in *pra-ṇamya*) would be unavoidable due to the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [Pāṇini 6.2.139]; to this we reply: even if that were so, since the word *bahulam* is included in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* [Pāṇini 2.1.32], there are instances where a *kāraka* is compounded with a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

This is precisely why the usage "sā hi tasya dhanakrītī" (she is his wife bought for wealth) is established; otherwise, by the rule *krītāt karaṇe pūrvapadāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.50], the form would have been *dīrghikrītī*. However, when there is a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied first; since the condition for the application of *ṣīṣ* (i.e., the presence of the letter *n*) is then absent, [the suffix *ṣyaṅ* does not apply].

The rule *bhāve dhanakrītā* is established in such a way that in cases like *nārasyāyanabhinnārāyaṇam*, where the substitution of *ṇ* is not desired, there is a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*); whereas in cases where it is desired, there is a compound with a word not ending in a case-suffix (*asubanta*). Thus, the statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "He from whom even the *nārās* (the waters) have their source (*ayana*) is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa," is consistent.

It should not be argued that this contradicts the etymological explanation of the names *Śiva* and *Paranārāyaṇa*, which demonstrates their status as *bahuvrīhi* compounds; for that [explanation] is intended merely to show the underlying meaning (*arthika-artha*) and does not purport to demonstrate their status as *bahuvrīhi*. Furthermore, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "gati-kāraka-upapadānām" is established through the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "upapadam" (Pāṇini 2.2.19) from "atiṅ" (2.2.20), and by the inclusion of the term "kṛt" in the rule "kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā bahulam" (2.1.32). This has been stated by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. To explain: the rule "atiṅ" is split into two parts; the compound previously mentioned in the two preceding rules is [restricted to] that which is not followed by a finite verb (*atiṅ*).

By the force of this [explanation], it follows that in the two preceding sūtras, the word *sup* (ending in a case-suffix) does not recur as a third-case ending; thus, the meaning of those [sūtras] is that *ru*, *ku*, *gati*, and *prādi* are compounded with a "competent" (*samartha*) word, and an *upapada* is compounded with a "competent" word. Similarly, in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* ("the agent and the instrument are compounded with a *kṛt*-suffix"), since a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) would not otherwise be obtained even by repeating *sup*, the inclusion of the term *kṛtā* is for the purpose of securing that the compound occurs only when the word is in the state of having a *kṛt*-suffix. By this, it is established that the compound occurs prior to the production of the case-suffix (*sub*). Therefore, regarding the word *nārāyaṇa*...

If [the term] *paramaśiva* is understood in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is entirely unobjectionable. Furthermore, regarding its status as a word based on both etymology and conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*) or as being metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*), the substitution of *ṇ* has already been established by the venerable Dīkṣitas themselves. Now, concerning the view that it is metaphorical, a certain point is investigated:

if the birth of Nārāyaṇa from Paramaśiva is indeed authoritative, then it is possible for Paramaśiva to possess the state of being characterized by the future condition of Nārāyaṇa; however, we do not see any evidence for that very point. To this, he says: ||32||
By the most excellent initiates consecrated to you,
this which has been proclaimed as the root— namely, that through the application of the characteristic of bearing the moon, you will exist in the state of Kṛṣṇa— is indeed beyond dispute.
The birth of Viṣṇu from the Moon-bearer is established by the Upaniṣads.

There is an alternative reading for the final quarter [of the verse]: "For the *Atharvaśikhā* is well known as having its origin from you. This is because in works such as the *Śivatattvaviveka*, this very statement from the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts—namely, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are all produced from you"—has been most thoroughly established as the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) in that regard. Furthermore, regarding what is accepted by you...

He states that even by reflecting on the meaning of the word *Nārāyaṇa*, his birth from Paramaśiva is understood: "O Śambhu, even through the purification of the meaning of Nārāyaṇa—the most excellent being whose name is cherished by those free from envy—it is well known that the birth of the Blessed Lord, the leader of Kamalā, occurred from you; this is as clear as day. For instance, the word *Nārāyaṇa* is established as a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) by the statement in the lexicon: 'Viṣṇu is Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore: 'The waters are called *nārāḥ*; the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara. They were his (*Nara's*) *ayana* (abode/origin)..."

It has been stated by him [in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*], "He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa," and so forth; and because the etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) of the word is established through such scriptural statements, there is no dispute that these terms are both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) when applied to Viṣṇu. Regarding this, the *Śruti* states: "The waters are *nārāḥ*; *nara* is Rudra, the Puruṣa, Kṛṣṇapiṅgala; they are his sons, and he is their refuge (*ayana*); therefore he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore: "From the form of the deity named Rudra, a physical manifestation (*mūrti*) is produced; by him, who identifies with the Supreme Form (*paramūrti*), the seed is cast into the fluid (*rasa*)."
Then that golden egg came into being, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns; Viṣṇu himself entered it through the majesty of my power.
He then assumed the name Nārāyaṇa.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa:
The waters are known as *sukṣemā*, and their essence (*rasa*) is to be understood; that essence is proclaimed as *nāra*.
In reality, Brahmā is not *rajas*; rather, *nara* is considered to be Śiva himself.
Therefore his course is called "Ayana," and by that he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
O tiger among men, even Brahmā entered into the form of fragrance.

From such statements in the Vāsiṣṭha, Liṅga, and other Purāṇas, it is understood that you, O Viṣṇu, are indeed [the Supreme], appearing under the name Nārāyaṇa—attained through the grace of Śiva, who is denoted by the word "Nara" and characterized as the abode of the attainment of the goals of worldly engagement and renunciation. Nor is this mere acquisition of the name [insignificant], for it is rooted in [the realization of] engagement and renunciation.

It may be asked: "How can it be said that [the name] was obtained through the grace of Śiva by virtue of being dependent on its etymological derivation (*yoga*)? Regarding the designation *Nārāyaṇa*, which possesses both etymological and conventional (*rūḍhi*) significance, even if the etymological component requires only the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it is possible for the conventional component to have been obtained through the grace of Śiva. [Objection: But surely, at the beginning of the *Manusmṛti*, it is stated: "Then the Blessed Lord Svayambhū, the Unmanifest, having manifested this [universe], appeared during the activity of the great elements and so forth..."?

The ocean of darkness appeared, which was beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, manifest, and eternal; that very one, being unmanifest and indefinable, shone forth by himself. Desiring to create various beings, he first brought forth the waters from his body and cast his seed into them. That became a golden egg, radiant as a thousand suns; within it, Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds. The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; since they were declared to be his place of movement (*ayana*), he is therefore called Nārāyaṇa.

Regarding the statement "He who is remembered as Yaṇa," it is recorded there that [the Lord] meditated upon the Self-born, Blessed One, the Dispeller of Darkness. By the word "that" (tat), which refers back to the Creator of the waters, His identity with Nārāyaṇa is clearly understood through the subsequent etymological explanation of the name Nārāyaṇa.

Consequently, since the status of being a source of valid knowledge (*āptatva*) is understood to belong to one created by Nārāyaṇa, how could He be created by Śiva? To this, he says: "The word 'āpaḥ' (waters), which by its own natural sense in the *Mūla-śruti* indicates Hari, has come to signify You."

How can they claim that the opening of the *Manusmṛti* refers to Mādhava (Viṣṇu), since it begins with Maheśvara? For, in the absence of words common to Viṣṇu alone, the opening of the *Manusmṛti*—which is perceived as common to both Śiva and Viṣṇu—is based on the *Nīlakaṇṭha-bhāṣya*, which establishes Rudra's nature as the one who cast the seed of virility that produced the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) within the ocean, according to the verse: "In the midst of the waters, the golden egg first came into being through the virility of Rudra. Thus, it is the basis for the *Manusmṛti*'s opening passage.

Since it must be stated that the passage refers specifically to Rudra in accordance with the Śruti and the previously cited statements from the Vāsiṣṭha, Laiṅga, and other Purāṇas, and since the etymological explanation of the name Nārāyaṇa found at the conclusion can be applied to Śiva as well by following the introductory context; and because, in reality, the term "tamonudaḥ" (dispeller of darkness) exists as a word in the fifth case (ablative) denoting Rudra—the presiding deity of the *tama-aṇu*—who is the limit of manifestation, Viṣṇu [is distinct] from Śiva, who is the "dispeller of darkness."

From the understanding of the meaning "he appeared" (*prādurāsīt*), it is clearly perceived that the opening of the *Manusmṛti* refers exclusively to Śiva. Likewise, in the passage "He meditated" (*so 'bhidhyāya*), the word "he" (*tat*) refers only to Śiva as the one who caused the manifestation, and not to Viṣṇu as the one manifested. This is in accordance with the Vedic citations and the statements from the *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Laiṅga*, and other Purāṇas quoted in the aforementioned commentary by Nīlakaṇṭha, which establish Rudra as the hurler of the seed (*vīryakṣeptṛ*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the fact that the state of being water (*aptva*) was created by Śiva; and even so, [the objection] is not raised here.

Through the statements of the *Hariṣyamāṇa*, *Padma*, and other Purāṇas, it is understood that the presiding over the quality of *tamas* belongs specifically to Saṃhārarudra, who is included within the triad of the Guṇamūrtis, and not to Paramaśiva. Furthermore, regarding the creatorship of Nārāyaṇa, statements such as from the *Atharvaśikhā*—"All this, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, are produced"—understand that this belongs to Paramaśiva alone and not to Saṃhārarudra. How, then, can the description of Nārāyaṇa as the creator of the one presiding over *tamas* be justified? It must be stated [that this refers to the form known as Rudra], based on statements from the *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Liṅga*, and other Purāṇas.

Furthermore, since the birth of Nārāyaṇa even from the Saṃhāra-Rudra is established by such passages as "From the Self, space was produced," which describe the process of creation; and moreover, because in statements from the Vāyu Purāṇa and other texts—such as "Having gratified that Father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were created first, and then Rudra"—it is clearly understood that the Saṃhāra-Rudra is the creator of Nārāyaṇa. Nor is there any contradiction with the word *tamonudaḥ*, for it is a nominative singular form ending in the suffix *ka* (according to the rule *prīkiraḥ kaḥ*), derived from a root beginning with *gu* (the *tud* class), and thus it remains [in its original case-ending].

And here, it is understood that [the Lord] is merely the one who manifests, not the one who causes manifestation; furthermore, this word "Bhagavat" as well as the word "Puruṣa" refer to the eternal Vāsudeva without any limiting adjuncts, as determined by the Purāṇic statement: "The word 'Bhagavat,' which denotes a state unique to Viṣṇu, is applied thus to the eternal Vāsudeva. Thus, it must be said that the status of being an authority belongs only to what is created by Viṣṇu. Moreover, even if one accepts that the word "tamonudaḥ" (dispeller of darkness) ends in the nominative case, there is no evidence for the claim that the manifestor is Viṣṇu alone, given the presence of the word "Bhagavat."

Even if one accepts that [the term] Viṣṇu is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) according to the previously stated words, nevertheless—by virtue of the traditional authority of Āśvalāyana stating, "All these indeed are his names," and by virtue of the statement in the *Harivaṃśa* beginning with "Govinda" and so forth as being your names—it follows that because what is conventionally established for Viṣṇu is not produced [as new] when applied to Śiva, it is likewise established for Śiva. Furthermore, it applies to Śiva by virtue of the etymological derivation (*yoga*) set forth in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "He is remembered as Svayambhū because he is self-born; and the Blessed One is remembered as 'Oṃ' because of his omniscience and his protection (*avana*). Thus, [the name] applies to Śiva as well.

Since it is not established that this term *yogarūḍha* (conventional-derivative) is unique to Viṣṇu, Śiva alone is the one who will manifest, in accordance with such scriptural passages as "From Him [comes] the golden staff" (*dasmādaṇḍaṃ hiraṇmayam*) and the statements in the Vāsiṣṭha and Laiṅga Purāṇas.

Furthermore, Śiva alone is the one who will manifest because of the co-occurrence of the word *tamonuda* (dispeller of darkness). For the word *tamonuda* denotes one characterized by the quality of dispelling darkness; and that quality of dispelling darkness is understood directly as belonging to Rudra—who is the restrainer of the *tamas* guṇa—just as the quality of dispelling obstacles belongs to Vighneśvara, and not to Brahmā.

It should not be argued that, because Rudra is likewise under the influence of his own qualities (*guṇa*), his status as the controller of the quality of *tamas* is unestablished. For even though Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are each under the influence of their respective qualities, Rudra’s role as the controller of *tamas* is established by the Purāṇas.

Thus, it is recorded in the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "The one eternal God, Sadāśiva, who is worshipped by Brahmā—the three-eyed one, the substratum of qualities, yet transcending qualities, imperishable and immutable—created from his right side his son Brahmā, from his left side Hari, and from his back Maheśāna."

The Lord created three sons; as soon as they were born—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—they spoke these clear words: "Who are you, and who are we? Śiva said to those sons, "You are the sons, and I am the father. O sons, for the sake of performing your tasks, you must resort to these three qualities (guṇas): Brahmā shall resort to *sattva*, Viṣṇu to *rajas*, and Maheśvara to *tamas*. As soon as this was said by the God, Brahmā took hold of *sattva*, but he was unable to sustain it; and although he was capable, he cast aside that quality (*tamas*) and then took hold of the quality of *rajas*.

"He could not be moved; he fell down and wept. Viṣṇu held the quality of Rajas with his left hand, while Rudra held that [quality] of Viṣṇu with his finger. And holding the Tamasic quality upon the footstool, he danced," and so forth—in these very words, regarding Brahmā...

Through the grace of Viṣṇu, there is the maintenance of the quality of *rajas*; through the grace of Rudra, there is the commonality of the quality of *sattva* for Rudra; but for Rudra himself, the quality of *tamas* is [present] in his footstool, as this is established explicitly by the mention of his "invisibility" (*adarśana*). Thus, it is clearly understood that Rudra is the controller of the quality of *tamas*. Nor is it even thus...

"This world was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, undiscernible, and indescribable, as if entirely immersed in sleep. Following this preceding verse, which establishes that at the time prior to creation only *māyā* remained, the word "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) in the subsequent verse, "Then the Self-born [Brahmā] dispelled the darkness," is understood to refer exclusively to *māyā*, and not to the *tamas-guṇa* (the quality of inertia), by virtue of which one might claim it refers specifically to Rudra. Even so, because the opening of the *Manusmṛti* must necessarily be understood as referring to Rudra when weighed against the previously cited scriptural and Puranic statements.

Furthermore, by the force of the syntactic unity of the concluding section, the opening of the *Manusmṛti* must also be understood as referring to Rudra alone; for in its conclusion, after teaching that the Supreme Person is the inner ruler (*praśāsitā*) of all, subtler than the subtlest, incomparable, and perceivable through the intellect in deep sleep—describing him as the Puruṣa who pervades all beings with five forms and perpetually causes the world to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay—the text demonstrates his pervasion of the universe through the five forms beginning with Sadyojāta.

By this, his nature as Paramaśiva is made manifest. Furthermore, it should not be argued that by the phrase "by the five forms" (*pañcabhirmūrtibhiḥ*), the five elements beginning with earth (*pṛthivyādi*) are intended rather than Sadyojāta and the others; for if that were so, the pervasion of the world by Nārāyaṇa through these five forms of earth and the rest would also be possible, and thus this would not be an exclusive characteristic (*aikāntikaliṅga*) of Paramaśiva. This is because the Taittirīya Śruti, which is the source of this Smṛti statement, declares: "Subtler than the subtle, the Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman... this sun is indeed that orb... obeisance to the golden-armed one (*hiraṇyabāhu*)."

By means of such passages as "He is indeed this Person, fivefold and five-souled, by whom all this is woven together— the earth and the intermediate space," etc., having designated the fivefold forms beginning with Sadyojāta through the mantras "Sadyojāta" and so forth for Paramaśiva, who was introduced as residing within the solar orb, [the text] demonstrates that very same Paramaśiva’s pervasion of the universe and its withdrawal by means of those five forms. This is indicated by the phrase "by the five forms" found in this Smṛti statement.

Indeed, the designation of the five forms beginning with Sadyojāta must necessarily be accepted. Now, one might object: the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) should be interpreted strictly according to the introduction (upakrama), for it is not proper to interpret the introduction according to the conclusion. For this very reason, in the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], under the sūtra "Because the Veda belongs to those born" (*śruter jātādhikārāt*), although the praise of the *Ṛgveda* and the others is understood from the introduction—"From Agni comes the *Ṛgveda*, from Vāyu the *Yajurveda*, and from Āditya the *Sāmaveda*"—the concluding statement, "It is recited loudly," [is shown to take precedence].

If it is argued that— having first established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the words "Ṛk" and so forth [in the concluding passage] denote the *Ṛgveda* and so forth by following the words "Ṛk," etc., which occur in the principal injunctive sentence, and then having established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the sūtra "Or rather, the Veda, because of the observation of the majority" (*vedo vā prāyadarśanāt*), that because the opening statement possesses greater force due to its non-contradiction with the aggregate, the concluding words "Ṛk" and so forth— even those occurring in the principal injunctive sentence— must denote the *Ṛgveda* and so forth in accordance with the words "Ṛgveda" and so forth [in the opening]— this is not so, because where one does not depend on the concluding statement...

The principle of the predominance of the introduction (*upakrama*) applies only where the determination of meaning depends on the introduction itself; however, in the present case, since the determination of the meaning of the introduction to the *Manusmṛti* must be stated in relation to its conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), the principle of the predominance of the introduction does not apply.

For this very reason, in the second chapter, under the rule "But when there is doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (*sandigdhe tu vākyaśeṣāt*), it was established as the final conclusion that the introduction "He scatters gravel" (*śarkarā upadadhāti*) is interpreted according to the conclusion "Clarified butter is indeed splendor" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). Therefore, in the present case, one must follow the conclusion.

Therefore, the interpretation as an *upakrama* (initial action) is indeed appropriate; thus, even in the view that "dispeller of darkness" (*tamo nuda*) is in the nominative case, the meaning is simply that "Rudra, the dispeller of darkness, appeared. However, in the ultimate sense, the nominative status of "dispeller of darkness" is impossible. This is because, having established the state of the world as Māyā in the preceding verse, "This was [then] unmanifest, enveloped in darkness," the subsequent verse, "From that [was born] the Self-existent One" (*tataḥ svayambhūḥ*), describes his essential nature as having come into manifestation. Consequently, it is impossible for him to have been the pre-established presiding deity of that darkness. Furthermore, immediately after the phrase "and of Vāyu... (*vāyor apīti*).

Furthermore, this would result in an inconsistency with the verse; for that verse is intended to exclude the distinction between the subject under discussion, Svayambhū, and the Supreme Lord who is characterized by attributes such as being perceivable by those beyond the senses (*atīndriyagrāhya*), and it does not intend to enjoin [Svayambhū] as the father himself, because the restrictive particle *eva* (only) subverts the injunctive force. For this very reason, in the section of the ninth chapter, fourth quarter (*navamādhyāya-caturthapāda*), it is stated that the four-horned nature of the horse is merely figurative (*vācikam*) based on the scriptural statement, and that "one should say 'twenty-six' according to the rule," where the injunctive force is restricted by the particle *eva*, and thus the injunctionality is established by what has been enjoined.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that even in the case of *prakṛti* (primordial matter), the portion "it manifested itself" (*svayamudbabhau*) is possible as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the property of being self-existent (*svayambhū*), as established in the preceding verse; thus, in your own view, if the term *tamonudaḥ*—which refers to the presiding deity over the darkness called *avidyā*, which is the *prakṛti* of the entire phenomenal world—is accepted as being in the nominative case and serving as an attribute of *svayambhū*, then the contingency of its being distinct from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) does not arise at all, nor is there any exclusion of such a distinction.

There is some logical connection here for the exposition; however, in my own position, since the manifestation of the Self-born Supreme Lord as the presiding deity of *tamas* is mentioned, there arises the possibility of a distinction [between them]. If the one who manifests were Śiva, then his being "self-born" (*svayambhū*) would be untenable; if he were Īśvara, the doctrine of multiple lords (*anekaiśvaravāda*) would follow. Therefore, in order to refute such views, the exclusion of difference must also be established; thus, the statement "this was once enveloped in darkness" (*āsīd idaṃ tamobhūtam*) serves as the introduction to the preceding verse.

It has been stated that the Supreme Lord alone, the presiding deity of *tamas*, is manifested at the beginning of creation in the form of the Nārāyaṇa-mūrti produced by a specific limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, He is designated as "Self-born" (*svayambhu*) in the preceding verse. This is consistent with the intention of the passage beginning with "He who... (*yo'sau*), which asserts that there is no other. Consequently, the word *tanmo nudaḥ*—ending in the *kvip* suffix and in the ablative case—is indeed the very one who brings forth the Existent (*sat*). Furthermore, upon reflecting on the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning creation, such as "From the Self, space was produced," [it follows that] those presiding over space and the other elements are always...

Therefore, the word *tamonudaḥ* (the dispeller of darkness) is formed with the *kvip* suffix and ends in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*). This is because it will be demonstrated later that the manifestation of Śiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā occurs sequentially, each arising from the one preceding it.

Furthermore, even at the beginning of the *Manusmṛti*, it is appropriate to adopt the meaning that "from Rudra, the dispeller of darkness, Viṣṇu manifested. Thus, in the passage "He meditated" (*so 'bhidhyāya*), by the previously stated reasoning, the pronoun *tat* refers to the one who causes manifestation.

Since only Rudra is mentioned [as the creator], it is established that the state of being water (*aptva*) is something created by Rudra. Now, one might object: "Even so, although Nārāyaṇa is the abode of the waters created by Rudra, how can his own origination from Rudra be obtained merely through the force of the name 'Nārāyaṇa'? If this is asked, we reply: No. When one reflects upon the meaning of the name 'Nārāyaṇa', which possesses as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the characteristic of being the abode of the waters created by Śiva—who is denoted by the word *nara*—it is established that the state of being water is understood there to be something created by Śiva. In that case...

Since the cognition of being created is possible without a prior cognition of the specific property that delimits that state of being created, one seeks that delimiting property. In the search for such a property, within the scriptural authority that makes known its state of being created—namely, the statement "He created water alone" and so forth—one finds that this statement is composed of words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), which refer to the presiding deity who is the substratum.

In accordance with Taittirīya and other Śrutis stating "From the Self, ether was produced," the word "water" (*ap*) is understood to denote water delimited by Nārāyaṇa as its presiding deity. Thus, although there is no sublation of the state of being created as predicated of the qualified entity (water as delimited by Nārāyaṇa), [the specific property of being created by Śiva remains unestablished].

Even though it is possible [to interpret the term] as a qualifier, the fact that Śiva is created by Nārāyaṇa is understood by the word "Nārāyaṇa" itself. Nor should it be argued that in the foundational Taittirīya Śruti, it is unestablished that words such as "ether" (ākāśa) denote elements together with their presiding deities; for there, since it must necessarily be stated that each subsequent element arises from its preceding element—which is already qualified by its respective presiding deity—it is therefore indispensable to accept, in accordance with that context, that words like "ether" denote elements together with their presiding deities.

For instance, although in such scriptural passages as "From the Self, space [was born]" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ*), only the elements such as space are mentioned and not the presiding deities of those elements, nevertheless, in the *Chāndogya* account of creation within the same context, the power of reflection (*īkṣaṇa*) is heard in the statements, "That fire reflected" (*tat tejo 'kṣata*) and "Those waters reflected" (*tā āpo 'kṣanta*). Since such reflection is impossible for an insentient agent, it must necessarily be admitted that the words "fire" and so forth in that passage refer to the respective presiding deities. And thus, the words "space" and so forth occurring in the *Taittirīya* scripture should likewise be understood by incorporating them into the account of creation found in the *Chāndogya*.

In accordance with that [context], it must indeed be stated that [the term "it"] refers to ether and the other elements as qualified by their respective presiding deities. Now, even so, since in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad the resolve of Brahman to become manifold—"It thought: May I be many, may I grow forth"—is heard first, the subsequent passage beginning with "That heat (tejas) thought" also describes the evolution of that very [Brahman] into the universe; it does not state a separate act of thinking performed by the presiding deities who possess the majesty of the elements such as heat. Otherwise, the resolve for becoming manifold heard at the outset would be restricted in scope solely to the creation of heat.

Because [otherwise] there would be the fallacy of over-narrowness (*saṅkoca*), it follows that words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth refer exclusively to Brahman as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of those respective elements, and not to the presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) of those elements. Nor should it be asked how the eternal Brahman can have an origin through the sequence of ether and so forth; for although an origin characterized by a change in essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*)—as in the case of clay and the like—is impossible, an origin characterized by a change in its qualifying attributes (*svaviśeṣaṇa-bhūta-dharma-anyathābhāva*) is possible even in the case of the eternal Brahman. For this very reason, one says: "Caitra was a cook," or "Time was."

If it is argued that expressions such as "now the sacrificer has arisen" are observed [in scripture], we say no; for even in this case, the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth must necessarily be understood as referring to the respective deities presiding over ether and the rest—specifically those distinguished by their respective deities—as well as to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) distinguished by those very things, in accordance with Purāṇic statements such as: "Sadāśiva and the others, known by the name Rudra, bring about the successive creation from each preceding stage to each succeeding one. Thus, the words "ether" and so forth refer to the Inner Controller who is qualified by ether and the rest, which are themselves qualified by the respective deities presiding over them.

In this very way, when described as qualified, the relationship of cause and effect—due to the absence of sublation and the presence of proof—indeed applies even to the qualifiers such as Sadāśiva and others. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be the consequence of the objects such as air having both [the element and its presiding deity] as their creators, with the respective inner controller (antaryāmin) being the creator of the ether and so forth; for just as a jar and the like are admitted to have both the potter and the Lord as their creators—either directly or through a succession—so too here, the consequence of dual authorship is accepted. Furthermore, this does not contradict Purāṇic statements such as "of the one named Rudra... regarding the ether.

Furthermore, the origin of air and the category of *vāyu* is not heard of at all; moreover, the origin of Viṣṇu and Brahmā—who preside over water and earth—respectively from Rudra and Viṣṇu—who preside over fire and water—is also not perceived as having any clear distinction [in this context]. Thus, how can it be asserted that, in accordance with this statement, the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth occurring in the Taittirīya Śruti refer to the Supreme Being as qualified by those respective presiding deities, especially when the Chāndogya account of creation mentions fire (*tejas*) as being first, even while following the Taittirīya Śruti?

The first objection does not hold, because, according to the *Śruti* stating "the golden egg" (*hiraṇmayam aṇḍam*)—which describes the creation and dissolution of ether and air like the essence (*sāra*)—and according to Purāṇic statements such as "of the one named Rudra who is its root," the creation and dissolution of ether and air must necessarily be mentioned in accordance with the *Taittirīya Śruti*. Nor does the second objection apply; for the meaning of the passage beginning with "of the one named Rudra" is as follows: the "form" (*mūrti*) of the deity named Rudra refers to his form as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the luminous form presided over by Rudra.

The alteration of case endings is according to Vedic usage (*cāndasa*). The meaning of "by him" is that [the seed] was produced from the essential nature of the entity *vāyu*, and by that Rudra—who identifies with the form of fire (*tejas*)—semen was cast into the water. Thus, in the description of Rudra casting his semen into the watery form, since the status of being the locus for the emission of semen cannot otherwise be accounted for by something not yet produced, it is understood that the entity *tejas* (fire), which is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the watery form presided over by Viṣṇu, has been produced; for it is this [entity] that possesses the capacity to instill the power to produce earth within the water.

Because of the capacity for the emission of water belonging to that very [Rudra] himself, the objection—that the production of the water-tattva is not heard of here, and even if it were so imagined, there is no evidence that Rudra alone created it—is refuted. Consequently, that seed-vigor (vīrya), presided over by Brahmā, transformed into the form of the Earth consisting of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as its inner controller (antaryāmin); this is the meaning of the phrase "the golden staff came into being. Thus, the doubt—how could the insentient seed-vigor, without being presided over by a conscious being, transform into the nature of the cosmic egg—is dispelled.

The meaning of the phrase "Viṣṇu entered that" (*viṣṇustatprāviśat*) is as follows: for the sake of creation, the *vīrya* (seed/energy) cast by Rudra was transformed into the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and in order to bring about the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha, Viṣṇu entered the state of water solely through the playful manifestation of Rudra’s power (*rudraśaktivilāsa*). Thus, it is established that the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the water-form presided over by Viṣṇu is born from the inner controller of the earth presided over by Brahmā. Consequently, the name "Nārāyaṇa" possesses its etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the sense of entering the principle of water (*jala-tattva*) obtained through the grace of Rudra.

Furthermore, by the phrase "known as Nārāyaṇa," this very point has been stated; this same idea is elaborated upon in the two verses beginning with "And this... and so forth. Consequently, because of Viṣṇu’s grace, for the purpose of creating the web of the phenomenal world consisting of gods, humans, and others, Brahmā also entered the principle of the earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*); thus it is stated. Likewise, in such statements as "of him who is named Rudra," it is clearly perceived that Viṣṇu himself is born from both Rudra and Viṣṇu. Nor does this contradict the Taittirīya Śruti, which says "From the Self, space [was born]," and so on, regarding him who is named Rudra.

It should not be said that in the statements of the *Tyādi-purāṇas* and other texts, the relationship of cause and effect is observed only between the respective inner rulers (*antaryāmin*) presiding over the respective elements—each qualified by their corresponding presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*)—according to the stated method, and not that each subsequent presiding deity is created by its preceding deity. This is because it has been stated that when a causal relationship is predicated of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it ultimately applies to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as well; furthermore, it was precisely the inner ruler of each element, as qualified by its respective presiding deity, who was spoken of.

Arising (*utpatti*) is not a change in essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*), but rather a change in its own qualifying attribute (*svaviśeṣaṇībhūta-dharma-anyathābhāva*); and this [change] culminates here precisely in a change in one's own body (*śarīra-anyathābhāva*), because no other kind is possible, or because even if another were possible, in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*), it would be appropriate to accept that the change in the body is what is intended. Furthermore, the respective presiding deities (*abhimāni-devatās*) such as Sadāśiva and others are indeed the bodily forms of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) Paramaśiva. "This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is the body of the God of gods"—this truth the bound souls (*paśus*), blinded by their fetters (*pāśa-gauras*), do not know.

They say that consciousness is knowledge (*vidyā*), and likewise that knowledge is consciousness. The entire universe, consisting of both knowledge and ignorance, is of the same nature as the all-pervading Lord, the Teacher of the Universe; of this there is no doubt, for the universe is under His control.
Both the existent and the non-existent—the entire world—is the body of the Supreme Being.
Just as the branches of a tree flourish when its root is watered, so it is with Him.
In the same way, through the worship of Śiva, his body nourishes the world;
the Self is the eighth form of that Śiva, the Supreme Soul.

"Because of such Purāṇic statements as 'Therefore, the universe is of the nature of Śiva, being the forms whose banner is pervasiveness,' it is established that the entire phenomenal world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, is the body of Paramaśiva; thus, the origin of Paramaśiva, who is the inner controller (antaryāmī), does not depend upon a transformation of His body composed of elements such as ether."

It must be stated that when [the body] comes into being, even a transformation of the body consisting of the respective presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) may be considered as its mode of origination, because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary]. This is supported by the natural force (*svārasya*) of employing specific terms denoting those respective presiding deities, such as "of the one named Rudra" and so forth; thus, [the body] consists of the respective presiding deities.

Because even the state of being otherwise (*anyathābhāva*) is to be accepted as having been stated [by the author], otherwise one would have to say, "Leaving aside the form of the god named Rudra, light is produced," whereas in fact, in the *Rudrayāmala*, the production of the deities presiding over each subsequent element from the deities presiding over each preceding element is clearly established. For it says:
"He who transcends the duality of 'is' and 'is not,' whose nature is beyond the range of speech and mind..."
Colorless yet endowed with color, formless yet the bearer of all forms.
The Supreme Self, the supreme abode, is a certain deity who is Śiva;
from Śiva arises Śakti, whose nature consists of the Kalā beyond Peace (śāntyatīta).
At first, she shines manifest in the ether as the god Sadāśiva himself.
Even Īśvara, beginning with Sadāśiva, is established within the element of air.
From Īśvara was born Rudra, the powerful one, who remained stationed in the wind;
from Rudra came Viṣṇu of great splendor, who was established in the state of water.

Brahmā was born from Viṣṇu and is established upon the earth; therefore, the origin of those respective elemental forms from the presiding deities of each preceding stage is indeed established for the sake of the consistency of this collection of statements. Furthermore, at the beginning of the *Manusmṛti*, by the verse "From that [Self-existent One]... (*tataḥ svayambhuḥ*), the birth of the internal ruler of water—who presides over Viṣṇu—from the internal ruler of fire—who presides over Rudra and is characterized by darkness (*tamas*)—is indicated; and by the verse "He, desiring... (*so 'bhidhyāya*), the word "he" (*saḥ*) refers to that dispeller of darkness.

Without touching the ego (ahaṃkāra), the emission of its creative power (*vīrya*) was deposited into the principle of water (*jalatatva*). Here, the mention of the creation of the *āptatva* (the state of being the "Attainer") is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since the creation presided over by that *āptatva* has already been described in the preceding verse through the account of Viṣṇu’s birth.

Consequently, although the entry of Viṣṇu into that *āptatva* was not explicitly stated, it should be inferred in accordance with the statements of other Purāṇas, such as "Viṣṇu entered into that. Following this, there is the birth of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the earth presided over by Brahmā; thus [it is said]: "That egg became golden."

The creation of ether and air mentioned here should also be concluded in accordance with the *Taittirīya* Śruti. Then, by the verse beginning "Then the waters [are] *nārāḥ*," the basis for the application of Viṣṇu’s name *Nārāyaṇa*—which was obtained through Rudra’s grace—is described as his entry into the water-element (*jalatattva*). Thus, since it is established that the word "waters" (*ap*) in the phrase "He created the waters alone" denotes the water-element presided over by Nārāyaṇa, [the definition of Rudra's status as a created being is determined by] Nārāyaṇa...

Since the status of being presided over by an authoritative being (*adhiṣṭhitāptatva*) is indeed the qualifying attribute, it is established that even Nārāyaṇa—who serves as the qualifier—is created by Rudra. Nor should it be argued that there is no evidence for the claim that Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of the five elements beginning with space; for the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the *Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa*, contains the following statement: "Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—these are the deities of the five elements proclaimed above, O you of virtuous vows. Furthermore, [it says]: "Sadāśiva is the embodiment of sound, and then Īśvara..."
Rudra is the embodiment of splendor, Janārdana is the embodiment of taste, and the four-faced one (Brahmā) is the embodiment of fragrance; these are the five embodiments.

Since the Purāṇic statement cited in the *Nīlakaṇṭha-bhāṣya* serves as authority on this point, one might object: "Even so, according to the reasoning stated above, by the force of the designation 'Nārāyaṇa,' it is understood that the Saṃhāra-Rudra alone is the creator of Nārāyaṇa, and not Paramaśiva—who, as you maintain, is the fundamental cause whose activity exists at the time when only the quality of *tamas* remains. Thus [it is said]: 'The divine, singular Nārāyaṇa is the god...'"

He explains how the application of the word *Nārāyaṇa*—which, as derived from the *Subālopaniṣad*, denotes the primal cause existing during the period when only the quality of darkness (*tamas*) remains—to the Supreme Śiva is justified: "O Lord of the Mountains, Hari’s birth [as described] in the *Manusmṛti*, which purifies the meaning of the term *Nārāyaṇa*, occurs from Guṇa-Rudra; it does not proceed from you. However, O best of sages, some deluded person, failing to understand the designations of both him and you, [claims otherwise]. But, O Brahmins, the form of Paraśiva is like fire within heated iron; it is distinct from other forms by its characteristics, just like a sage.
O lords of sages,
O you of excellent vows, the names of the Supreme Reality are, by proximity, also the designations for the three forms and for Rudra as well.
By such statements from the Sūta-saṃhitā, having introduced the majesty of Saṃhāra-Rudra:
"This very Lord Īśa is a mass of splendor, free from all affliction."
He is the Lord without beginning or end, the Sustainer, the one who withdraws all beings, and the all-pervading.
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, permeated by the nature of the Supreme Lord,
perpetually presided over by His power, and likewise marked by His insignia.

Furthermore, from such statements in the Śiva Purāṇa as "having that name, that form, performing those functions, engaged in those activities, and observing that command," it is understood that Paramaśiva and Saṃhārarudra possess identical names, forms, and deeds; thus, like Saṃhārarudra, Paramaśiva also [is established] by virtue of the designation "Nārāyaṇa."

Since it is possible to understand that Nārāyaṇa is the creator, therefore, by the force of the designation "Nārāyaṇa"—which possesses as its basis for application (pravṛttinimitta) the characteristic of being the abode of that which is attained through the creation of Śiva, who is denoted by the word "nara"—it is understood that the status of Paramaśiva as the creator of Nārāyaṇa remains entirely unimpaired. Now, even if this is so, in the ancient [texts]...

If the rule *pūrvapadāt* in all grammatical treatises were intended as an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be no possibility at all of the substitution of *ṇ* in words such as *rāmanāma*; whereas if it were intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), that which was applicable by the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* would be excluded by this restriction. Thus, the "ringing of the bell" [of the former position] would now become like a flower in the sky.

Since, in your own school of thought, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in that instance is to be prevented precisely by its inclusion in the list of words beginning with *kṣubh*, he says: "For those who follow the path set forth by us, no fault arises that would contradict the earlier commentators; whereas you, possessing minds as fierce as those of mutual adversaries, have become a source of confusion for the learned."

For truth (*ṛta*) is indeed the great authority. Let it be so; for by the very authors of ancient treatises—such as the authors of the *Prakriyākaumudī*, the *Manoramā*, and the *Svarasiddhāntacandrikā*—who successively refuted their predecessors, the principle that "error is a human attribute" has been clearly demonstrated.

For this very reason, even among grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), great errors are observed here and there; we shall show merely a few instances of these. For example, from the word *yuvan* with the suffix *śas*, by the rule *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.133), the semivowel *v* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*; then, after the formation of the *pūrvarūpa* and the subsequent long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*, the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108)—which prohibits further *saṃprasāraṇa* when one has already occurred—would apply because the preceding *saṃprasāraṇa* has just taken place. Thus, after the application of *rutva* and *visarga*, the form *yūnaḥ* is produced. This is the procedure (*prakriyā*) stated in all grammatical treatises. Such is the case.

It appears as if a lotus in the sky; for in the case of [the form] *yūnaḥ*, the application of the rule *na samprasāraṇe* is simply impossible, because the *samprasāraṇa* has been superseded by both the *pūrvarūpa* and the *savarṇadīrgha*. Nor can the *pūrvarūpa* be treated as the final element (*antavad-bhāva*) or the *savarṇadīrgha* as the initial element (*ādivad-bhāva*).

It should be stated that there is the possibility of [the rule] *anta-samprasāraṇa* applying because of the inclusion of the term *samprasāraṇa* by way of its presence (*bhāva*); however, this is not the case, because the prohibition of [the presence of] the state [of being an internal element] is indicated by the statement that [the rules for] *ṣatva* and *tuk* are "not established" (*asiddha*) with respect to one another, which implies that the operation based on the [presence of the] individual phonemes is not established. Otherwise, in forms such as *dhītya*, since the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* would—by way of its presence—be treated as the initial element, and thus the short vowel would also be present, the *tuk* would be established by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*; consequently, the statement regarding the non-establishment of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with respect to *tuk* would be redundant. For this very reason, in cases such as *vṛkṣe u ha* or *vṛkṣe iha*, the single-substitute resulting from *guṇa* (which begins with *ā*) is treated as the initial element.

A long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrgha* does not occur here; nor should one object that in examples such as *hṛtaḥ* and *jitaḥ*, where the root *hṛ*, the root *ji*, and the root *jyā* take the suffix *kta*, and after the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) according to the rules *vacisvapiyajādīnām* and *grahijyā*, the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) would fail to apply because the *pūrvarūpa* cannot be grasped by the mention of *samprasāraṇa*. This is because the very formulation of the rule *halaḥ* indicates that a long vowel occurs even for that which stands in the place of a *samprasāraṇa*. Nor can it be argued that, by relying on this indicator (*jñāpaka*) as being general in scope, [the rule applies] to all instances of *samprasāraṇa*.

It cannot be argued that an operation is accepted as occurring even when [the substitute] stands in the place of every [element], for even so, in the case of *yūnoḥ*, because of the intervention by the *yakāra* and *ukāra* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment as the original), the condition of being followed by a semivowel (*samprasāraṇaparatva*) cannot possibly apply to the *yakāra*. Therefore...

In this way, even if [the rule] *ādi-vat-tva* (the status of being like the first) were to apply, there would still be no resolution; for even then, the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) effected by the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if it were the original) under the rule *acaḥ parasmin* cannot be avoided. For this very reason, in the commentary on the sūtra *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti*, the authors of the Bhāṣya have provided a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) stating "except when *śit* follows."

In the case of the words *glāyanti* and *mlāyanti*, the possibility that the substitution of *kā* (for *glai* and *mlai*) would behave as the initial element (*ādivadbhāva*)—thereby resulting in the long vowel *ā*—is raised and refuted by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*. Now, one might argue: "The repetition of the term *samprasāraṇa* in the rule *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.32), despite its presence in the preceding rule *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (6.1.30), is intended to prohibit the *saṃprasāraṇa* prescribed for *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* even when they occur in a different location. This indicates that in a word such as *satyūnaḥ*, the intervention caused by *sthānivadbhāva* does not constitute a fault. If this is argued, we say no; for the intervention created by a rule located in another part of the grammar, namely *vyadhividāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), is indeed a fault, as seen in the form *vivyādha*.

In examples such as *vivyadha* (*ṛep.*?), when the first *y* has undergone *samprasāraṇa*, the *v* immediately preceding it would again be subject to *samprasāraṇa* by that same rule; thus, the repetition of the term "samprasāraṇa" is justified as being intended to prohibit that. However, in the case of *yūnaḥ*, [the situation is] interrupted...

Because it is impossible for [the rule] to indicate that *dhā* is defective; for, since the *samprasāraṇa* [prescribed] by the rule *vyatho liṭi* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *halādiśeṣa*, and because of the rule that an exception and its general rule (*utsarga*) must have the same domain of application, there is no possibility at all of the *samprasāraṇa* occurring in place of the letter *v*. Therefore, how could [the rule] serve the purpose of prohibiting that?

If it is argued that the mention of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) serves a further purpose, we say no; for under the theory of classes (*jātipakṣa*), the rule *vyatho liṭi* applies, and since the letter *va* does not fall within the scope of *halādiśeṣa*, the principle of *yena nāprāpta* (the rule by which [another] would not have applied) is absent. Under the theory of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), however, because the grammatical system differs with each individual instance, there exists a separate rule concerning the letter *ya*.

If that [rule] does not apply, then because there is no distinction between the *yakāra* and *vakāra*, the rule *vyatho liṭi* would apply; since the *vakāra* is not subject to *halādiśeṣa*, the *yena nāprāpta-nyāya* (the maxim of "that which was not already applicable") does not hold. In the view that rules apply to individual instances (*vyaktipakṣa*), because the scripture differs for each instance, even if the single scripture concerning the *yakāra* serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to *halādiśeṣa*, the scripture concerning the *vakāra* lacks even a scent of being such an exception. For this very reason, in the *Kāśikā* on the word *vivyadha*, the *samprasāraṇa* of the *vakāra* is prohibited by the rule [beginning with] *na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam*, because of [the presence of] *vyatho liṭi* [which would otherwise have applied]. *Halādiśeṣa*.

However, in the case of [the view that the rule] is a *pavāda* (exception), the contradiction with the *Kāśikā* is quite evident. Thus, regarding what Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita stated—that the rule *vyatho liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.3.65) is an exception (*apavāda*) to *halādiśeṣaḥ*—that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), or else it refers to the intention of the scripture concerning the letter *y* under the theory of individuality (*vyaktipakṣa*). Let those of refined intellect understand this for themselves. By this, [it is shown that] in the *Manoramā*, having raised the objection that in the word *sudhyupāsya* there should be a *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) by the rule *samprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), he first provided a solution by means of the Vārttika: "When there is the state of being preceded by a *samprasāraṇa*, there is the inclusion of the homogeneous vowels."

Some say that [the substitute] in the place of a *samprasāraṇa* is not such [a *samprasāraṇa*]; that is incorrect. As for what was said—that the [form] *yūnaḥ* would be unestablished—that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is clear to those of subtle intellect. Even if one relies on the general indicator (*jñāpaka*) "hal" [in P. 1.1.70], which implies that the substitute in the place of a *samprasāraṇa* is also included under the term *samprasāraṇa*, the obstruction caused by *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of *yūnaḥ* remains unavoidable; thus, the failure to establish that form (*yūnaḥ*) cannot be remedied. Now, as for the objection: "Is it not true that the maxim *na hi kāryanimittatvenāśrayate* (for [a rule] does not depend on something as the cause of its own operation) applies here?"

By the rule *vrataḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.34] regarding one who sleeps on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍilaśāyī*), and by the inclusion of the word *āṅ* in the list of roots beginning with *kūṭ*, it is indicated that the locative case in rules such as *ktici ca* [Pāṇini 1.1.5] must be understood as a "locative of cause" (*nimitta-saptamī*). For if one were to rely on the locative as a "locative of location" (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), then in forms such as *chinnaṃ* and *bhinnaṃ*, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution would not apply because the suffix *kta* is not followed immediately after the letter *d*. Therefore, one must resort to the locative of cause; and thus, since the root *śīṅ* is marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅit*), its *guṇa* substitution does not occur precisely because it is caused by that *ṅ*, and consequently, the prohibition by the rule *ktici ca* applies to the form *śayi*.

The grammatical indication *tarīti* is indeed untenable; for since the root *kṛ* is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ*, the *guṇa* substitution caused by that [indicatory letter] is prohibited, making its inclusion in the list beginning with *kuṭ*—which serves the purpose of extending the status of being *ṅit* via the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ añṇiti* to prohibit *guṇa*—also untenable. Thus, these two indications and their textual readings inform us of this *paribhāṣā*. Consequently, the *guṇa* substitution in the case of the roots *śī* and *kuṅ* is not caused by the indicatory letters of *śī* and *kuṅ*, and so the indications and readings are rendered consistent. Furthermore, the utility of this *paribhāṣā* is seen in the derivation of *cyavate*.

If you argue that in examples such as *plavate* and likewise in *yūnaḥ*, since the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution) has both [the preceding and following] as its substituends (*ubhayasthānika*), it lacks the status of having a subsequent cause (*paranimittakatva*), and thus the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* finds no scope—this is not so. For the *paribhāṣā* "na hi kāryī" (the substitute does not behave like the original when it itself is subject to an operation) is not accepted because it serves no purpose. Nor should it be said that forms such as *cyavate* constitute a purpose [for that *paribhāṣā*]; for that is established otherwise. To explain how: in *kadati*, the locative case is indeed subsequent (*parasaptamī*), and thus the *guṇa* is established in *cyavate* and the like. Nor should it be argued that [the *paribhāṣā* is necessary] in cases such as *bhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ*, where [the *guṇa* would be blocked] by the letter *d*.

If it were argued that the prohibition [of *guṇa*] would not apply due to the intervention [of a letter], then by the fact that the root *kṣnu* is marked with the *kit* designation, it is indicated (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition of *guṇa* will indeed occur even when there is an intervention of a single phoneme. Now, if the *paribhāṣā* "the cause of an operation is not itself affected by that operation" (*na hi kāryī*) were not accepted, the form *aririṣati* would not be established. To explain: from the root *ṛ*, with the suffix *san*, after the application of the rule *sani mīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadām aca is* and the subsequent *guṇa* by *pūṅrañjaśāṃ sani*, we arrive at *aris*. Then, because it begins with a vowel (*ajādittva*), the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* applies, causing reduplication (*dvitva*) of the syllable *ri*; following this, by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the form *aririṣati* is obtained. In that case, if the *paribhāṣā* were not accepted, the vowel *i*—which is the subject undergoing the operation (*kāryin*)—would become the cause (*nimitta*) for the reduplication.

If one were to accept the formal designation (*rūpātideśa*) by the rule *na dvirvacane'ci*, then when the *guṇa* substitute for the *śit* [affix] results in the form of the vowel *ṛ*, and the syllable *is-* undergoes reduplication, the form would be *arīṣati*. However, if the *paribhāṣā* is accepted, since the vowel *i* lacks the status of being caused by a *cit* [suffix], the rule *na dvirvacane'ci* does not apply.

If it is argued that the desired form is established [by this rule], we say no; for in the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), one must adopt one of the methods—such as *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so forth—to explain the meaning as: "When a reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed, a substitute for an *ac* vowel standing in the place of another shall be treated as non-substituted (*sthānivadbhāva*) when an *ac* vowel follows which is the cause of the reduplication. Otherwise, in forms such as *cakrakaḥ*, once the reduplication is performed, the *yaṇ*-substitution and other operations of the subsequent portion would not take place; rather, there would only be *prakṛtibhāva*. Thus, when there is a requirement regarding what is to be reduplicated—as in "when a reduplication is to be performed" (*dvitve kartavye*)—one must state, by virtue of proximity, either "of the *ac*" or "of the substitute. And so, in *ariri...* [the rule applies].

In the case of *ṣaṭ*, since the letter *ī* (the substitute for *nī*) or its resulting *guṇa* vowel possesses that [original] status (*tadvitva*), and because it begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), the doubling (*dvitva*) applies specifically to the second single vowel; thus, the rule "na dvirvacane’ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59) does not apply. However, in forms such as *cakratuḥ*, because even the vowel *ṛ* participates in the doubling by virtue of the maxim "doubling of a monosyllabic root" (*ekāco dvirvacananyāya*), the rule does apply. Consequently, since forms such as *aririṣati* are established even without this *paribhāṣā*, there is no need to accept it; on the contrary, if the *paribhāṣā* were accepted, a fault would be observed. For instance, in cases such as *śrāyasau*, *gautamau*, *caturau*, and *anaḍvāhau*, regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)...

By virtue of the *parādivadbhāva* (the treatment of the preceding element as if it were the beginning of the following), the augment *num* and the suffix *ām* would apply [to the reduplicated stem]. However, these two are to be prevented by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) under the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57), which accounts for the intervention [of the substitute]. If this *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim) were accepted, then *sthānivadbhāva* itself would not even be applicable there. Thus, after explaining the *paribhāṣā* "kāryī" (the operation applies to that which possesses the cause) along with its indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) and purpose in the *Kaustubha* on the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, the *Kaustubha* on the rule *acaḥ parasmin* explains that in cases such as *śrāyasau* and *gautamau*, *num* and *ām* are prevented by the intervention caused by *sthānivadbhāva*.

One should understand how there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. Therefore, in forms such as *yūnaḥ*, the rule "there is no *samprasāraṇa*" simply does not apply. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam*, it is stated that the repeated mention of *samprasāraṇa* is for the purpose of prohibiting the *samprasāraṇa* that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *śvayuvamaghonām ataddhite* even in the case of *yūnaḥ*. It further states: "Even when this [prohibition] is being uttered, it is not established... and so forth.

Thus, it has been refuted according to the manner stated above. Therefore, another effort must be undertaken to establish the form *yūnaḥ*; for the meaning of the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam* is not "when a *saṃprasāraṇa* follows, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*," but rather "once a *saṃprasāraṇa* has occurred within a single *aṅga*, there is no further *saṃprasāraṇa*. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam*, the authors, having raised the objection regarding the non-establishment of the form *yūnaḥ* according to the aforementioned method, introduced the requirement of "belonging to the same *aṅga*" (*samānāṅga-grahaṇa*).

Having introduced the *Vārttika* "vyami," they resolved the matter with this intention. For this very reason, in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, it is stated that if the genitive form *acaḥ*—which is carried over from the rule *acaḥ parasmin*—were absent, then even the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the root *svap* before an affix beginning with *ṅ* would be prohibited in forms such as *asūṣupat*. Consequently, the vowel *u* would not be heard in the reduplicated syllable. Having thus argued, one might raise the objection: "Even if the *samprasāraṇa* is prohibited prior to the doubling, once the doubling has occurred, let there be *samprasāraṇa* again in the reduplicated syllable. To this, [the author] says: "No."

In the *Kaustubha* and *Manoramā*, the objection regarding the rule "when there is a *samprasāraṇa*, [there is] *samprasāraṇa*" has been refuted; however, one must necessarily admit that its intended meaning is: "when a *samprasāraṇa* has already occurred, there is no further *samprasāraṇa*. This is because the prohibition "when a *samprasāraṇa* follows, there is no *samprasāraṇa*" is impossible due to the intervention [of other elements]. Nor does this lead to an over-extension in forms such as *upoṣuṣaḥ* or *upeṣuṣaḥ*, where within a single *aṅga* [the roots] *vac*, *svap*, etc., [are involved].

It should not be argued that, by [the rule] *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam*, there would not be a double *samprasāraṇa*—one for the *v* of the root *vas-* and one for the *v* of the suffix *vasi-*; for, by the principle "in a single member," once a *samprasāraṇa* has been performed with respect to a certain suffix having been treated as *nit*, a further *samprasāraṇa* does not occur again with respect to that very same [suffix].

Because this is what is intended to be expressed, there is no fault in cases such as *upoṣuṣaḥ* and so on; for while the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel *u* in the verbal root occurs by reason of the *sup* suffix, the substitution of the vowel *u* in the element *vas* occurs by reason of suffixes such as *śas*. Nor does it follow that, even under this view, the semivowel substitution of the letter *y* would occur first in forms such as *yūnaḥ*.

It should not be argued that [the rule] "the first *saṃprasāraṇa* belongs to the subsequent [vowel]" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that when a *saṃprasāraṇa* follows, there is no further *saṃprasāraṇa*, because you do not accept this meaning; for, by the indicative force (*jñāpaka*) of such rules as "the suffix *ti*" in *yūnaḥ*, "an elder with a youth" in *vṛddho yūnā*, and "elision in the case of a youth" in *yūni luk*, even in our own view, the first...

It might be argued that one could simply state that "the semivowel (yaṇ) of another [vowel] alone undergoes *samprasāraṇa*. Furthermore, it should not be said that even in our own view, the intervention [of other sounds] does not cause a fault due to the very force of the specific mention of forms such as *yūnaḥ*; for if that were the case, then by the very force of the specific mention of forms such as *yūnaḥ*, the semivowel *yakāra* would not undergo *samprasāraṇa*.

Since it is impossible to say [that], the demonstration of the application of the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe* by way of making known that the intervention [of a vowel] is not a defect is refuted by its prolixity and is fruitless; in my view, however, by the force of the specific mention [in the rule], first the subsequent [vowel] undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, and thus by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *ya*—this is the distinction. In reality, however, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) based on the maxim "when the end is barred, the penultimate position [is affected]," the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the subsequent semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) is established in cases such as *yūnaḥ*; and this is not...

It should not be argued that if this *paribhāṣā* were accepted, the rule "na samprasāraṇe" (P. 6.1.37) would be redundant; for such a consequence is desired (*iṣṭāpatti*). For this very reason, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ṣyaṅaḥ samprasāraṇam" (P. 6.1.13) have enumerated the brevity of form resulting from the composition of the rule "na samprasāraṇe" as the primary purpose of this *paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, if this *paribhāṣā* is accepted, the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ" (P. 7.2.106) applies only to forms such as "saḥ" and "tau," because the *takāra* there is in the position immediately preceding the final letter (*antyasadeśa*); however, it does not apply in cases such as "kyasya."

One might ask: "How can this be so, since faults such as [the rule] 'it would apply [to the *takāra*]' because the final *takāra* lacks a common locus (*sadeśatva*) have already been illustrated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra regarding the *samprasāraṇa* of *ṣyaṅ*? This must be addressed by noting that this [particular] Bhāṣya represents the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument). For this very reason, in the concluding Bhāṣya on that sūtra, after beginning with the statement, "Just because there are beggars, pots are not left uncooked," it says: "Therefore, for the sake of those purposes which are the applications of this Paribhāṣā, this Paribhāṣā must be formulated; as for the faults, they must be remedied."

By the statement beginning with "it is established by the mention of the acute accent" (*ktvodāttanirdeśāt siddham*), the faults are avoided as follows: where the application of this *paribhāṣā* is intended, such as in the rule *adasaḥ seḥ*, the mention of the acute accent must be made; where it is not intended, such as in *tadoḥ saḥ sāu*, the mention of the acute accent need not be made. Thus, the formation of forms such as *yūnaḥ* is established by this very *paribhāṣā*. Therefore, the derivation of forms like *yūnaḥ* by relying on the principle that "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when another *samprasāraṇa* follows" is impossible even for the teacher Ākhaṇḍala (Patañjali); the same applies to other cases as well.

Errors are found in abundance here and there; however, for fear of prolixity, we shall desist.
