Therefore, even if the word *nārāyaṇa* is etymologically derived from the Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), the substitution of the nasal *ṇa* is indeed easily established. Now, one might object: even so, since it is extremely possible to describe words denoting Viṣṇu as being etymologically applicable to Maheśvara—who is the very form of Maheśvara—and since the Upaniṣadic passages such as "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed" establish that Viṣṇu also possesses the status of the creator of the universe...

If it is asked how the universal proclamation (*khaṇṭāghoṣa*) that Śiva alone is the most excellent by virtue of being the creator of the world is consistent [with other texts], we reply: just as the creatorship of Viṣṇu is established by Vedic statements such as "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," so too is the creatorship of Paramaśiva established by a collection of Upaniṣadic passages such as the *Atharvaśikhā*, which states, "All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and the Indras—is produced from Him. Thus, when there is mutual contradiction between the Upaniṣads, the former [should be understood] word by word...

In that manner, in order to avoid the futility of the entire mantra beginning with "tad ātmanaḥ," one must describe the Upaniṣads—which establish the preeminence of Nārāyaṇa according to the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts—as well as the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Bhagavadgītā*, and so forth, as being intended to establish the preeminence of Paramaśiva. And this has been described in great detail by the sovereign Appayadīkṣita, who acted like a royal swan in discerning the milk from the water of the essence and non-essence of all the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other scriptures, in his works such as the *Śivatattvaviveka*.

Since this has been treated at great length in other treatises, we have not exerted ourselves therein; thus, everything is consistent. Now, he offers the *Tattvamālā*, an ornament for the word *Nārāyaṇa*, at the lotus-feet of Paraśiva.
I offer this *Vasantatilaka*— a garland of the essence of nectar adorned with the words of Nārāyaṇa—
at the pair of Śambhu’s fresh feet, which grant satisfaction even when the arrangement of the syllables is inverted by a child.

May this *Tattvamālikā*, which serves as an ornament for the feet of Nārāyaṇa and belongs to Śambhu, composed by Śeṣādri, endure as long as the moon, stars, and sun exist. Hari Om. May I become the sacrificial priest for Rāmasvāmin. The lords of the Colas, who render the speech of disputants like parched grain, shine eternally throughout the three worlds like mere droplets of water in the ocean.

Just as in this world there are those known as "reservoirs of the Sindhu river's waters" from which water is drawn by the thirsty, so too are your disciples; for even though they have drunk but a drop of the nectar of your words—which were churned by the Lord of the Gods (Indra) using Śeṣa as the primary mountain—they shine forth like the kings of sages. O Best of the Wise, who among those in the three worlds truly knows whether these [disciples] are [merely] kings of sages or [the actual] kings of sages? For even after drinking but a drop of the honey from the lotus of your mouth, they become vessels for the speech of victory over all disputants. [Regarding] food and such...

If even those devoid of merit become radiant-hearted through devotion to you, how much more so those whose hearts shine with such devotion? If disciples—whether pure in their inner being or otherwise—are taught all the sciences by you, they too become the best of the wise;

regarding this, Śeṣādri has been cited as our example. Whether by an improper path or indeed by the proper path, those who worship the compassionate Śambhu most certainly attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this, the gods and the asuras speak.
May my mind, having become a bee, delight forever in the pair of lotus-feet of those lords of sacrifices, Rāma. Salutations to Śrī Sāmba, the Supreme Brahman.
Salutations to the two lotus-feet of Śrī Guha. This *Nārāyaṇatattvamālikā* was composed by Aruṇācalaguru, a resident of the city named Aṇahara, which is a suburb of the city of Kuśalava.
